weeks.label: Week 1 - Cardiac Physiology, ECG & Cardiac Pharmacology

lectures.name: Cardiac Electrical Physiology
lectures.title: Circulation, the Cardiac Cycle & Cardiac Electrical Physiology
lectures.framing: How blood moves through a series pulmonary circuit and a parallel systemic circuit, how one cardiac cycle fills and empties the ventricle, and the ion currents that make the heart beat. The organising idea: pressure gradients open and close the valves, and ion gradients set the rhythm.
lectures.keypoints: EF = SV/EDV (normal 50–60%; EDV 120 mL, ESV 50 mL). S1 = AV valves close, S2 = semilunar valves close. Veins hold ~70% of blood volume. Capillary pressure ~20 mm Hg – any compartment above that compromises perfusion. Cardiac AP: phase 0 Na+ in, phase 2 Ca2+ plateau, phase 3 K+ out; SA node self-excites from -55 to -60 mV to a -40 mV threshold, and the AV node delay (0.13 s) is the longest step.

blocks.html:
Blood flow through the heart
  • Venous return → atria → AV valves → ventricles → semilunar valves → arteries

rows:
Pulmonary circulation – low pressure
• Oxygenation
• Carbon dioxide removal/ventilation

Systemic circulation – high pressure
• Oxygenated blood
• Redistribution

blocks.alt: Cut-away of the heart showing the four chambers and valves
blocks.cap: The four chambers and their valves: right side (blue) receives venous return, left side (red) ejects to the aorta.

blocks.html:
Oxygen delivery
  • Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × oxygen content
  • Oxygen content = oxygen bound to Hb + dissolved oxygen
  • Oxygen content = (O2 saturation × Hb × 1.34) + (pO2 × 0.3)
  • Microvascular perfusion at the tissue level is important for oxygen delivery at a cellular level
  • Oxygen delivery must meet requirements for oxygen consumption
  • 200 mL of O2 in every 1 L of blood, but only use 250 mL
  • Venous pO2 depends on the balance between supply and demand

rows: Separates the right and left ventricle
Low pressure system (20/10) – RV less muscular than LV

High pressure system (120/80) – can change blood-flow distribution
• Dehydration/hypervolemia: less skin and kidney perfusion to retain water
• Exercise: vasodilation of skin and muscles
In series – output of RV and LV matched

blocks.alt: Pulmonary and systemic circuits in series
blocks.cap: The pulmonary and systemic circuits are in series, so RV and LV output must match.

blocks.alt: Systemic organ beds arranged in parallel
blocks.cap: Organ beds of the systemic circulation sit in parallel, which lets flow be redistributed between them.

blocks.alt: Distribution of cardiac output to organs at rest
blocks.cap: Distribution of blood to organs at rest: share of the 5 L/min cardiac output and flow per 100 g for each organ.

blocks.html: The vasculature – 100 000 miles!

rows:
• High pressure system (120/80)
• Rapid transit
• Distensible – become less elastic with increasing age
• Elastic arteries = conducting arteries; elastic fibres (pressure reservoir)
• Muscular arteries = distributing arteries; smooth muscle (vasoconstriction)

• Resistance vessels – vasoconstriction, vasodilation
• Thick, elastic, muscular walls
• Control of microvascular blood flow to various organs

• Large cross-sectional area
• Exchange system – nearby cells extract nutrients/deposit wastes
• Slow, non-pulsatile flow
• Length = 0.3–1 mm
• Capillary pressure = 20 mm Hg
• Capillary refill evaluates microvascular flow clinically; chronic vasoconstriction, hypovolemia, or obstructive shock will delay the refill

• Capacitance vessels – hold 70% of blood volume
• Low pressure system
• Compliant
• Able to contract and dilate
• Valves propel blood back to the heart – varicose veins if incompetent

blocks.lead: Where’s the blood? Most of it sits in the veins.

blocks.alt: Average pressure across arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins
blocks.cap: The biggest pressure drop is across the arterioles – the resistance vessels.

blocks.alt: Pressure versus cross-sectional area along the vascular tree, with vessel diameters
blocks.cap: Cross-sectional area peaks at the capillaries, which is why flow there is slow.

blocks.html:
Capacitance
  • Total body fluid = 60% of body weight
  • Blood volume = 5 L
  • Vasodilation → increased capacitance
  • Vasoconstriction → decreased capacitance
  • Only a finite ability to compensate: after maximum constriction, any additional blood loss will unmask hypovolemia, which may present as a sudden deterioration
Compensation in a low-flow state
  • Arteriolar vasoconstriction
  • Venoconstriction
  • Redistribution of flow to vital organs
  • Increased oxygen extraction
  • Decrease in venous pO2

blocks.html:
The cardiac cycle
  • SYSTOLE = CONTRACTION (atrial systole, ventricular systole)
  • DIASTOLE = RELAXATION AND FILLING OF VENTRICLES
  • Graph below is of the L side of the heart; the R side looks very similar but with much lower pressures
  • Electrocardiogram = electrical conduction; phonocardiogram = heart sounds
  • Ventricular systole: isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection
  • Ventricular diastole: isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling → atrial systole

blocks.alt: Wiggers diagram: aortic, atrial and ventricular pressure, ventricular volume, ECG and phonocardiogram
blocks.cap: Line up each valve event with the ECG and heart sounds: S1 at AV valve closure, S2 at aortic valve closure.

rows:
1. Atrial systole
a wave · P wave · S4 may be heard

• AV valves open
• Pulmonary/aortic valves closed
• There is a delay between electrical and mechanical events in the heart
• Normally a small contribution to ventricular filling

• Increased ventricular volume
• In some clinical situations atrial systole is more important for filling:
– High HR: less diastolic time
– Stiff ventricle: does not fill well passively
• Atrial fibrillation: atria have no organized contraction; HR irregularly irregular; no atrial systole

2. Isovolumetric contraction
c wave · QRS complex · S1

• Ventricles begin to contract
• AV valves close
• Pulmonary/aortic valves closed

• Maximum ventricular volume unchanged
• End-diastolic volume (EDV): volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole, before the heart contracts; 120 mL

• Increase in ventricular pressure closes the AV valves
• Increase in atrial pressure as the valves push upwards into the atria

• AV valves closed
• Pulmonary/aortic valves open
• Blood ejected

• Ventricular pressure forces valves open
• Stenosis: narrow valve that does not open properly; requires higher pressure
• Increase in pulmonary/aortic pressures as they receive blood
• Gradient between LV and aorta is small

4. Reduced ejection
v wave · end of T wave

• Ventricles begin to repolarize
• AV valves closed
• Atrial filling continuing

• Ventricles begin to relax
• AV valves closed
• Pulmonary/aortic valves close
• Active, energy-dependent process; if ventricles do not relax well, they do not fill well (diastolic dysfunction)

• Ventricular volume unchanged
• End-systolic volume (ESV): volume remaining at the end of systole; 50 mL

• Decrease in ventricular pressure
• Aortic/pulmonary pressures > ventricular pressures, so aortic and pulmonary valves close

• Fall in ventricular pressure opens the AV valves
• Atrial pressure falls as the atrium passively gives blood to the ventricle

• AV valves open
• Pulmonary/aortic valves closed

blocks.html:
Ejection fraction
  • Ejection fraction (EF): the proportion of blood ejected from the ventricles; a continuum measured with echocardiogram, nuclear medicine scans, or cardiac catheterization
  • EF = SV/EDV, where SV = EDV – ESV
  • Normal = 50–60% · moderately impaired = 30–35% · severely decreased < 25%
  • Heart failure: heart muscle slowly weakens and loses its ability to pump blood
  • Patients with systolic heart failure have a reduced EF
  • Patients may have heart failure with a normal EF – diastolic failure, heart failure with normal/preserved EF (HFpEF)
Pressure–volume loop

blocks.alt: Left ventricular pressure-volume loop with its four phases
blocks.cap: I isovolumetric relaxation, II filling, III isovolumetric contraction, IV ejection; loop width = stroke volume.

blocks.alt: Pressure-volume loops in systolic and diastolic failure
blocks.cap: Systolic failure shifts the loop right (dilated ventricle); diastolic failure steepens the filling curve (↓ distensibility), raising EDP at the same volume.

blocks.html:
Pulmonary edema
  • Wet lungs
  • Hydrostatic pressure from the L heart (LVEDP) is transmitted back to affect microvascular pressure in the lungs
  • Qf = Kf[(Pmv − Ppmv) − σf(πmv − πpmv)]
  • Lungs stiffer – more work to breathe (dyspnea)
  • Decreased oxygen (hypoxia)
  • Infiltrates and air space on CXR
Normal pressures

blocks.alt: Normal chamber pressures and oxygen saturations
blocks.cap: Normal pressures (mm Hg) and O2 saturations: RA 1–5, RV 25/5, PA 20/10, LA 3–12, LV 120/12, aorta 120/70.

blocks.alt: Ventricular filling and emptying shown as a beaker: EDV, stroke volume, ESV
blocks.cap: Stroke volume is the difference between EDV and ESV.

blocks.html:
Heart sounds
  • S1 = closure of mitral and tricuspid valves – mitral closes before tricuspid; can be heard clinically as a split S1
  • S2 = closure of aortic and pulmonary valves – aortic closes before pulmonary; A2 and P2 split
  • S3 = rapid filling phase of ventricular diastole – children and young adults may have a normal S3
  • S4 = atrial filling phase of diastole

Aortic pressures
  • Systolic pressure: maximum aortic pressure during contraction
  • Dicrotic notch: dip separating the systolic and diastolic parts of the aortic waveform; closure of the aortic valve
  • Diastolic pressure: minimum aortic pressure during diastole
  • Mean arterial pressure (MAP): average BP during a single cardiac cycle; provided by NIBP cuff or invasive arterial monitoring
    • MAP = DP + 1/3(SP – DP) = 93 mmHg
    • MAP = CO × TPR
  • Pulse pressure = systolic BP – diastolic BP; decreased with a decrease in CO or an increase in vascular resistance
Central venous pressure
  • a wave = atrial contraction
  • c wave = early ventricular contraction that bows the valves up into the atrium
  • v wave = atrial pressure during filling, just before the AV valve opens
  • Jugular venous pressure: the indirectly observed pressure over the venous system via visualization of the internal jugular vein
    • Normal mean JVP = 6–8 cm H2O; the vertical distance above the midpoint of the RA
    • Increased JVP from regurgitant tricuspid valves – every RV contraction forces blood backwards towards the neck veins
  • Central venous catheter – a measure of pressure, NOT volume (but could hint at volume); internal jugular or subclavian vein to a transducer

Clinical questions
  • When would RV and LV output NOT be matched? Septal defect → a hole in the heart causes a mismatch
  • LVEDV 100 mL, SV 50 mL → EF = SV/EDV = 50/100 = 50% (normal)
  • LVEDV 200 mL, SV 50 mL → EF 25%; LVESV 150 mL → SV normal, CO maintained; systolic heart failure
  • LVEDV 100 mL, SV 25 mL → EF 25% → low SV, low CO
  • Decreased capillary refill – possible reasons:
    • Cold – vasoconstriction
    • Hypovolemic – compensatory response to maintain BP and perfusion
    • Low cardiac output – decreased perfusion to non-vital organs
    • Septic patients are vasodilated with normal capillary refill, but “cold sepsis” can decrease CO and cause relative hypovolemia
  • Pressure in the capillaries? ~20 mm Hg → above this gives pulmonary edema
  • If surrounding tissue pressure exceeds this? Decreased perfusion at the cellular level – capillaries get squished:
    • Intracranial hypertension → brain damage and ultimately brain death; high ICP > 20 mm Hg
    • Intra-abdominal hypertension → decreased kidney perfusion, bowel ischemia, respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse (abdominal compartment syndrome – treated with abdominal decompression); high IAP > 20 mm Hg
    • Compartment syndrome of an extremity → fasciotomy to relieve swelling and pressure
    • Endotracheal tube cuff → high cuff pressure can affect flow to the tracheal mucosa; necrosis and tracheal stenosis
  • Esophageal balloon for bleeding varices – inflate to? 20 mm Hg (enough to stop bleeding, safe against esophageal necrosis and ischemia)
  • High intra-ocular pressure (glaucoma)? > 20 mm Hg
  • Can a failing left heart with high LV diastolic pressures affect the right heart? Yes → LA pressure high; RV must generate higher pressures to move blood across the pulmonary circulation
  • Most common cause of right heart failure: left heart failure

blocks.title: The 20 mm Hg rule
blocks.html: Capillary pressure is ~20 mm Hg, so any compartment above 20 mm Hg (ICP, IAP, IOP, extremity compartment, ET cuff) starts to squeeze capillaries shut – and 20 mm Hg is also the safe inflation pressure for an esophageal balloon.

Module questions
  1. S1 represents: tricuspid and mitral valve closure → valves opening cannot be heard except with valve pathology
  2. S2 represents: pulmonary and aortic valve closure
  3. Most blood volume is in: veins and venules → capacitance vessels
  4. Systemic CO is 5 L/min; pulmonary blood flow is: 5 L/min → systemic and pulmonary flow are matched
  5. Most oxygen in blood is: bound to hemoglobin → makes oxygen saturation an important measure of oxygenation
  6. Ejection fraction: EF = SV/EDV
  7. On the diagram, at which point are the mitral and aortic valves both closed? C

blocks.alt: Pressure-volume loop with labelled points A to F for module question 7
blocks.cap: Module question 7: both mitral and aortic valves are closed at point C.

blocks.html:
Anatomy module questions
  • 15. 58-year-old woman with acute pericarditis from untreated streptococcal infection; needle drainage. Deepest layer the needle passes to enter the pericardial cavity? Parietal pericardium
  • 16. Match the structures on the chest radiograph: 1 = SVC, 2 = IVC, 3 = RA, 4 = RV, 5 = LV, 6 = aorta, 7 = pulmonary trunk

blocks.alt: Chest radiograph with numbered cardiac structures
blocks.cap: Question 16: 1 SVC, 2 IVC, 3 RA, 4 RV, 5 LV, 6 aorta, 7 pulmonary trunk.

blocks.html:
• 17. 69-year-old woman, catheter inserted into the femoral artery and advanced to the aorta. First chamber entered? Left ventricle
  • 18. 65-year-old man, chest pain unrelieved by rest or nitroglycerin; thallium stress test shows reduced perfusion of the lateral wall of the ventricle that pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Artery most likely occluded? Right marginal artery → supplies the lateral RV and apex; the RV pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs
  • 19. 52-year-old man implanted with a pacemaker. Defective conductive tissue? Sinoatrial (SA) node → initiates the impulse; the pacemaker of the heart
  • 20. 67-year-old man; angiogram shows stenosis of the large vessel at the white arrow. Most likely complication? Reduced brachial blood pressure on the left → stenosis of the L subclavian artery (from the aortic arch) decreases brachial BP in the L upper extremity

Cardiac electrical physiology
  • Action potential: a rapid change in electrical balance across a physiological membrane
  • Resting stage: membrane is polarized
  • Depolarization: membrane potential moves towards zero
    • Threshold potential: voltage at which an AP is triggered – V.G. Na+ channels open, Na+ flows into the cell
  • Repolarization: return of the membrane potential to its resting value – V.G. K+ channels begin opening, K+ flows out; V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated
  • Hyperpolarization: membrane potential moves to more negative values – K+ continues to leave as V.G. K+ channels close slowly
  • Absolute refractory period: another AP cannot be generated
  • Relative refractory period: a stronger than normal stimulus is required; some V.G. Na+ channels have recovered
  • Local anesthetics (lidocaine, procaine) block APs in pain fibres by acting directly on V.G. Na+ channels, making them more difficult to open

blocks.alt: Nerve action potential: threshold, depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization
blocks.cap: Threshold, depolarization, repolarization and hyperpolarization relative to the resting membrane potential.

blocks.html:
Membrane potential
  • Due to an imbalance of charged ions inside and outside cell membranes – a gradient for ions to diffuse down
  • How an ion affects membrane potential depends on: its charge, the membrane permeability to it, and its relative concentration on each side
  • K+: high intracellular (140 mEq/L), low extracellular (4 mEq/L)
  • Na+: low intracellular (14 mEq/L), high extracellular (140 mEq/L)
  • Maintained by the Na+/K+ pump and “leak” channels that let ions travel down their gradients (far more permeable to K+ than Na+) → resting membrane potential = -90 mV

blocks.alt: Na+/K+ ATPase pump and K+/Na+ leak channels
blocks.cap: The pump moves 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in; leak channels are far more permeable to K+.

blocks.html: The cardiac action potential

blocks.alt: Chemical gradients across the cardiac myocyte membrane
blocks.cap: Chemical gradients: Na+ and Ca2+ want to move in, K+ wants to move out.

blocks.alt: Net electrical gradient across the cardiac myocyte membrane at -90 mV
blocks.cap: Net electrical gradient: the inside of the cell sits at -90 mV.

blocks.html:
• Fast channels = V.G. Na+ channels – responsible for the rapid spike of the AP
  • Slow channels = V.G. Ca2+ channels – slower to open; prolong the plateau of positive membrane potential

rows: V.G. Na+ channels open, Na+ flows into the cell

V.G. K+ channels open, K+ flows out of the cell
V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated

V.G. Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ flows into the cell
Ca2+ influx essentially balances the K+ efflux → unchanging potential
These channels begin to open in Phase 0 and close in response to increased cytosolic Ca2+

V.G. Ca2+ channels close
V.G. K+ channels continue to open, K+ flows out of the cell
Return to the resting membrane potential

blocks.title: Never give a rapid K+ bolus
blocks.html: Cardiac depolarization depends on the balance of ions across the membrane; derangements can cause heart failure and life-threatening arrhythmias. Always exercise caution with ion-containing solutions – a rapid K+ bolus will almost certainly cause cardiac arrest and death.

Rhythmicity
  • The heart has a system that generates rhythmical electrical impulses
  • SA node fibres are capable of self-excitation; RMP = -55 to -60 mV
  • Leak of Na+ and Ca2+ into SA node cells is greater than in other cells (skeletal or cardiac muscle) → gradual rise of membrane potential (less negative)
  • Threshold potential = -40 mV → V.G. Na+ channels open, AP initiated
  • Repolarization: V.G. Na+ channels inactivate, V.G. K+ channels open
  • Other parts of the conduction system can also depolarize spontaneously, but at a slower intrinsic rate than the SA node
    • AV node may take over as pacemaker if the SA node is not working
    • If these fail too → cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest, requiring an emergent artificial pacemaker (on the chest wall or via a wire into the RV)

blocks.alt: Sinus nodal fibre versus ventricular muscle fibre action potentials
blocks.cap: The sinus nodal fibre has no stable resting potential: it drifts up to threshold (-40 mV) on its own; ventricular muscle rests near -85 mV.

blocks.html:
Conduction timing
  • SA node to most ventricular muscle cells takes 0.19 s:
    • SA node → AV node = 0.03 s
    • AV node → Purkinje system = 0.13 s
    • Purkinje system → ventricular muscle = 0.03 s
    • Transmission through muscle cells = 0.03 s
Important ions
  • Na+: influx causes cell-to-cell conduction/depolarization through the myocardium
  • Ca2+: influx causes myocardial contraction and cell-to-cell conduction/depolarization in the AV node
  • K+: efflux causes repolarization of myocytes

blocks.alt: Cardiac conduction system: sinus node, internodal pathways, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches
blocks.cap: The conduction path from the sinus node through the AV node and bundle to the left and right bundle branches.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart LR A["SA node"] -->|"0.03 s"| B["AV node"] B -->|"0.13 s"| C["Purkinje system"] C -->|"0.03 s"| D["Ventricular muscle"] D -->|"0.03 s"| E["Through muscle cells
total 0.19 s"]

lectures.name: Introduction to ECG
lectures.title: ECG Basics and Interpretation
lectures.framing: The ECG records the heart’s depolarization as seen from 12 viewpoints; a wave moving toward a positive electrode writes an upward deflection. Everything else – leads, axis, localising an infarct – follows from that one rule, read in a fixed order: rate, rhythm, axis, hypertrophy, ischemia.
lectures.keypoints: PR 120–200 ms, QRS 80–120 ms, QT ≤ 440 ms (M) / ≤ 460 ms (F). Rate by 300-150-100-75-60-50. Normal axis -30° to +90° (leads I and aVF). Localise STEMI by lead group: anterior V1–V4 = LAD, inferior II/III/aVF = RCA, lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 = circumflex, confirmed by reciprocal changes. Mobitz I = progressive PR (benign); Mobitz II = constant PR with drops (pacemaker).

blocks.html:
Electrocardiogram basics
  • Electrocardiogram (ECG, EKG): records the electrical activity of the heart – myocardial contraction
  • As a wave of depolarization (positive charges) within the myocytes flows TOWARD a positive electrode, a positive (upward) deflection is recorded
  • Most of the QRS reflects the LV because of its high mass – current flows from top to bottom, then R to L

blocks.alt: P, QRS and T waves mapped to atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization and repolarization
blocks.cap: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; ST (plateau) and T (rapid phase) = ventricular repolarization.

blocks.alt: Depolarization wave travelling toward an electrode, producing an upright deflection
blocks.cap: Depolarization moving toward the electrode (the eyes) records an upright deflection.

blocks.alt: Depolarization wave travelling away from an electrode, producing a negative deflection
blocks.cap: Moving away from the electrode records a negative deflection.

blocks.alt: Depolarization wave travelling perpendicular to an electrode, producing a biphasic deflection
blocks.cap: Travelling perpendicular to the electrode gives a small biphasic complex.

blocks.html:
ECG paper
  • Smallest divisions = 1 × 1 mm; heavy black squares = 5 × 5 mm
  • Horizontal axis = time: 1 mm = 40 ms, 5 mm = 200 ms
  • Vertical axis = amplitude/voltage: 10 mm = 1 mV
  • Calibration signal = 1 box wide × 2 boxes high
  • Lead changeover marker = small spike

blocks.alt: Normal 12-lead ECG on standard grid paper
blocks.cap: A normal 12-lead ECG: note the grid, the calibration pulse and the lead changeover markers.

rows: Pause at the AV node before ventricular depolarization

80–120 ms
• Q: first downward deflection; often absent
• R: first upward deflection
• S: any downward wave preceded by an upward wave
• QS: no upward wave
Normally level with baseline – pathology if elevated or depressed
Late phase of rapid ventricular repolarization

Less than half the R-to-R interval at normal rates
Males ≤ 440 ms; females ≤ 460 ms
Prolonged by genetics, drugs, electrolytes, hypothermia
Can be normal or a sign of hypokalemia

blocks.alt: Labelled normal ECG complex: P, Q, R, S, ST, T, U
Local myocyte electrogram phases compared with the surface ECG
blocks.cap: Depolarization (1), plateau (2) and repolarization (3) of the myocyte map onto QRS, ST segment and T wave.

blocks.html:
The 12 standard ECG leads

6 limb leads (R arm, L arm, L leg) + 6 chest leads.

• Pushing the leads to the centres of their triangles forms six intersecting lines of reference
    • Lie in a flat frontal (coronal) plane
    • Each limb lead records from a different angle – a different view of the same cardiac activity
  • Lateral leads (left arm positive): I, aVL
  • Inferior leads (left leg positive): II, III, aVF → QRS should be positive
  • aVR → QRS should be negative
  • Modified electrode positions on the trunk (shoulders, abdomen) are commonly used to monitor patients in various settings

blocks.alt: The six limb leads shown on a figure: I, II, III, aVF, aVL, aVR
blocks.cap: Each limb lead looks at the heart from a different angle in the frontal plane.

rows: 5th intercostal space, L anterior axillary line
blocks.lead: Chest wall leads (unipolar) – lie in a horizontal (transverse) plane; each chest electrode is positive, projects through the patient’s back (negative), and is oriented through the AV node.

blocks.alt: Frontal-plane limb lead axes and horizontal-plane chest lead vectors
12-lead ECG layout coloured by region: lateral, inferior, septal, anterior
blocks.cap: Standard layout: I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral; II, III, aVF inferior; V1–V2 septal; V3–V4 anterior.

blocks.html:
ECG interpretation

Work through the tracing in the same order every time.

300-150-100-75-60-50"] --> B["Rhythm
P before each QRS? QRS after each P?"] B --> C["Intervals

blocks.html:
Rate
  • Count large boxes between beats: say “300, 150, 100” … “75, 60, 50”
  • Or calculate: rate = cycles per 10-second strip × 6
  • Sinus bradycardia: rate < 60/min · sinus tachycardia: rate > 100/min

blocks.alt: Table of large boxes between beats versus interval and heart rate

blocks.html:
Rhythm
  • Identify the basic rhythm, then scan for prematurity, pauses, irregularity and abnormal waves
  • Check for: P before each QRS, QRS after each P, PR intervals (for AV blocks), QRS interval (for BBB)
  • If axis deviation, rule out hemiblock
Axis
  • Normal = -30° to +90°; check lead I and aVF; check lead II for left axis
  • QRS above or below baseline gives the axis quadrant
  • For axis in degrees, find the isoelectric QRS in a limb lead of the axis quadrant – use the “Axis in Degrees” chart
  • Axis rotation in the horizontal plane – find the transitional QRS

blocks.alt: Axis quadrants from the QRS direction in leads I and aVF
blocks.cap: Lead I and aVF both upright = normal; I up, aVF down = LAD; I down, aVF up = RAD; both down = extreme RAD.

blocks.alt: Axis-in-degrees chart: isoelectric lead for each axis
blocks.cap: Find the isoelectric limb lead, then read the axis in degrees for that quadrant.

rows: Long notched or biphasic P wave
Large S in V1 + large R in V6 > 35 mm

blocks.html:
Ischemia and infarction
  • Check for: Q waves (necrosis/past infarction), inverted T waves (ischemia), ST elevation (infarction), ST depression (ischemia)
  • Reciprocal changes: ST elevation ± ST depression on the mirror side of the STEMI location = true STEMI
  • Find the location of the pathology, then identify the occluded coronary artery
  • STEMI locations: big LII, little LI, ASS, ALL

rows: Loss of R wave in V1, V2 or V3

blocks.title: Two STEMIs to recognise on sight
blocks.html:
• “The boot”: elevation in II, III, aVF (inferior STEMI) – patients with RV involvement have vitals “in their boots”
  • “Widow maker”: elevation in V1–V4; affects the entire LAD

Pericarditis
  • Flat/concave elevated ST segments in more than one coronary distribution
  • PR interval depression
  • ST segment and T wave elevated off baseline

Rhythm disorders

Irregular rhythms lack a constant duration between paced cycles.

rows: At least 3 different P-wave morphologies in the same lead
Escape rhythms – response of an automaticity focus to a pause in SA node pacemaking

A junctional focus in the AV node takes over as pacemaker
Inverted P wave immediately before, after, or buried within each QRS
A ventricular automaticity focus takes over as pacemaker
Tachyarrhythmias – rapid rhythms from very irritable automaticity foci

Continuous rapid sawtooth atrial complexes from a single rapid-firing atrial focus
Many flutter waves needed to produce a ventricular response

Rapid series of smooth sine waves from a single rapid-firing ventricular focus
Usually a short burst leading to ventricular fibrillation

Jagged baseline of tiny spikes from multiple atrial foci
Ventricular QRS response is irregular

Multiple ventricular foci → totally erratic rhythm without identifiable waves
Needs immediate treatment
P wave after the QRS complex
Usually delay in the AV node; influenced by autonomic tone

PR > 200 ms; no dropped QRS
All P waves conducted
Usually the AV node, or high parasympathetic tone

Progressive PR prolongation, then a dropped QRS
Cycle after the block has the shortest PR
Often benign; no pacemaker unless symptomatic

Constant PR; spontaneous dropped QRS
PR after the block same as before
Higher progression to complete AVB; usually pacemaker indicated

AV dissociation – no P wave produces a QRS
Regular P waves; regular QRS, slower than the P waves
Ventricular rate 40–60/min → junctional focus; 20–40/min → ventricular focus

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Mediastinum and the Heart
lectures.framing: A map of the chest’s middle compartment and the heart inside it. The organising idea is the sternal angle: it splits superior from inferior mediastinum, and from there each structure – chamber, valve, coronary branch, nerve – has a fixed place and a fixed job.
lectures.keypoints: Sternal angle (T4/T5) separates superior from inferior mediastinum and marks the carina. L recurrent laryngeal loops under the aortic arch; the R loops the subclavian. Pericardial pain refers via the phrenic (C3–C5); cardiac ischemic pain via T1–T4/5. LAD = anterior 2/3 of the septum; posterior interventricular (RCA) = posterior 1/3. VSD is the most common heart defect. Bundle of His is the only electrical link between atria and ventricles.

blocks.html:
Anatomy of the mediastinum
  • Mediastinum: the middle space between the two pleural sacs
  • All thoracic structures are within the mediastinum except the lungs

blocks.alt: The mediastinum between the two pleural sacs, in dissection, surface projection and CT
Divisions of the mediastinum: superior, and inferior split into anterior, middle, posterior
blocks.cap: The sternal angle to the T4/T5 disc divides superior from inferior mediastinum.

rows: Superior thoracic aperture to the sternal angle anteriorly and the inferior border of T4 posteriorly
Thymus gland · brachiocephalic veins · SVC · arch of aorta and branches · vagus nerve · L recurrent laryngeal nerve · ligamentum arteriosum · phrenic nerve · trachea · esophagus
Divided into anterior, middle and posterior:
Anterior: between the sternum and pericardial sac
Thymus gland (children, adolescents) · fat (adults) · lymph nodes · internal thoracic vessels and branches
Heart · ascending aorta · pulmonary vessels · terminal SVC · phrenic nerves
Posterior: from the pericardial sac and lung roots to the thoracic vertebral bodies
Descending aorta · thoracic duct · azygos venous system (collateral pathway from the IVC in the abdomen) · esophagus · sympathetic trunk · thoracic splanchnic nerves

blocks.alt: Superior mediastinum and its contents
Anterior mediastinum: thymus, fat, lymph nodes, internal thoracic vessels
Middle mediastinum: pericardium, phrenic nerves, pericardiophrenic vessels
Posterior mediastinum contents

blocks.html: Arteries and veins of the mediastinum

blocks.alt: Arteries (aorta and arch branches) and veins (brachiocephalic, SVC, azygos system) of the mediastinum
blocks.cap: Left: aortic arch branches. Right: brachiocephalic veins, SVC and the azygos/hemiazygos system.

blocks.alt: Great vessels: arch branches, brachiocephalic veins, SVC, pulmonary vessels, ligamentum arteriosum

blocks.html:
Nerves of the mediastinum
  • R/L phrenic nerves: arise in the neck from C3–C5 to innervate the diaphragm; often embedded in fat around the pericardial sac
  • R/L vagus nerves: descend from the neck into the superior mediastinum; found posterior to the root of the lung, which distinguishes them from the phrenic nerves
  • L recurrent laryngeal nerve: branch of the L vagus supplying many laryngeal muscles; loops under the arch of the aorta and ascends between trachea and esophagus to the larynx
  • R recurrent laryngeal nerve: loops around the R subclavian artery and ascends between trachea and esophagus; it is NOT in the superior mediastinum
  • Sympathetic chain: bilateral trunks either side of the vertebral column from skull base to coccyx
    • Typically 12 ganglia (postsynaptic cell bodies) in the thoracic portion of each trunk
    • Most presynaptic sympathetic fibres synapse in ganglia along the trunk
  • Thoracic splanchnic nerves: presynaptic nerves that pass through the thoracic sympathetic trunk without synapsing, continue through the diaphragm into the abdomen to supply abdominal organs
    • Greater: 5th–9th ganglia · lesser: 10th–11th · least: 12th thoracic ganglion

blocks.alt: Nerves of the mediastinum: vagus, recurrent laryngeal, phrenic, sympathetic chain, greater splanchnic

blocks.html:
Other structures in the mediastinum
  • Trachea: from the larynx into the superior mediastinum, anterior to the esophagus; ends at the carina at the level of the sternal angle, bifurcating into R and L primary bronchi; it is NOT part of the posterior mediastinum
  • Ligamentum arteriosum: remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosum, which shunted blood from the pulmonary trunk to the inferior surface of the aortic arch
  • Esophagus: from the pharynx, posterior to the trachea; runs the entire length of the thorax before piercing the diaphragm to enter the stomach
  • Thoracic duct: main lymphatic duct; begins in the abdomen, enters the thorax to the R of the aorta, ascends to the base of the neck and drains at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins

blocks.alt: Trachea, ligamentum arteriosum, esophagus and thoracic duct

blocks.html:
Pericardium
  • Pericardial sac: protective, fluid-filled, triple-layered sac around the heart and roots of the great vessels
  • Fibrous pericardium (outer): dense, inelastic connective tissue attached to the diaphragm to anchor the heart; protects it and prevents overstretching
  • Serous pericardium: thin, double-layered membrane that secretes serous fluid
    1. Parietal pericardium: lines the internal aspect of the fibrous pericardium
    2. Visceral pericardium: lines the heart and roots of the great vessels
  • Pericardial cavity: serous fluid between the layers reduces friction as the heart moves
  • Sensory: phrenic nerve (C3–C5) – pain radiates to the ipsilateral supraclavicular region (top of the shoulder)
  • Sympathetic: cardiopulmonary splanchnic nerves (T1–T4) · parasympathetic: vagus nerve

blocks.alt: Sagittal view of the pericardial layers and cavity with needle entry site
blocks.cap: The arrow marks the infrasternal approach for pericardiocentesis.

blocks.html:
Clinical note
  • Pericarditis: painful inflammation making the pericardial surface rough → friction heard as a rustling sound with a stethoscope
  • Pericardial effusion: passage of fluid into the pericardial cavity
  • Cardiac tamponade: compression of the heart; potentially lethal
    • Can occur from cardiomegaly, or an illness/wound that lets blood or fluid enter the pericardium
    • With extensive effusion the sac cannot let the heart fully expand → limits filling and reduces CO
  • Pericardiocentesis removes fluid to relieve pressure: wide-bore needle into the 5th or 6th intercostal space near the sternum or via the infrasternal angle

Anatomy of the heart
  • Located in the inferior, middle mediastinum; rests on the diaphragm between the lungs and the ribs
  • The apex lies on the left
  • Generates and conducts electrical impulses for contraction so blood can be transported to the lungs and throughout the body

blocks.alt: Anterior surface of the heart: chambers, great vessels, coronary and interventricular sulci
Anterior view of the heart with auricles, pulmonary trunk and sulci labelled

rows:
Right atrium
receives deoxygenated blood from the body

• R auricle and anterior portion contain pectinate muscles
• Crista terminalis separates the pectinate muscles from the smooth posterior wall
• Fossa ovalis: remnant of the fetal foramen ovale that shunted blood to the L heart
• Three veins deliver blood: SVC (upper body), IVC (lower body; largest vein), coronary sinus (heart tissue – enters between the right AV valve and the IVC opening)

Right ventricle
pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs

• Tricuspid valve bases attach to a fibrous ring that resists dilation; free cusp edges attach to chordae tendineae
• Papillary muscles anchor the tricuspid valve; with the chordae they stop the cusps being pushed back into the atrium during contraction
• Septomarginal trabecula carries part of the conducting system → coordinated RV contraction
• Trabeculae carneae: muscular ridges
• Blood leaves via the conus arteriosus (smooth part just below the pulmonary semilunar valve) into the pulmonary trunk

Left atrium
receives oxygenated blood from the lungs

• Smooth interior; walls slightly thicker than the RA
• Forms most of the base of the heart
• L auricle is small and contains pectinate muscles; the rest is smooth-walled
• Four pulmonary veins (R/L superior, R/L inferior) deliver oxygenated blood

Left ventricle
pumps oxygenated blood to the body

• Mitral valve chordae attach to two large papillary muscles on the LV wall, which contract with the LV
• Larger and thicker-walled than the RV – pumps systemically under greater pressure
• Numerous small trabeculae carneae
• Ejects through the aortic semilunar valve (left, right and posterior cusps) into the ascending aorta

Interior of the right ventricle: tricuspid valve, chordae, papillary muscles, septomarginal trabecula, conus arteriosus

Ascends through the diaphragm; returns deoxygenated blood from the lower 2/3 of the body to the RA

Separates RA and LA
Fossa ovalis (fetal remnant of the foramen ovale) prominent on its R side

ASDs: frequently incomplete closure of the foramen ovale (patent foramen ovale) – may go unnoticed with no consequence; if big enough, left-to-right shunting → right-sided hypertrophy and dilation of the pulmonary trunk

Separates RV and LV
Thin posterosuperior membranous part and a predominant muscular part

VSDs = most common heart defect: consequences depend on size and shunted volume – pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure can occur
High incidence in Down syndrome

blocks.html:
Valve function
  • AV valves: open in diastole, closed in systole
  • Semilunar valves: closed in diastole, open in systole

blocks.alt: Superior view of the four valves in diastole and systole
blocks.cap: Diastole: AV (bicuspid, tricuspid) valves open, semilunar valves shut; systole: the reverse.

blocks.alt: Figure from the valve function section

blocks.html:
Coronary circulation
  • The heart has its own circulation – it is fed oxygenated blood first
  • The first two branches of the ascending aorta, at the aortic sinuses, are the R and L coronary arteries

rows: Ascends to the SA node – supplies the pulmonary trunk and SA node
Inferior R margin and apex – supplies the RV and apex
Posterior interventricular groove to the apex – RV, LV and the posterior 1/3 of the septum
From near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery to the AV node
Anterior interventricular groove to the apex – RV, LV and the anterior 2/3 of the septum; anastomoses with the posterior interventricular artery (RCA)
Continues in the coronary sulcus to the posterior heart – LA and LV; gives rise to the L marginal artery; anastomoses with the RCA

blocks.alt: Right and left coronary arteries and their branches

blocks.html:
Cardiac veins
  • Great cardiac vein – runs with the LAD and circumflex → coronary sinus
  • Middle cardiac vein – runs with the posterior interventricular artery → coronary sinus
  • Small cardiac vein – runs with the R coronary artery → coronary sinus
  • Coronary sinus (main vein) – runs left to right posteriorly in the coronary groove, receiving the great, middle and small cardiac veins before draining into the RA

blocks.alt: Anterior and posterior cardiac veins: great, middle, small cardiac veins and coronary sinus

blocks.html:
Conduction system
  • When impulses propagate through cardiac muscle, the myocytes contract
  • Sinoatrial (SA) node (“pacemaker”): R atrial wall at the junction of the SVC and RA
  • Atrioventricular (AV) node: inferior interatrial septum; conducts impulses in one direction only
  • AV bundle (bundle of His): the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles; branches into R/L bundle branches
  • Purkinje fibres: large conduction myofibrils continuous with the muscle mass
  • Septomarginal trabecula (moderator band): from the inferior interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle of the RV; carries conduction fibres through the RV

flowchart TD A["SA node
AP produced"] --> B["Three internodal tracts"] B --> C["AV node
one-way conduction"] C --> D["Bundle of His"] D --> E["R and L bundle branches
through the interventricular septum"] E --> F["Apex of the heart"] F --> G["Purkinje fibres"] G --> H["Ventricular contraction"]

blocks.alt: Conduction system and sequence of excitation from SA node to Purkinje fibres
blocks.cap: Impulse is delayed at the AV node before passing down the bundle branches to the apex.

blocks.html:
Extrinsic innervation of the heart
  • Sympathetics: cardiopulmonary splanchnics (T1–T4/5) from the sympathetic chain to the cardiac plexus (a diffuse network of delicate fibres from the trachea to the aortic arch)
    • ↑ HR and force of contraction; dilation of the coronary vessels
    • General visceral afferents carry pain (ischemia, metabolic by-products) retrograde along the sympathetic nerves to the dorsal roots of T1–T4/5
    • Referred pain: the brain may misinterpret this as coming from the T1–T4/5 dermatomes
  • Phrenic nerves give sensory innervation to the pericardial sac – pericarditis pain can be referred to C3–C5
  • Parasympathetics: primarily the vagus nerve
    • ↓ HR and force of contraction; constriction of the coronary vessels
    • Transmits cardiac reflexes to tension/pressure (baroreceptors) or O2 levels (chemoreceptors)

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart LR A["Myocardial ischemia
metabolic by-products"] --> B["Visceral afferents
along sympathetic nerves"] B --> C["Dorsal roots T1-T4/5"] C --> D["Referred to T1-T4/5 dermatomes"] E["Pericardial inflammation"] --> F["Phrenic nerve"] F --> G["Referred to C3-C5
top of shoulder"]

blocks.alt: Sympathetic and parasympathetic supply to the heart and their effects
blocks.cap: Sympathetic ↑ SA pacing, force and coronary dilation; vagal ↓ pacing, force and constricts coronaries.

lectures.name: Introduction to Cardiac Physiology
lectures.title: Normal Heart Sounds and Classifying Cardiac Murmurs
lectures.framing: Two normal sounds mark valve closure; two extra sounds and every murmur point to a specific abnormal load or valve. The organising idea: describe a murmur by timing, location, intensity and shape, and the diagnosis narrows itself.
lectures.keypoints: S1 = mitral + tricuspid close; S2 = aortic + pulmonary close. S3 = volume-loaded ventricle (early diastolic, can be normal when young); S4 = stiff ventricle (late diastolic, atrial kick). Regurgitant = leaky, stenotic = tight. Grade IV = thrill; diastolic murmurs top out at IV.

rows: Rush of blood into the LV

Volume-loaded ventricle: mitral regurgitation, severe diastolic dysfunction
Can be normal in young patients
Atrial contraction forces blood through the AV valves, striking the LV

blocks.html:
Classifying cardiac murmurs
  • Murmur: an audible sound from increased blood flow through normal cardiac structures, or turbulent flow through abnormal ones
  • Regurgitant valve = leaky · stenotic valve = tight

Describe every murmur by:

  1. Timing: systole, diastole, or both
  2. Location of maximum intensity: sternal border (tricuspid), base (aortic, pulmonary), apex (mitral)
  3. Intensity: grading scales (below)
  4. Shape: ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) or holosystolic for systolic murmurs; decrescendo for diastolic murmurs

rows: Audible with stethoscope tilted off the chest wall
Audible with stethoscope away from the chest
blocks.lead: Intensity grading – systolic murmurs go to VI, diastolic only to IV.

flowchart TD A["Murmur"] --> B{"Timing?"} B -->|"Systolic"| C{"Location?"} B -->|"Systolic and diastolic"| D["Pericardial rub
triphasic · scratchy · loudest at border"] B -->|"Diastolic"| E["Aortic regurgitation
or mitral stenosis"] C -->|"Base"| F["Aortic stenosis · ASD
HCM"] C -->|"Border"| G["Tricuspid regurgitation · VSD
HCM"] C -->|"Apex"| H["Mitral regurgitation · MVP
HCM"]

blocks.alt: Algorithm for classifying a murmur by timing, precordial location and associated findings
blocks.cap: Split first by timing, then by where it is loudest; the tables separate the candidates by radiation, apex beat, S2 and extra sounds (e.g. AS radiates to the carotids with a single S2; MR radiates to the axilla).

lectures.name: The Heart as a Pump
lectures.title: Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump
lectures.framing: Cardiac output is heart rate × stroke volume, and stroke volume is set by three levers – preload, afterload and contractility. Each lever helps a normal heart; the recurring lesson is how a failing heart stops responding to them.
lectures.keypoints: CO = HR × SV (5 L/min; SV 60–70 mL). Tachycardia shortens diastole, when the LV is perfused → demand ischemia. Frank-Starling: ↑ EDV → ↑ SV up to an optimal sarcomere length. Afterload by Laplace: tension = P × r / (2 × wall thickness); pressure overload → concentric, volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy. Contractility is independent of preload and afterload. A failing heart is insensitive to preload but very sensitive to afterload.

blocks.html:
Determinants of cardiac output
  • Cardiac output (CO): blood pumped in one minute; increases with oxygen demand (exercise, fever); normal = 5 L/min
  • CO = HR × SV
  • Cardiac index: relates heart performance to body size – CI = CO/body surface area (L/min/m2)

blocks.alt: Cardiac output depends on heart rate and stroke volume; stroke volume on preload, afterload and contractility
blocks.cap: CO = HR × SV, and SV is set by preload, afterload and contractility – the structure of this lecture.

blocks.html:
Heart rate
  • Heart rate (HR): contractions per minute; normal resting HR = 70–80 bpm
  • The SA node pacemaker sets HR; normal intrinsic resting SA node rate = 110
  • Parasympathetic input (vagus) decreases HR – athlete resting HR = 50–60 bpm
  • Sympathetic input increases HR
  • Heart transplants are denervated:
    • No PSNS innervation – higher HR from the intrinsic SA node rate
    • No SNS innervation – circulating catecholamines can still cause tachycardia
  • Force-frequency relationship (Bowditch/treppe phenomenon): ↑ HR increases the force of contraction, but only up to a maximum rate; not as effective for failing ventricles
  • ↑ HR decreases diastolic time → decreased CO and decreased cardiac perfusion

blocks.alt: Rate-tension relation in control versus failing myocardium
blocks.cap: Force rises with rate up to ~180/min in normal muscle; the failing heart gains almost nothing.

blocks.alt: Aortic pressure and left versus right coronary blood flow through systole and diastole
blocks.cap: Left coronary flow happens mainly in diastole – so tachycardia, which shortens diastole, starves the LV.

blocks.html:
Changes in HR
  • Bradycardia = HR too low → low CO if SV does not increase
  • Tachycardia = HR too high → ↑ myocardial oxygen consumption, ↓ myocardial perfusion (occurs mainly during diastole for the LV), ↓ time for diastolic filling; demand ischemia
  • Increasing age → ↓ maximal HR (220 – age) and maximal oxygen consumption; stiffer aorta and ventricles

Stroke volume and preload
  • Stroke volume (SV): blood pumped in one contraction; normal = 60–70 mL
  • Preload (EDV): the blood that fills the ventricles during diastole and stretches them to their greatest dimensions
  • Starling’s law: the more a muscle fibre is stretched, the greater its contractile energy
    • There is an optimal sarcomere length; beyond it there is no further increase in tension
    • ↑ preload/EDV → ↑ SV
  • Frank-Starling curves: show how changes in ventricular preload change SV

blocks.alt: Frank-Starling curve: stroke volume against end-diastolic volume with sarcomere lengths
blocks.cap: SV climbs with EDV as sarcomeres approach their optimal length, then plateaus.

rows: A more compliant ventricle holds more blood at a given pressure than a noncompliant one
↑ afterload → ↑ preload: less blood ejected, more residual blood adds to EDV
More blood ejected in systole → less left to add to EDV
Atrial “kick” forces extra blood into the ventricle
Excessive thoracic pressure can reduce venous return to the RV

blocks.html:
Clinical relevance of preload
  • EDV cannot be easily measured or monitored
  • Too little EDV → the heart is underfilled
  • Too much EDV → the heart is overstretched → decompensation, ↑ LV diastolic pressure and congestion (pulmonary edema)
  • A failing ventricle is less responsive to EDV

blocks.alt: Stroke volume versus preload in normal and failing hearts, with the congestion threshold
blocks.cap: The failing heart's curve is flat: more preload pushes it past the congestion line without adding much stroke volume.

blocks.html:
Case: hockey player with acute blood loss who feels faint

Expected vital signs

  • Heart rate: increased to help maintain CO
  • Blood pressure: initially maintained by the sympathetic nervous system, then decreased from blood loss
  • Oxygen saturation: normal – the lungs are functioning
  • Respiratory rate: increased due to fear
  • Temperature: decreased; may become hypothermic, especially if given blood products
  • Urine output: decreased to preserve water and circulating volume

How is he compensating?

  • Reduced urine output and vasoconstriction to maintain SV
  • Decreased capillary refill – blood is sent to vital organs rather than the extremities
  • Management: stop the bleed (pressure); elevate the legs and give fluids or transfusions to increase SV; surgical intervention

blocks.alt: Injured hockey goaltender bleeding on the ice
blocks.cap: The case: acute hemorrhage in a previously healthy athlete.

flowchart TD A["Acute blood loss"] --> B["↓ blood volume → ↓ preload"] B --> C["↓ stroke volume"] C --> D["Sympathetic activation"] D --> E["↑ heart rate"] D --> F["Vasoconstriction
↓ capillary refill"] D --> G["↓ urine output
preserve volume"] E --> H["BP initially maintained"] F --> H G --> H H -->|"Ongoing loss"| I["BP falls"] I --> J["Stop bleed · elevate legs
fluids or transfusion · surgery"]

blocks.html:
Afterload
  • Afterload: the wall tension or stress the ventricle must develop to open the aortic valve and eject blood into the aorta
  • Law of Laplace: tension = (pressure × radius)/(wall thickness × 2)
  • Clinically simplified to pulmonary arterial pressure (right) or MAP (left)
  • RV = lower afterload – generates less pressure to eject
  • Decrease afterload clinically by decreasing pressure – vasodilator, intra-aortic balloon pump for LV failure; beware hypotension
  • A normal heart tolerates afterload changes well; a failing heart is very sensitive to afterload
  • ↑ RV afterload: pulmonary embolism with R heart failure – acute response: ventricular dilation, ↑ EDV + ESV, ↓ SV
  • ↑ LV afterload: hypertension (↑ aortic pressure) – chronic response: concentric hypertrophy, ↑ wall thickness
    • Good → compensatory, decreases afterload (wall stress)
    • Bad → stiffer ventricle, more prone to ischemia, difficult to perfuse

blocks.alt: Stroke volume versus afterload in normal, moderate and severe heart failure
blocks.cap: The more the heart fails, the more steeply SV falls as afterload rises.

blocks.lead: Hypertrophy: an increase in ventricular mass and cell volume.

blocks.alt: Growth stimuli driving physiologic, concentric and eccentric hypertrophy, apoptosis and sarcomeric disorganization

blocks.html:
Ventricular remodeling
  • Changes in mass, volume and shape of the ventricles as a compensatory response to increased load
  • Occurs in myocardial infarction, hypertension and valvular heart disease
  • Molecular mechanisms: aldosterone, angiotensin II, cytokines (TNF, IL-6)
  • Includes interstitial fibrosis, collagen deposition and apoptosis

Compliance
  • Relates to the stiffness of the ventricle
  • Compliance = Δ volume / Δ pressure
  • Decreased compliance: hypertrophy, ischemia, scar tissue
  • Increased compliance: dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Compliance can change both acutely and chronically
  • Stiff ventricles need higher pressures to fill – can lead to hypertension

blocks.alt: Diastolic LV pressure-volume curves in control, aortic stenosis, aortic insufficiency and HCM
blocks.cap: HCM and AS curves rise steeply (stiff); aortic insufficiency sits far right (dilated, compliant).

blocks.html:
Contractility
  • Contractility (inotropy): the intrinsic property of cardiac muscle cells to shorten in response to a stimulus (action potential)
  • Independent of preload and afterload – based on the intrinsic strength of contraction of heart muscle
  • Shortening of cardiac muscle results in ejection of blood
  • Increased with sympathetic nervous system activation
  • An increase in contractility increases SV for any given preload
  • Systolic heart failure: downward/right shift and flattening of the curve; will not respond properly to volume
    • Fluid to increase preload – may increase SV and CO, but may also increase end-diastolic pressure and cause pulmonary edema
    • Decrease afterload – only if a patient is hypertensive
    • Increase contractility – does not improve long-term mortality

blocks.alt: Family of Frank-Starling curves: exercise, rest, heart failure, fatal myocardial depression
blocks.cap: Higher contractility shifts the curve up and left; heart failure flattens it, so extra filling buys little extra performance.

blocks.html:
Module questions
  • 8. Most common cause of right heart failure: left heart failure → pulmonary embolism, chronic lung disease, idiopathic pulmonary hypertension and chronic hypoxemia due to altitude may also cause it
  • 9. JVP elevated to the angle of the jaw may be caused by: all of the above → volume overload, right heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation raise RA pressure and JVP; cardiac tamponade is pressure in the pericardium that impairs venous return and CO
  • 10. A noncompliant (stiff) ventricle is associated with aortic stenosis, chronic hypertension, acute cardiac ischemia and HFpEF, EXCEPT: mitral stenosis → raises LA pressure and a gradient across the mitral valve; the LV is not directly affected – the problem is filling from atrium to ventricle
  • 11. Patients with a disproportionate fall in CO when they develop atrial fibrillation: all of the above → anything making the ventricle stiff increases the importance of atrial systole (aortic stenosis, stiff noncompliant ventricle, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); a stenotic mitral valve does not open easily, so atrial contraction provides an extra “kick”
  • 12. Acute large PE, hemodynamically unstable (tachycardia, hypotension, low urine output, decreased capillary refill). Echo MOST likely shows: dilated right ventricle → acute PE abruptly increases RV afterload; the RV fails and acutely dilates; the LV is affected only indirectly if the septum is pushed toward it
  • 13. Chronic mitral regurgitation is associated with: all of the above → backflow into the LA during systole, reflected into the pulmonary vasculature; LA enlargement, LV enlargement from volume overload, tendency to pulmonary edema, eccentric hypertrophy
  • 14. Compliance is the relationship between: pressure and volume

lectures.name: Microcirculation and Lymphatics
lectures.title: Microcirculation, Vascular Flow and BP Regulation
lectures.framing: How the capillary bed exchanges material and fluid, and how flow and pressure are controlled – from Poiseuille’s law through the baroreflex to local metabolites. The organising idea: Flow = ΔP/R, and nearly every control mechanism works by changing R at the arterioles.
lectures.keypoints: R = 8ηl/πr⁴ – radius to the fourth power dominates. Optimal O2 delivery at hematocrit ~40%. Net fluid out at the arteriolar end, in at the venous end; small ↑ interstitial pressure → 10-fold ↑ lymph flow. Aortic baroreceptors = vagus; carotid sinus = glossopharyngeal. Parasympathetics do not innervate vessels. Neurogenic shock = hypotension + bradycardia from lost T1–T4 sympathetic outflow. NO → cGMP → vasodilation; sildenafil blocks PDE5; bosentan blocks endothelin receptors.

blocks.html:
Macro- vs microcirculation
  • Macrocirculation: transports material between organs – long distances, movement within vessels
  • Microcirculation: distributes and exchanges material within organs – short distances, movement within capillaries; a network of arterioles, capillaries and venules
  • Precapillary sphincters regulate blood flow into the capillary beds
  • Arteriovenous anastomoses shunt blood directly to the venules – temperature regulation

blocks.alt: Capillary bed with arteriole, precapillary sphincters, metarteriole, thoroughfare channel and AV anastomosis
blocks.cap: Precapillary sphincters gate the bed; the metarteriole and AV anastomosis let blood bypass it.

blocks.html:
Bulk flow and diffusion
  • Bulk flow: movement of fluid along a vessel due to a pressure gradient; resistance depends on vessel geometry and blood viscosity
  • Diffusion: movement of material across a vessel wall due to a concentration gradient
    • Factors: blood flow, concentration gradient, endothelial area, endothelial permeability
    • Capillary endothelia have a high permeability; molecular movement depends on molecular weight, temperature and viscosity
    • Major factors of material exchange: diffusion distance, capillary density
  • Fick principle: ↑ flow → more arterial O2 available per minute → more exchange by diffusion (dO2/dt)
    • Uptake = flow × ([arterial O2] – [venous O2])
    • Used to assess CO by measuring arterial and venous O2
  • Multi-directional flow in adjacent capillaries enhances uniform exchange
  • The lung is an ideal exchange organ: large surface area, short diffusion distances, fast flow

Poiseuille’s law
  • Q = πPr⁴ / 8ηl or R = 8ηl / πr⁴
    Q = flow rate · R = resistance · P = perfusion pressure · r = vessel radius · η = blood viscosity · l = vessel length
  • Blood flow in vessels is generally laminar; entering a smaller vessel, a parabolic flow profile develops
  • Plasma skimming: natural separation of RBCs from plasma at bifurcations, dividing blood into relatively concentrated and dilute streams → low hematocrit entering the smaller capillaries
  • Factors increasing turbulence: low/high blood viscosity (disrupt laminar flow), vessel obstructions (increased CO in pregnancy, atherosclerotic plaques, stenotic heart valves)

blocks.alt: Plasma skimming at a vessel bifurcation: RBC core and cell-free layer
blocks.cap: The branch taking the cell-free edge layer gets fewer RBCs – the basis of plasma skimming.

blocks.html:
Hematocrit and viscosity
  • Hematocrit: volume of blood occupied by packed RBCs; men = 45%, women = 40%
  • Makes blood viscosity 3–4× that of water; provides the basis for laminar flow
  • Low hematocrit: not enough O2-carrying capacity per volume
  • High hematocrit: viscosity too high for adequate flow
  • Optimal O2 delivery occurs when the hematocrit/viscosity ratio is maximized
  • ↑ hematocrit in normal RBCs → small ↑ viscosity; in sickle cells → huge ↑ viscosity – they cannot deform at low PO2

blocks.alt: Viscosity and hematocrit/viscosity ratio against hematocrit
blocks.cap: The hematocrit/viscosity ratio peaks near 40% – the optimum for oxygen delivery.

blocks.alt: Viscosity versus hematocrit for normal RBCs, sickle cells at low PO2 and rigid spheres
blocks.cap: Sickle cells at low PO2 behave almost like rigid spheres: viscosity climbs steeply.

blocks.html:
Determinants of fluid exchange
  • Transmural differences in tissue/capillary fluid pressures and oncotic pressures:
    • Net fluid OUT at the arteriolar end of the capillary
    • Net fluid IN at the venous end
  • Changes in resistance in one vascular bed alter perfusion pressure and flow:
    • ↑ vascular resistance → ↓ perfusion pressure and capillary flow
    • ↓ vascular resistance → ↑ perfusion pressure and capillary flow
  • Ultrafiltration: capillary pressure drives fluid out of the vessels
    • Some returns to the circulation by plasma oncotic pressure
    • Some remains in the interstitium – high capillary hydrostatic pressure and loss of large molecules from vessels (capillary damage, angiogenesis) lead to edema
Lymphatics
  • A one-way drainage returning lymph to the bloodstream to maintain circulatory homeostasis
  • Distal endothelial cells overlap, letting proteins and fluid enter the lymphatic vessel
  • Lymph reaches the subclavian veins mainly via surrounding muscle contraction and elastic recoil of the lungs
  • Distal lymphatics = valves, no smooth muscle · tubular lymphatics = some smooth muscle

blocks.alt: Lymphatic capillaries with pores and valves joining a collecting lymphatic
Overlapping lymphatic endothelial cells held by anchoring filaments, forming valves
blocks.cap: Overlapping endothelial flaps open to let fluid and protein in, then close as one-way valves.

blocks.html:
Interstitial compliance
  • High interstitial compliance: ↑ volume → small ↑ interstitial pressure – subcutaneous tissue
  • Low interstitial compliance: ↑ volume → large ↑ interstitial pressure – brain
  • When interstitial pressure is increased by -5 mm Hg (i.e. from about -5 toward 0 mm Hg), lymphatic flow increases 10-fold, which helps reduce edema

blocks.alt: Interstitial volume versus pressure for high and low compliance tissues, and lymph flow versus interstitial pressure
blocks.cap: Lymph flow rises 10-fold as interstitial pressure climbs from normal (-8 to 0 mm Hg).

blocks.html:
Module questions
  • 29. The microcirculation is a network of: arterioles, capillaries, venules
  • 30. Cardiac output can be assessed with: the Fick principle
  • 31. Major factors of material exchange: diffusion distance, capillary density
  • 32. Fluid diffusion across the capillaries occurs due to: fluid pressure gradient, oncotic pressure
  • 33. NOT correct about lymphatics? (a) one-way drainage for interstitial fluid; (b) essential for circulatory homeostasis; (c) valves like veins to prevent backflow; (d) lymph moved toward the heart mainly by skeletal muscle contraction and respiratory movement; (e) lymphatic flow is reduced when interstitial pressure is elevated ← false: flow can increase tremendously with only slight increases in interstitial pressure

Regulation of the circulatory system
  • Change the rate of blood flow: Flow = ΔP / R
    • ΔP = MAP – mean RA pressure
    • Flow = CO = HR × SV
    • R = systemic vascular resistance (SVR)
    • Each organ can regulate its own blood supply by regulating vessel resistance
  • Change concentrations in the blood – electrolytes
  • Change the relative distribution of blood flow – small regional changes in arteriole diameter are compensated by vasoconstriction or vasodilation in other beds, preserving SVR and MAP
  • Vascular compliance: the relationship between the volume of blood in a vascular segment and its pressure; veins are 20–30× more compliant than arteries

Acute BP control – autonomic nervous system (rapid)
  • Baroreceptors: mechanoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus that sense changes in arterial wall tension
    • Aortic arch baroreceptors = vagus nerve
    • Carotid sinus baroreceptors = glossopharyngeal nerve
  • Low BP: ↓ baroreceptor signalling via afferents to the nucleus tractus solitarius (medulla) → ↑ parasympathetic inhibition, ↑ sympathetic outflow (spinal cord T1–4, sympathetic trunk ganglion, cardiac accelerator nerve) → norepinephrine → ↑ HR, contractility, SV; vasoconstriction → ↑ BP

blocks.html:
Case: neurogenic shock
  • 30-year-old woman fell from a 3rd-floor balcony; displacement of C5/C6; no other major injuries; previously well, no medications
  • Exam: BP 70/30, HR 45, RR 26, T 37.0, SpO2 96% on room air, urine output < 20 cc/hr; no movement or sensation below the collar line
  • Why is she in shock? Neurogenic shock – spinal cord injury with autonomic dysregulation; C5/C6 is above T1–T4, which is critical for sympathetic outflow
  • Loss of sympathetic tone with an unopposed parasympathetic response → hypotension with bradycardia

Chronic BP control – renal and hormonal (slow)
  • Aldosterone regulates blood volume, BP and blood Na+, K+ and H+; ↑ extracellular K+ stimulates the adrenal cortex to ↑ aldosterone
  • Aldosterone = Na+ retention
  • ADH/AVP = water reabsorption
  • ANP = Na+ secretion

blocks.alt: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system response to dehydration or hemorrhage
blocks.cap: ↓ volume and BP → renin from JG cells → angiotensin I → (ACE in lung) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction and aldosterone → Na+/water retention → BP restored.

blocks.alt: ADH negative feedback loop for water deficit
blocks.cap: Water deficit → ↑ osmolarity → osmoreceptors → ADH → ↑ water reabsorption in the collecting ducts → ↓ water excreted.

rows: Binds α-receptors in blood vessels throughout the body
Binds β2-receptors in vessels of skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and liver
Production stimulated by ↓ BP and ↓ Na+; ↑ thirst
Released from the posterior pituitary; ↑ water reabsorption in the kidneys
Released by stretched atrial muscle cells; ↑ GFR and ↓ Na+ reabsorption in the collecting ducts

blocks.html:
Local control of vascular resistance and flow
  • Metabolic hypothesis: vasodilator metabolites mediate changes in local vascular resistance (vascular tone)
    • K+, H+ and adenosine levels track the rate of metabolism
    • ↑ VO2 → ↑ vasodilator metabolites → ↓ resistance, ↑ blood flow
  • Autoregulation: control of blood flow for individual organs – flow is held constant regardless of pressure (within limits)

blocks.alt: Vasodilator factors released in proportion to tissue metabolism dilating arterioles
blocks.cap: Release is proportional to O2 consumption; removal is proportional to flow – so flow settles where supply matches demand.

blocks.alt: Cerebral autoregulation: flow constant between MAP 50 and 150 mm Hg
blocks.cap: Flow stays flat between ~50 and 150 mm Hg; below it, ischemia; above it, forced dilation and vasogenic edema.

blocks.html:
Active regulation – response to metabolic demand
  • Flow rises in proportion to oxygen consumption

blocks.alt: Blood flow rising linearly with oxygen consumption

blocks.html:
Reactive regulation – response “after the fact”
  • Reactive hyperemia: the transient ↑ in organ blood flow after a vessel occlusion (ischemia)
    • The size of the increase is directly proportional to how long flow was stopped
    • The additional flow after occlusion causes ischemia-reperfusion injury to the heart

blocks.alt: Reactive hyperemia after short and long occlusions
blocks.cap: A longer stop in flow produces a larger hyperemic overshoot.

blocks.html:
Vascular smooth muscle
  • ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → muscle contraction
  • Ca2+ influx via V.G. channels, receptor-mediated activity (hormones) and stretch channels (basal tone)
  • ↑ [Ca2+]i → vasoconstriction; ↑ cAMP and IP3, ↓ cGMP
  • ↓ [Ca2+]i → vasodilation; ↑ NO and cGMP
Nitric oxide (EDRF) = vasodilator
  • Shear stress or receptor-dependent EDNO agonists ↑ endothelial [Ca2+]i → activates eNOS: O2 + L-arginine → NO + L-citrulline
  • NO diffuses from endothelial cells into smooth muscle cells
  • NO stimulates guanylate cyclase: GTP → cGMP
  • Sildenafil (Viagra) inhibits phosphodiesterase 5 from converting cGMP to GMP – loss of cGMP breakdown

GTP → cGMP"] F --> G["Smooth muscle relaxation

blocks.cap: NO also inhibits platelets and monocyte adhesion.

blocks.cap: Sildenafil blocks PDE5, so cGMP accumulates and smooth muscle relaxes.

blocks.html:
Endothelin (ET-1) = vasoconstrictor
  • Big-ET-1 is converted to ET-1 by endothelin converting enzyme (ECE)
  • ET-1 binds ETA and ETB → second messenger signalling via IP3 → smooth muscle contraction
  • Bosentan (dual receptor antagonist) treats pulmonary hypertension – inhibits ETA and ETB
  • NO mitigates ET-1 – can inhibit ECE and increase cGMP

blocks.alt: Endothelin receptors on endothelium and smooth muscle and their interaction with nitric oxide

lectures.name: Cardiac Pharmacology

blocks.html:
Circulatory system: function and organization
  • Function: transport materials required by cells; transport hormones and metabolites; transfer heat from the core of the body to the surface; remove nitrogenous wastes and CO2 from the body
  • Organization: cardiopulmonary circulation (in series), systemic circulation (in parallel); arterial system (high pressure), venous system (low pressure)
  • Overall goal: provide blood flow to organs in response to their needs
Vessels
  • Elastic arteries — closest to the heart; most elastin to withstand high pressure and recoil
  • Muscular arteries — less elastin, more smooth muscle
  • Arterioles — significant smooth muscle content; the greatest change in pressure occurs in the arteriole bed
  • Capillary beds — link arterioles and venules; lined by a single layer of cells, allowing diffusion of materials from capillary to tissues and vice versa; in direct contact with the single-cell-layered alveolar sacs in the lungs
  • Venules, veins — move blood back to the heart
Flow, pressure and resistance
  • Flow = ΔP / R; SVR = ΔP / CO
  • R = 8ηl / πr4 (η = viscosity, l = vessel length, r = radius)
  • Worked example: renal blood flow 500 mL/min, renal arterial pressure 100 mm Hg, renal venous pressure 10 mm Hg → R = ΔP / flow = (100 − 10 mm Hg) / 500 mL/min = 0.18 mm Hg/mL/min
  • Mean arterial pressure — the average arterial pressure through one arterial cycle: MAP = CO × SVR = DP + 1/3(SP − DP) = 93 mmHg
Laminar vs turbulent flow
  • Laminar: slowest flow closest to the vessel wall, increasing velocity towards the centre
  • Turbulent: disorganized flow at points of vessel obstruction; flow rate decreased, perfusion pressure increased
  • Increases turbulence: low blood viscosity, high blood viscosity (as written in source)
Hematocrit, viscosity and resistance
  • Hematocrit contributes to blood viscosity, which is why blood flow is laminar
  • Resistance is directly proportional to viscosity → an abnormally high hematocrit raises viscosity and vessel resistance
  • In anemia, reduced hematocrit → reduced resistance

Acute vs chronic blood pressure regulation
  • Acute — neuronally controlled, responds rapidly to changes in BP → baroreceptors
  • Chronic — hormonal, through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system → primary role of the kidneys
AVP and ANP
  • AVP: dehydration detected as increased extracellular osmolality → AVP released from the posterior pituitary → increases water permeability of the collecting ducts and water reabsorption → ↑ blood volume, ↑ BP
  • ANP: peptide hormone released by atrial muscle cells in response to increased stretch from increased blood volume → increases GFR and decreases sodium reabsorption in the collecting ducts → ↓ blood volume, ↓ BP

blocks.html:
Local control of blood flow
  • Metabolites — metabolic hypothesis: vasodilator metabolites regulate vascular tone
  • Autoregulation — constant blood flow over a wide range of blood pressures
  • Active regulation — in response to changes in blood flow reflecting metabolic demand
  • Reactive regulation — occurs “after the fact”
  • Reactive hyperemia — when flow in a vessel stops and then resumes, flow rises above the pre-blockage level
Vascular smooth muscle tone
  • Vasoconstriction: increased intracellular calcium initiates a second messenger pathway that results in decreased cGMP
  • Vasodilation: decreased intracellular calcium leads to increased cGMP
  • Nitric oxide maintains high cGMP in smooth muscle by increasing guanylyl cyclase activity (GTP → cGMP)

ACE inhibitors (ACEI) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB)
  • ACEI (“-pril”) — block ACE: ↓ production of angiotensin II and block metabolism of bradykinin (bradykinin → vasodilatation is enhanced)
  • ARB (“-sartan”) — block the AT1 (angiotensin II) receptor; no effect on bradykinin
  • Both impair angiotensin II actions: vasoconstriction, ↑ aldosterone (→ ↑ Na+ retention), ↑ sympathetic activity
Mineralocorticoid antagonists (MRA)
  • Aldosterone is an adrenal steroid hormone, stimulated for release by angiotensin II
  • Binds mineralocorticoid receptors → Na+ and water retention, K+ excretion; also inflammatory and fibrosis effects
  • MRAs have a cardioprotective effect in systolic heart failure — stop aldosterone from retaining water

blocks.alt: Renin-angiotensin pathway showing the sites of ACE inhibitors and AT1 receptor antagonists
blocks.cap: ACE inhibitors act at ACE (blocking both angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown); AT<sub>1</sub> antagonists act at the receptor. The boxed actions below are what both impair.

blocks.html:
Spironolactone vs eplerenone
  • Spironolactone is inexpensive
  • Eplerenone has less risk of gynecomastia; in general reserve it for patients with severe/painful gynecomastia
  • 3-year heart failure studies: improved mortality with the addition of an MRA to usual therapy
  • Translation to clinical practice: spironolactone prescription rates climbed, as did rates of admission for hyperkalemia

blocks.alt: Survival curves over 36 months, spironolactone vs placebo
blocks.cap: Survival separates in favour of spironolactone over 3 years of follow-up.

blocks.alt: Cumulative hospitalization for heart failure, eplerenone vs placebo
blocks.cap: Eplerenone lowers heart failure hospitalization (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.47–0.70, P<0.001).

blocks.title: MRAs and hyperkalemia
blocks.html: When MRA prescribing rose, admissions for hyperkalemia rose with it. ACEI, ARBs, spironolactone and eplerenone all predispose to hyperkalemia — watch potassium, especially in renal insufficiency.

Digoxin
  • Inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → via Na+/Ca2+ exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → ↑ contractility
  • Indirect vagal effect → ↓ intrinsic rate of SA node, slows conduction through AV node → ↓ HR
  • Narrow therapeutic window — toxic threshold
  • Long t1/2 (36 hours) with normal kidney function; longer with kidney dysfunction, since it is renally excreted
  • Many drug interactions, which may increase digoxin levels
  • No effect on overall mortality, but fewer admissions for pulmonary edema (decreased morbidity)
  • Higher doses/drug levels do not improve symptoms, but may increase mortality and worsen outcomes
  • Does not convert atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm; rate control is poor during exercise or with SNS activation

blocks.alt: Digitalis inhibiting the myocyte Na+/K+ ATPase, with the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and sarcoplasmic reticulum
blocks.cap: A: digitalis blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase; B: the retained Na+ reduces Ca2+ extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger; C: more Ca2+ is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

blocks.html:
Nitrates
  • Formulations: IV infusion, sublingual tablet/spray, transdermal patch
  • Easily absorbed anywhere, but short half-life, so IV must be continuous
  • Tablets as isosorbide dinitrate (Isordil) — hepatic conversion to mononitrate; longer t1/2
  • Tolerance and rebound: mechanism unclear; occurs with frequent dosing or long-term use
  • Preventable with a nitrate-free interval: dosing with a 10-hour gap — patch ‘off at night’, qid or tid schedule

blocks.alt: Nitric oxide from endothelium or from nitrates activating guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle
blocks.cap: Nitrates and nitroprusside bypass the endothelium and supply NO directly to smooth muscle: GTP → cGMP → relaxation.

blocks.html: Nitrates are contraindicated in low blood pressure and with PDE-5 inhibitors.

Calcium channel blockers
  • Dihydropyridines (“-pine”, e.g. nifedipine) — ↓ arterial resistance → ↓ afterload, but reflex tachycardia
  • Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — ↓ arterial resistance and ↓ heart rate and/or contractility → no reflex tachycardia, due to the concomitant effect on heart rate

blocks.cap: Nifedipine acts on the vessel only (reflex tachycardia); diltiazem/verapamil also slow the heart, so there is no reflex tachycardia.

Module questions: cardiovascular drugs
  • 50. Digoxin, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MRAs and beta blockers have all been shown to decrease mortality in systolic (decreased EF) heart failure EXCEPT: digoxin
  • 51. ED patient with tongue and oropharyngeal swelling and difficulty swallowing — angioedema; admitted to ICU after otolaryngology consult. Of furosemide (Lasix, diuretic), spironolactone, perindopril (ACEI), metoprolol (beta blocker) and atorvastatin (statin), the MOST likely cause: perindopril, ACEI
  • 52. Diffuse muscle pain (especially thighs, shoulders, lower back) and weakness over two days, elevated creatine kinase. If an adverse drug event, the MOST likely medication: atorvastatin, statin
  • 53. Chronic cough — if medication-related, the MOST likely medication: lisinopril, ACEI
  • 54. Ramipril (ACEI), nitroglycerin transdermal patch, valsartan (ARB), spironolactone (MRA) and eplerenone (MRA) may all predispose to hyperkalemia EXCEPT: nitroglycerin transdermal patch

blocks.html:
Steps in cholinergic transmission
  1. Synthesis of ACh: acetyl CoA + choline
  2. Storage in vesicles: 10 000–50 000 ACh molecules per vesicle
  3. Release into the synapse: depolarization, triggered by Ca2+ influx
  4. Cholinergic receptor activation
  5. Rapid inactivation: breakdown of ACh by membrane-bound acetylcholinesterase, and recycling of choline

blocks.alt: Acetylcholine synthesis, release, breakdown by acetylcholinesterase and choline reuptake
blocks.cap: The ACh cycle: made from choline + acetyl CoA, broken down in the cleft by AChE, choline taken back up to make more.
