blocks.title: Anticholinergic vs sympathomimetic
blocks.html: Both give dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and CNS changes. Sweating separates them: the anticholinergic patient is dry (“dry as a bone”); the sympathomimetic patient (e.g. cocaine) is sweaty.

Case: Jurassic Park (1993) — the sick triceratops
  • Confusion and disorientation
  • Dilated pupils
  • Dry mouth
  • Not sweating
  • Enlarged abdomen — ileus, distended bladder

This is pharmacologic — which pattern?

  • a) Sympathomimetic: ↑ HR/BP, dilated pupils, CNS changes, sweating
  • b) Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: muscarinic effects (sweating, nausea/vomiting, secretions); nicotinic effects (variable HR/BP, muscle weakness/paralysis)
  • c) Muscarinic agonist: SLUDGE, constricted pupils, ↓ HR
  • d) Nicotine poisoning: dry mouth, dilated pupils, paralysis
  • e) Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic): dry mouth, dilated pupils, not sweating/dry skin, ileus/bladder distension, confusion/disorientation, ↑ HR/BP — matches the triceratops

Module questions: autonomic drugs
  • 55. Mr. Thompson, 45, with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, has difficulty swallowing and drooling of saliva; fed a liquid diet through a gastrojejunostomy. Glycopyrrolate (Robinul) is used to dry his secretions — similar to atropine but does not cross the blood–brain barrier. Side effect you would NOT expect: increased muscle weakness (atropine = muscarinic receptor blocker)
  • 56. 19-year-old: T 39.7°C, HR 142, RR 20, BP 165/96; flushed, warm dry skin; agitated and incoherent; pupils 6 mm (mydriasis), sluggishly reactive; soft abdomen, absent bowel sounds; ate jimson weed seeds (four other teenagers en route with the same symptoms). Most similar drug class: belladonna alkaloid (blocks muscarinic receptors) → toxidrome effects; Benadryl and Gravol also have these effects
  • 57. Neurotransmitter released by the preganglionic neurons innervating the adrenal medulla: acetylcholine
  • 58. 15-year-old after a seizure at home: HR 135 (sinus tachycardia), BP 158/68, RR 30, T 39.8°C (febrile); pupils dilated (7 mm); pale and sweaty. Drug effect type: sympathomimetic — similar to anticholinergic (antimuscarinic), but patients with anticholinergic toxidrome do NOT sweat; cocaine may present this way, as it blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at nerve terminals
  • 59. 1985 Tokyo subway: difficulty breathing with bronchorrhea, drooling, runny nose and eyes, sweating, nausea, involuntary muscle movements, weakness (some paralysis), involuntary urination, vomiting, confusion, convulsions, coma. Sarin is most likely: acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → muscarinic and nicotinic effects; used in chemical warfare; crosses the BBB causing confusion, seizures, coma
  • 60. Botulinum toxin (Botox) blocks release of ACh vesicles from cholinergic neurons; used clinically as an injection and a potent toxin. NOT expected in botulism: small miotic pupils — pupils would be dilated due to loss of ACh release
  • 61. IV infusion went interstitial; medication leaked into tissue and the skin is necrotic. The medication most likely is an alpha receptor agonist: potent alpha agonists are run through a large central vein (jugular, subclavian); peripheral IVs can be used in an emergency, but extravasation causes profound vasoconstriction → tissue ischemia and necrosis. If caught early, an alpha blocker can be infiltrated into the area to try to prevent skin damage

62–64. Isoproterenol: synthetic catecholamine, β1 agonist = β2 agonist, no α effect. Norepinephrine: endogenous catecholamine, α agonist with only slight β effects clinically. Fenoterol: +++ β2, + β1, no α. Labetalol: α blockade plus β1 and β2 blockade.

  • 62. MOST helpful for bradycardia: isoproterenol — β1 agonists increase HR, CO and contractility
  • 63. Most helpful for hypotension: norepinephrine — α agonists cause vasoconstriction and increased BP
  • 64. Most helpful for bronchodilation: fenoterol — β2 agonists cause bronchodilation

blocks.title: Extravasated alpha agonist
blocks.html: Run potent alpha agonists through a central vein where possible. Leakage into tissue → profound vasoconstriction → ischemia and necrosis; infiltrate an alpha blocker early to limit skin damage.

Case of the week: Howard, 72

Presents to the ED with exertional breathlessness, progressively worse over 2 months. Occasional palpitations, no chest pain. More breathless lying flat, eased sitting up. Non-productive cough; no fevers, weight loss or other concerns.

  • Medical history: hypertension for ~5 years; otherwise unremarkable; no diabetes or dyslipidemia
  • Medications: amlodipine 5 mg/day
  • Allergies: penicillin (rash)
  • Social: lives with wife, fully independent; retired accountant; occasional glass of wine; stopped smoking 40 years ago (previously 5–10/day for 10 years)
Examination
  • Alert and orientated, afebrile, generally well; short of breath when talking
  • Vitals: HR 150 bpm; BP 125/75 mm Hg; RR 20/min; SpO2 92% on room air
  • Cardiac: normal heart sounds, no murmurs, elevated JVP, mild ankle swelling
  • Respiratory: fine crackles at both bases; lung fields resonant except the bases, which are dull to percussion
Immediate investigation priorities
  • a) ECG: yes — records the rate, determines the rhythm, may give clues to structural abnormalities
  • b) CXR: yes — confirm or refute volume overload suggested by history/exam; exclude other causes of breathlessness (pneumonia)
  • c) CT pulmonary angiogram: no — unless suspicion of pulmonary embolism is raised for another reason
  • d) Bloodwork: yes — may help exclude precipitating causes
  • e) Coronary angiogram: no — no chest pain or other reason to suggest it would help immediately

blocks.alt: 12-lead ECG: narrow-complex tachycardia with flutter waves (highlighted in lead II)
blocks.cap: Narrow complexes at a rapid rate; the highlighted segment of the lead II rhythm strip shows the flutter waves.

blocks.html:
ECG interpretation
  • Tachycardia: yes
  • Bradycardia: no — the ECG shows a tachycardia
  • Atrial fibrillation: no — although the rhythm is irregularly irregular, there are flutter waves consistent with atrial flutter
  • Atrial flutter: yes — “flutter waves”
  • Atrial tachycardia: no — visible flutter waves
  • Ventricular tachycardia: no — the complexes are narrow
  • Acute MI: no — no clues on this ECG
Chest X-ray
  • Clinical information: short of breath; no previous films for comparison
  • Heart mildly prominent; small bilateral pleural effusions; increased interstitial markings in both lower lungs, suggesting cardiac decompensation
  • Summary: interstitial pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions

blocks.lead: Bloodwork — his baseline results are within normal limits.

blocks.html:
Why bloodwork before treatment (all true)
  • Electrolyte disturbances can cause abnormal cardiac rhythms
  • Thyroid abnormalities can cause abnormal rhythms — in particular thyrotoxicosis causes atrial arrhythmias
  • Anemia can cause tachycardia, and may cause problems with management
  • Elevated leukocytes may raise concern for another illness such as infection — atrial fibrillation often presents alongside another illness, particularly infections such as pneumonia
Diagnosis: atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response and heart failure — priorities
  • a) Correction of the rhythm: no — does not have to occur immediately
  • b) Correction of the rate: yes — reducing ventricular rate is likely to help
  • c) Treatment of heart failure: yes — initially diuretics to relieve congestion
  • d) Anticoagulation: yes — to reduce thromboembolism risk; confirm the patient is not anemic before starting
Rate control options (after oxygen and diuretics)
  • a) Beta blocker (e.g. metoprolol): yes, with caution — excellent for ventricular rate control, but negative inotropes, so low doses initially in heart failure
  • b) Non-dihydropyridine CCB (e.g. diltiazem): no — can rate-control, but negative inotropic effects make it not first choice
  • c) Dihydropyridine CCB (e.g. amlodipine): no — vasodilatory, no rate-limiting activity
  • d) Digoxin: yes — reasonable initially while acutely unwell as not negatively inotropic; ideally substituted with a beta blocker once improved

blocks.html:
Case wrap-up

Treated in the ED with diuretics, relieving excess fluid; ventricular rate improved with beta blockers; anticoagulated to reduce thromboembolism risk. With diuresis and rate control he improved and was discharged on a beta blocker, oral furosemide, oral anticoagulation and an ACE inhibitor. Follow-up with his family physician in 2 weeks to recheck electrolytes and renal function on the new medications; cardiology outpatient follow-up in 2 months with an echocardiogram to assess cardiac function.

lectures.title: Cardiovascular Pharmacology
lectures.framing: A physiology review (flow, resistance, blood pressure control) followed by the drugs that act on it: the RAAS blockers, digoxin, nitrates, vasodilators, calcium channel blockers and beta blockers, then the autonomic (cholinergic and adrenergic) drugs. The organising idea: know where each drug acts in the pathway, and its effects, indications, contraindications and toxicities follow.
lectures.keypoints: Digoxin is the one HFrEF drug (vs ACEI, ARB, MRA, beta blockers) that does not reduce mortality — it reduces admissions for pulmonary edema. ACEI block bradykinin breakdown (dry cough, angioedema); ARBs have no effect on bradykinin and are used when ACEI cause cough. ACEI, ARBs and MRAs all predispose to hyperkalemia; nitrates do not. Nitrates are contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors and need a nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance. Non-dihydropyridine CCBs are contraindicated in systolic heart failure. Anticholinergic toxidrome = dry skin; sympathomimetic = sweaty; AChE inhibitors (sarin) = muscarinic + nicotinic effects.

lectures.name: Intro to Valvular Disease, Heart Sounds, and Clinical Assessment
Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease
lectures.title: Investigations in Cardiovascular Disease
lectures.framing: How to investigate suspected ischemic heart disease, from history to catheter. The organising idea: match the test to the pretest probability and to the question (anatomy vs. function vs. viability) – no testing when risk is low, functional stress testing when it is intermediate, angiography when non-invasive results are high-risk.
lectures.keypoints: Hx and PEx are the most important investigations; don't test asymptomatic low-risk patients (Framingham < 10%). Troponin is the most sensitive and specific marker of myocardial injury (rise 2-4 h, peak 12 h, normal by 5-10 days). Gold standards: MRI for chambers/global function, echo for valves, cardiac catheterization for coronary anatomy. CTCA is a test of exclusion (NPV 99%). Withhold caffeine/theophylline 48 h before dipyridamole; dobutamine is preferred for stress echo. LV function is the strongest predictor of survival – LVEF normal > 50%, prognosis falls below 30-35%.

blocks.html:
Ischemia: insufficient blood supply to a specific organ

The ischemic cascade — abnormalities appear in a fixed order as supply falls behind demand:

  1. First detectable abnormality: a perfusion abnormality at the cellular level
  2. Abnormalities of ventricular function
  3. Abnormalities detected on an ECG – ischemic ST depression
  4. Angina: chest pain related to myocardial ischemia, caused by coronary arterial narrowing/reduced blood flow to the heart

blocks.alt: Ischemic cascade curve
blocks.cap: The ischemic cascade: as exercise and myocardial O<sub>2</sub> demand rise, perfusion abnormality comes first, then regional diastolic → regional systolic → global LV dysfunction, then ischemic ST depression, and angina last. Symptoms and ECG are late markers.

blocks.html:
Approach to suspected ischemic heart disease

Hx and PEx are the most important investigations for ischemic heart disease.

  • Testing is NOT recommended in asymptomatic, low-risk patients → use the Framingham risk score
  • Severe CAD requiring intervention in asymptomatic patients is rare
  • False positive tests result in: inappropriate anxiety, adverse consequences related to work and insurance, complications from further diagnostic testing
History
  • Predictors of CAD: age, male gender, chest pain symptoms – most powerful
  • Also: diabetes, smoking (½ ppd), hypercholesterolemia, ECG changes (Q waves, ST-T changes)
Physical exam
  • Angina pectoris: substernal squeezing chest pain (5-30 minutes); occurs with stress, emotion, or physical activity; relieved with rest or nitroglycerin
  • Levine sign: chest hand-clutching; the universal sign of distress in angina pectoris and myocardial infarction; pain > 20 minutes

blocks.title: ECG limitations
blocks.html:
• Underdiagnosis: a normal ECG does not exclude myocardial ischemia/infarction (though a normal ECG throughout the course of an acute MI is uncommon) → leads to undertreatment
  • Overdiagnosis: ST elevation from other conditions – acute pericarditis, acute myocarditis, Brugada syndrome, early repolarization (normal), Prinzmetal's angina → exposes the patient to unneeded risk from overtreatment

Laboratory investigations
  • Complete blood count: hemoglobin
  • Renal function: creatinine, microalbumin (especially if using contrast)
  • Electrolytes: Na+, K+
  • Glucose: diabetes, HbA1c
  • Hypercholesterolemia: LDL, HDL, apolipoprotein B-100 (ApoB; main protein in LDL; not in ER)
  • High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP): inflammation marker; atherosclerosis

Cardiac biomarkers reflect acute damage to the myocardium: chemicals/enzymes are irreversibly released from injured muscle cells over a period of hours-days.

blocks.alt: Interpretation of an elevated troponin
blocks.cap: Interpreting troponin > 99th percentile URL: a rise and/or fall with acute ischemia = acute MI (type 1: plaque rupture/erosion; type 2: supply-demand imbalance, e.g. severe hypertension, sustained tachyarrhythmia); without ischemia = acute myocardial injury (acute HF, myocarditis); a stable level = chronic injury (structural heart disease, CKD).

lectures.name: Pericardial Disease
lectures.title: Pericardial Disease
lectures.framing: Three pericardial syndromes – acute pericarditis, effusion (with or without tamponade) and constriction – compared across the same headings. The organising idea: inflammation causes pain, fluid and stiffness each impair diastolic filling, and the rate of change decides how sick the patient is.
lectures.keypoints: Viral is the most common cause. Acute pericarditis = 2 of 4 (pleuritic pain, rub, widespread ST elevation/PR depression, effusion); treat with NSAID + colchicine 3 months. Rate of accumulation, not volume, decides symptoms (200–300 mL fast vs 2 L slow). Tamponade: Beck’s triad, pulsus paradoxus > 10–12, electrical alternans → drain. Constriction: Kussmaul’s sign, pericardial knock, equalized pressures, square root sign; pericardiectomy earlier is better.

blocks.html:
Function of the pericardium
  • Prevents spread of infection between the lungs and heart
  • Maintains cardiac position within the thorax
  • Lubricates the movements of the heart

rows: Enteroviruses, herpesviruses, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HIV, COVID-19
Primary tumours (rare), metastatic tumours (lung cancer, breast cancer, lymphoma)
Direct injury (penetrating trauma), indirect injury (non-penetrating trauma), post-pericardiotomy syndrome, radiation-induced
Lupus-like syndromes (methyldopa, INH, phenytoin), chemotherapy agents
Post-MI (acute, Dressler syndrome), amyloidosis, aortic dissection
blocks.lead: Causes of acute pericarditis and pericardial effusion

blocks.html:
Causes of constrictive pericarditis
  • Pericarditis/idiopathic (45% of cases)
  • Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (25%)
  • Chest irradiation (mantle radiation for lymphoma; 20%)
  • Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, end-stage renal disease, malignancy
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (most common in developing countries)

rows:

Complications:
• Recurrent pericarditis
• Chronic pericarditis
• Constrictive pericarditis
• Associated myocarditis

Increased pericardial fluid (normal = 50 mL)
Slower accumulation = better tolerated – up to 2 L before symptoms
Faster accumulation = more symptomatic – symptoms with only 200–300 mL

Compromised cardiac function from a thickened, rigid, fibrous pericardium secondary to acute pericarditis
Thickened, calcified, stiff; loses compliance:
• Cannot expand when the heart fills (diastole)
• Impaired cardiac filling
• High intracardiac pressures
• Equalization of pressures in all 4 chambers

Chest pain: sharp, pleuritic
• Worse with inspiration
• Worse supine, better leaning forward
± fever
± signs of systemic disease (malignancy, autoimmune conditions, hypothyroidism)

“Tamponade physiology” when fluid impairs cardiac filling (30% of patients)
Pre-syncope, syncope
Dyspnea
Pedal edema
Hiccups (phrenic nerve irritation)
Dysphagia
Symptoms of the underlying cause

From elevated filling pressures:
Fatigue/weakness · ↓ exercise tolerance
RHF: pedal edema, ascites
LHF: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, cough
Similar to other CVD states – need a high index of suspicion

Pericardial friction rub: triphasic (atrial contraction, ventricular expansion – diastole; ventricular contraction – systole), scratchy, can be transient
↑ WBC
↑ inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
↑ myocardial injury markers (CK, troponin)

Small–moderate: no signs on exam
Large: Ewart’s sign below the L scapula (dullness, ↓ breath sounds)
Tamponade:
• Beck’s triad – low BP, high JVP (prominent x, blunted y), muffled heart sounds
• Pulsus paradoxus > 10–12 mm Hg: BP variation with respiration

↑ JVP (prominent y descent)
• Kussmaul’s sign: no expected fall, or a rise, in JVP on inspiration
Pericardial knock: early diastolic, loud, high-pitched – rapid equalization of filling pressures
Hepatomegaly/features of cirrhosis
Ascites, peripheral edema

ESC 2015 – need 2 of:
• Pleuritic chest pain
• Pericardial rub
• New widespread ST elevation or PR depression
• Pericardial effusion
Supportive: ↑ inflammatory markers; pericardial inflammation on CT or MRI

CXR: ↑ cardiac silhouette if > 250 mL; “water bottle heart” if very large
Echo: presence and size of effusion; signs of cardiac compression/tamponade

ECG: LA enlargement, AF, non-specific T changes, low voltages
Echo: normal systolic function, diastolic dysfunction, plethoric IVC, septal bounce, respirophasic septal motion; pericardial thickness hard to see on TTE
CXR/CT: pericardial calcification
Cardiac MRI: thickness, enhancement after gadolinium, respirophasic septal motion
Catheterization: elevated, equalized pressures in all 4 chambers; “square root sign” (early diastolic filling); ventricular interdependence

• High-dose NSAIDs (1–2 weeks) + proton pump inhibitor to prevent ulcers
• Colchicine (3 months) – ↓ recurrences
• Steroids (tapering) – autoimmune
• Immune modulators – anakinra, IVIG, azathioprine
• Pericardiectomy
• Exercise restriction for 3 months

Treat the underlying cause
Drain the fluid: pericardiocentesis (percutaneous) or pericardial window (surgical)
Therapeutic: tamponade physiology (IV fluids or pressors stabilize BP while preparing to drain); suspected purulent effusion
Diagnostic: large effusions where malignancy or infection is suspected

Treat the heart failure: diuretics, low-salt diet
Treat inflammation, especially with late gadolinium enhancement on MRI: NSAIDs/colchicine/steroids/anakinra (IL-1 inhibitor)/azathioprine
Surgical pericardiectomy – earlier is better

blocks.title: Beck’s triad = tamponade
blocks.html: Low BP + high JVP + muffled heart sounds, with pulsus paradoxus > 10–12 mm Hg and electrical alternans. Stabilize with IV fluids or pressors, then drain urgently.

Stage 3 (3–several weeks): flattened T waves invert
Stage 4 (several weeks onwards): ECG returns to normal
↓ voltages: QRS < 5 mm in limb leads, < 10 mm in precordial leads
Electrical alternans: QRS size varies beat to beat – the heart is swinging

blocks.html:
Pericardial fluid analysis
  • Colour: hemorrhagic, chylous (white, milky), purulent
  • CBC: ↑ RBC in trauma and malignancy
  • ↑ protein: TB, malignancy
  • Culture, acid-fast bacilli: TB
  • Cytology: abnormal in malignancy, but low yield
  • ↓ glucose: infection, rheumatoid arthritis, TB, malignancy
  • LDH ↑ in fluid but normal in serum = malignancy

blocks.alt: Exudate versus transudate criteria for pericardial fluid
blocks.cap: Exudate: protein > 3.0 g/dL, fluid:serum protein > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, glucose ratio < 1.0 – malignancy, infection, post-pericardiotomy, collagen vascular disease.

blocks.html:
Case 1: sharp chest pain after a viral illness
  • 32-year-old man: sharp chest pain, worse with inspiration and lying down, only comfortable sitting up and leaning forward
  • No SOB, palpitations, light-headedness or fainting; recent 2 days of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea
  • No prior medical issues, medications, allergies; no smoking/marijuana/alcohol/IV drugs; no family history
  • Exam: BP 124/56 (similar both arms), HR 95, SpO2 99%, RR 20, afebrile; scratchy sound in systole and diastole; JVP normal, no pedal edema, chest clear, no rashes, no inflamed joints
  • Labs: WBC 17, ESR 65, CRP 15 (all elevated); troponin normal
  • ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression, PR elevation (aVR)

blocks.alt: Case 1 ECG with diffuse ST elevation and PR depression

blocks.html:
• CXR: normal · Echo: trace pericardial effusion
  • Meets the “2 of 4” criteria (pleuritic pain, rub, widespread ST elevation/PR depression, effusion)
  • Diagnosis: acute pericarditis in the setting of viral illness
Case 2: breathless with muffled heart sounds
  • 55-year-old woman: progressive SOB (exertion → rest); light-headed walking; no ankle swelling, chest pain, palpitations or syncope
  • 6-month “nagging” cough, sometimes hemoptysis (“smoker’s cough”); unintentional 15 lb weight loss; no fevers or night sweats; no medications or allergies
  • Exam: looks uncomfortable; BP 85/73, HR 120, SpO2 95%, RR 38, afebrile; JVP elevated; muffled heart sounds; chest clear
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, electrical alternans · CXR: ↑ cardiac silhouette · Echo: large effusion, swinging heart, signs of tamponade
  • Management: urgent bedside pericardiocentesis
    • Fluid: bloody, low glucose, fluid:serum LDH 0.8 (high), protein high (malignancy)
    • Cytology: lung adenocarcinoma · CT chest: mass consistent with lung adenocarcinoma

Module questions
  • 48. 4 causes of pericarditis: viral/bacterial infections, lupus, metastatic tumours, renal failure, post-pericardiotomy syndrome, chemotherapy agents
  • 49. Which is part of the diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis – pericardial rub, ST elevation in the inferior leads only, chest heaviness, elevated troponin? Pericardial rub → the others are pleuritic chest pain, new widespread ST elevation or PR depression, and pericardial effusion
  • 50. Beck’s triad: low BP, high JVP, muffled heart sounds
  • 51. 4 common causes of constrictive pericarditis: pericarditis, idiopathic, post-cardiotomy, chest irradiation (mantle radiation for lymphoma), rheumatologic (RA, lupus), end-stage renal disease, malignancy, TB (most common in developing countries)

lectures.name: Endocarditis

blocks.html:
Definition

Endocarditis: infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, one or more heart valves, or an indwelling cardiac device, with local collection of fibrinous material and superimposed infection.

Epidemiology
  • Incidence 1970-2000: 5-7 cases per 100 000 person-years
  • Incidence since 2000: 15 cases per 100 000 person-years
  • Typical patient: male, mean age 67 years
  • Younger patients: developing countries, underprivileged socioeconomic demographic

rows: Congenital heart disease: bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, ventricular septal defect
Acquired valvular heart disease: rheumatic heart disease, previous endocarditis, prosthetic cardiac valves
Immunocompromised, IVDU, indwelling vascular catheters or devices, septicemia
Dental procedures, body piercing, skin wounds, systemic sepsis, genitourinary instrumentation, endoscopies

blocks.html:
Microorganisms: native valve
  • Streptococcus: S. pneumoniae, S. bovis
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Enterococcus
  • HACEK organisms (7-21 day incubation time): Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Haemophilus aphrophilus, Haemophilus paraphrophilus; Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans; Cardiobacterium hominis; Eikenella corrodens; Kingella kingae
  • Culture negative: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), Bartonella quintana, Brucella, Chlamydia, Legionella, Tropheryma whipplei
Microorganisms: IVDU
  • S. aureus, G-ve rods; usually the tricuspid valve (right side)

blocks.lead: Prosthetic valve endocarditis: organisms in order of frequency (CNST = coagulase-negative staphylococci).
rows: CNST > S. aureus > G-ve bacilli > Enterococcus = fungi = diphtheroids > HACEK > polymicrobial > Streptococcus spp
CNST > S. aureus = Enterococcus = fungi > Streptococcus spp > HACEK = polymicrobial > G-ve bacilli = diphtheroids
Streptococcus spp > S. aureus > CNST > Enterococcus > G-ve bacilli = HACEK = polymicrobial > diphtheroids > fungi

blocks.title: Pattern to remember
blocks.html: Early prosthetic valve IE is dominated by CNST (skin flora seeded at surgery); by late (> 60 days) the order reverts toward the native-valve pattern, led by streptococci.

Pathophysiology: how a vegetation forms
  • Normal valvular endothelium is smooth and resistant to bacterial colonization
  • Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) follows damage to the vascular surface:
    • Systemic disease states (rheumatic carditis)
    • Mechanical injury by catheters or electrodes
    • Injury from repeated injections of solid particles in IVDU
  • Transient bacteremia → microorganism-NBTE interaction
  • Platelet aggregation and evolution of the vegetation
  • Biofilm formation: makes the vegetation more resistant to antibiotic therapy

blocks.alt: Pathogenesis of infective endocarditis: bloodstream access, adherence, persistence, proliferation, dissemination
blocks.cap: Pathogenesis: pathogens gain transient access to the bloodstream (IV line, injection, mouth), then (b) adhere to an injured or inflamed valve surface, (c) persist, (d) proliferate into a vegetation and (e) disseminate as emboli.

flowchart TD A["Normal valve endothelium
smooth, resists colonization"] --> B["Damage to vascular surface"] C["Rheumatic carditis"] --> B D["Catheters or electrodes"] --> B E["Injected solid particles in IVDU"] --> B B --> F["Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis
NBTE"] G["Transient bacteremia
dental, piercing, wounds, GU, endoscopy"] --> H["Microorganism-NBTE interaction"] F --> H H --> I["Platelet aggregation
vegetation evolves"] I --> J["Biofilm formation
resists antibiotics"] I --> K["Septic emboli
systemic spread"]

blocks.html:
Symptoms
  • Acute: fulminant septic illness with emboli, valve destruction, and cardiac decompensation
  • Subacute: non-specific constitutional symptoms: anorexia/weight loss, fevers/chills/night sweats, fatigue/general malaise, flu-like illness, cardiac decompensation (shortness of breath, edema)
Clinical findings
  • Peripheral stigmata: septic emboli, finger clubbing, subungual hematoma, splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots, Janeway lesions
  • Cardiac decompensation: tachycardia, new murmur, peripheral edema, weight gain (fluid retention), pulmonary edema
  • Sepsis: fever, organ-specific infective syndromes secondary to emboli

blocks.lead: History and physical exam: search every system for emboli and heart failure.
rows: Level of consciousness, mental status, vitals
Fundoscopy for Roth spots, conjunctival hemorrhage, neck stiffness, oral mucosal petechiae
Stroke, focal neurological symptoms (vegetations may have spread systemically)
JVP, S3, regurgitant murmur, volume status
Septic emboli to lungs: cough, sputum production
Septic emboli to joints: joint pain
Bloody diarrhea from septic emboli, abdominal pain

blocks.alt: Clinical manifestations and complications of infective endocarditis by organ
blocks.cap: Where the emboli land: Roth spots (retina), embolic stroke with hemorrhagic conversion and pyogenic brain abscess, septic pulmonary emboli, splenic infarcts, peripheral infarcts of the fingers; in the heart, a perforated aortic leaflet, a mitral vegetation and a vegetation on a pacemaker lead.

blocks.html:
Differential diagnosis
  • With bacteremia: intravascular catheter infection, cardiac device infection, prosthetic joint infection, hematogenous osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis, infected arterial aneurysm
  • Without bacteremia: systemic lupus erythematosus, Hodgkin's disease

Investigations
  • Bloodwork: CBC, coagulation, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, cancer antigen profile, liver enzymes, lactate, albumin, cardiac enzymes, ESR, complement, rheumatoid factor
  • Pan-culture: 3 blood cultures for extended growth (2 bottles, 3 sites, 3 times in the first hour if very sick), urine culture, sputum culture
  • ECG and CXR: may show conduction disease that can accompany abscess formation, or septic emboli
Echocardiography (as soon as possible once IE is suspected)
  • Evaluate valvular dysfunction, assess hemodynamic severity of valve lesions, assess underlying ventricular function, detect associated abnormalities (shunts)
  • Follow-up of patients with persistent or recurrent bacteremia or other clinical deterioration
  • False negatives if vegetations are small or have already embolized
  • Warranted even when an associated condition already requires a protracted antimicrobial course (e.g. vertebral osteomyelitis)

rows:
Negative or technically inadequate TTE with high clinical suspicion
Concern for intracardiac complications
Significant valvular regurgitation, to decide need for surgery
Cardiac device and persistent fever, even without new murmur or bacteremia
Superior for cardiac complications: abscess, leaflet perforation, aortic pseudoaneurysm, intracardiac fistula
Blood culture positive for IE with a typical organism from 2 separate blood cultures
Persistently positive blood cultures for any organism (at least 2 positive cultures of samples drawn > 12 h apart)
Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase I IgG antibody titer > 1:800
Vascular phenomena: arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions
Echocardiogram positive for IE: vegetation, abscess, new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve, or new valve regurgitation
Immunological phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor, glomerulonephritis
Microbiological evidence (incl. a positive blood culture) not meeting major criteria

Firm alternative diagnosis present
Signs/symptoms resolve with 4 days of antibiotic therapy
No pathological evidence of IE at surgery (with 4 days of antibiotic therapy)
Criteria for possible IE not met

+ TTE"] B --> C["Count Duke major and minor criteria"] C --> D{"2 major, 1 major + 3 minor,
or 5 minor?"} D -->|"Yes"| E["DEFINITE IE"] D -->|"No"| F{"1 major + 1 minor,

blocks.html:
Treatment: antibiotics
  • 6-12 weeks of IV antibiotics
    • Native valve endocarditis: IV vancomycin + IV cefepime
    • Prosthetic valve endocarditis: IV vancomycin + IV cefepime
    • Culture-negative endocarditis: IV vancomycin, IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin or doxycycline
Treatment: indications for surgery
  • Heart failure: valve dysfunction or intracardiac fistula causing pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock
  • Persistent infection: enlarging vegetation or persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antibiotic therapy
  • Complication of infection: local uncontrolled infection resulting in abscess, heart block, or penetrating lesion
  • Prevention of embolism: mobile vegetation > 10 mm, especially on the anterior mitral leaflet and after a previous embolic episode

blocks.alt: Algorithm for timing of surgical intervention in infective endocarditis
blocks.cap: Timing of surgery: a major ischemic stroke or intracranial hemorrhage delays surgery at least 4 weeks; HF from valve dysfunction, resistant organism (S. aureus, fungi), heart block/abscess, persistent infection or relapsing PVE means early surgery; large mobile or recurrent-embolizing vegetations mean consider early surgery; otherwise continue antibiotics, reassess and consider re-imaging.

blocks.html:
Prophylaxis
  • Amoxicillin, or clindamycin with a penicillin allergy
  • Dental procedures: dental extractions; subgingival scaling; manipulation of the gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or oral mucosa
  • High-risk patients: prosthetic heart valve/valve repair, prior endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or residual shunt
  • Moderate risk: unoperated heart valve disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Case example: IE with embolic and valvular complications

A 55-year-old man presented with fatigue, weight loss, and back pain. Blood cultures grew viridans group streptococcus; imaging showed osteomyelitis of L2-L3. Started on ceftriaxone 2 g daily, then developed clinical signs of biventricular failure.

Echo findings

  • Mildly dilated LV with normal systolic function; mildly dilated RV with normal systolic function
  • Thickened mitral valve; large (24 mm × 4 mm) mobile echodensities consistent with vegetations; moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation
  • Thickened aortic cusps with a large (15 mm × 5 mm) mobile echodensity on the left coronary cusp; large central orifice from aortic cusp destruction; severe aortic regurgitation

Course in hospital

  • Stroke: CT showed multifocal hemorrhages of the right parietotemporal lobe from septic emboli with hemorrhagic transformation; MRI showed right parietal hemorrhages with a possible small mycotic aneurysm
  • Surgery: aortic and mitral valve replacement; abscess of the mitral valve leaflet
  • Prolonged QTc and an episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; ICD implanted

Meet the patient: bicuspid aortic valve in heart failure

A 48-year-old man presents to the ED with worsening dyspnea: increasing exertional dyspnea, peripheral edema and orthopnea progressive over 2 months; now limited by dyspnea on minimal exertion. His family physician prescribed antibiotics 2 weeks ago for a presumed lower respiratory tract infection.

History

  • Appendectomy age 18
  • Diabetes mellitus diagnosed 1 year ago; metformin 500 mg BID
  • Seasonal allergies: OTC cetirizine
  • Lives with his wife in a rural community about an hour from hospital
  • Smokes 10-15 cigarettes/day for 30 years

Examination

  • Diaphoretic and tachypneic at rest
  • HR 110 bpm; BP 102/64 mm Hg; RR 24/min; SpO2 89% on room air, 94% on 2 L by nasal prongs; T 36.6°C
  • Normal S1, diminished S2, no S3/S4. III/IV late-peaking systolic murmur at the left sternal border, with a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur loudest in the 3rd/4th intercostal space
  • Carotid pulse diminished with slow upstroke; brachio-radial delay; JVP 6 cm above the sternal angle; 1+ bilateral lower-extremity edema
  • Chest: equal expansion, widespread crackles with mild wheeze. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or masses. Neuro: alert, oriented, no focal deficits

Test results

  • ECG: sinus tachycardia 110 bpm, LVH criteria; no Q waves or significant ST changes
  • CXR: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe vascular redistribution, Kerley B lines
  • Labs: CBC, creatinine and electrolytes normal; troponin 80 (14)
  • ABG: pH 7.38, PO2 65 mm Hg, PCO2 40 mm Hg, HCO3 23 mEq/L

Case questions

1. Volume status? Overloaded/hypervolemic, suggested by the history and confirmed by elevated venous pressure, lung crepitations and peripheral edema. (Other options: euvolemic, hypovolemic.)

2. Most likely valve pathology? Bicuspid aortic valve disease: aortic stenosis + aortic regurgitation. Late-peaking systolic murmur, diminished S2, diminished carotid upstroke and brachio-radial delay indicate significant AS; an early diastolic decrescendo murmur loudest in the 3rd/4th intercostal space fits AR.

  • Distractors: rheumatic mitral disease (MS + MR); carcinoid heart disease (pulmonic stenosis + TR); endocarditis of mitral and aortic valves (AR + MR); endocarditis of tricuspid and pulmonic valves (TR + PR)

3. Preferred diagnostic test? Transthoracic echocardiogram: he presents with heart failure, and echo shows whether it is ventricular or valvular; TTE is preferred over TEE because it is non-invasive.

  • Coronary angiogram: may help later if this proved a myocardial problem, to separate ischemic from non-ischemic causes
  • Treadmill stress ECG: breathless at rest, could not perform it; likely non-diagnostic
  • Nuclear myocardial perfusion scan: cannot exclude valvular disease
  • Cardiac MRI: could separate ventricular from valvular disease, but he cannot currently lie flat

4. Initial management (pick two)? Supplemental oxygen by face mask (he is hypoxic) and IV diuretic (he is volume overloaded).

  • Other options: non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP); intubation and ventilation
  • Beta-blockade: his tachycardia is a physiological response to heart failure; rate-controlling him now could cause further decompensation
  • IV nitroglycerin: helpful in heart failure but contraindicated in severe aortic stenosis

He improves. Echo: low-normal LV systolic function (LVEF 50-55%), bicuspid aortic valve with severe stenosis and moderate regurgitation.

5. Next step? Admit for further investigation: he is clinically in heart failure and needs diuresis and work-up of his valve disease. Discharging on oral furosemide with GP or cardiology follow-up is wrong.

After diuresis, catheterization shows an 80% proximal LAD and a 90% mid RCA stenosis.

6. Refer for? Cardiac surgery: aortic valve replacement + coronary artery bypass (what he received).

  • PCI to LAD and RCA alone: does not fix the dominant valvular problem
  • Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty: only temporary improvement in AS, and may worsen his moderate AR (also rules out PCI + valvuloplasty)
  • TAVI: a good procedure but not appropriate for him now: he is young and valve life expectancy is short (also rules out PCI + TAVI)

7. Mechanical vs bioprosthetic valve? Mechanical valves are more durable and long lasting but require chronic anticoagulation with warfarin. Younger patients should be primarily considered for mechanical valves unless anticoagulation is contraindicated. (The question also asks you to list complications of both valve types.)

8. Two months after mechanical AVR + CABG he develops ongoing fevers and chills. Likely diagnosis? Prosthetic valve endocarditis, which can be early or late. He needs blood cultures and an echocardiogram, possibly a TEE.

blocks.title: Fever after valve replacement
blocks.html: New fever in a patient with a prosthetic valve is prosthetic valve endocarditis until proven otherwise: blood cultures and echo (low threshold for TEE) before antibiotics are assumed to be for something else.

Atherosclerosis

Atherosclerosis: a systemic disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which plaque (fatty substances, cholesterol, cellular waste products, calcium, fibrin) builds up slowly, over decades, in the inner lining of the arteries, causing them to thicken or harden.

blocks.alt: Histology of arteries with progressive atherosclerotic narrowing
blocks.cap: Arterial cross-sections (H&E) from normal to progressively larger intimal plaque, until only a pinhole lumen remains.

blocks.html:
Arterial wall layers
  • Tunica intima (inner layer): single layer of endothelial cells; where atherosclerosis occurs
  • Tunica media (middle layer): involuntary smooth muscle that expands and contracts

blocks.alt: Layers of the arterial wall: intima, media, adventitia
blocks.cap: Endothelium and internal elastic lamina form the intima; smooth muscle forms the media; the external elastic lamina separates media from adventitia.

blocks.html:
Atherogenesis: the process of atherosclerotic plaque formation
  • An exaggerated repair process (long-term, low-grade inflammation)
  • Players: platelets, macrophages, endothelium, smooth muscle cells, extracellular matrix, lipids, growth factors, cytokines
  1. Chronic endothelial injury: hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, homocysteine, hemodynamic factors, toxins, viruses, immune reactions
  2. Endothelial dysfunction (increased permeability, leukocyte adhesion); monocyte and platelet adhesion and emigration
  3. Smooth muscle emigration from media to intima; macrophage/histiocyte activation
  4. Macrophages and smooth muscle cells engulf lipid (cholesterol derived from the blood) → fatty streaks (e.g. aorta), the precursor lesion of an atherosclerotic plaque
  5. Smooth muscle proliferation, collagen and other ECM deposition, extracellular lipid → raised plaques

Histology: foamy macrophages/histiocytes and cholesterol clefts.

blocks.alt: Response-to-injury sequence of atherogenesis
blocks.cap: Response to injury: endothelial injury → monocyte and platelet adhesion → smooth muscle migration into the intima → lipid-laden cells form a fatty streak → fibrofatty atheroma with collagen, lymphocytes and lipid debris.

flowchart TD A["Risk factors
hyperlipidemia, HTN, smoking, homocysteine,
hemodynamic, toxins, viruses, immune"] --> B["1 Chronic endothelial injury"] B --> C["2 Endothelial dysfunction
permeability, leukocyte adhesion"] C --> D["Monocyte and platelet adhesion
and emigration"] D --> E["3 Smooth muscle migrates media to intima

blocks.alt: Timeline of atherosclerotic lesion progression by decade
blocks.cap: Plaque evolution over decades along a background of endothelial dysfunction: foam cells → fatty streak → intermediate lesion → atheroma (growth mainly by lipid accumulation), then fibrous plaque (smooth muscle and collagen) → complicated lesion/rupture (thrombosis, hematoma).

blocks.alt: Structure of a fibrous atherosclerotic plaque
blocks.cap: Plaque anatomy: a fibrous cap (smooth muscle cells, macrophages, foam cells, lymphocytes, collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, neovascularization) over a necrotic centre (cell debris, cholesterol crystals, foam cells, calcium), sitting on the media.

blocks.alt: Histology showing foamy macrophages and cholesterol clefts
blocks.cap: Plaque histology: foamy (lipid-laden) macrophages on the left; needle-shaped empty cholesterol clefts on the right.

blocks.html:
• Risk factors accelerate progression
  • Overall risk increases exponentially when risk factors are combined
  • Pathogenesis is multifactorial; the relative importance of specific genetic and external factors varies between individuals

blocks.alt: Bar chart of 10-year ischemic heart disease risk with combined risk factors
blocks.cap: Estimated 10-year ischemic heart disease risk climbs as factors stack: 8.7% (men) / 5.5% (women) at SBP 120 and cholesterol 220, up to 57.5% / 56.4% with SBP 160, cholesterol 260, HDL 35, diabetes and smoking.

blocks.html:
Important terms
  • Stenosis = narrowing
  • Ischemia = reduced blood supply
  • Necrosis = process of tissue death
  • Necrotic = adjective describing dead tissue
  • Infarction = process of tissue death due to ischemia (ischemic necrosis)
  • Infarct = lesion resulting from infarction

Manifestations of atherosclerosis
  • Plaque tends to develop in areas of turbulent flow (e.g. the carotid bifurcation)
  • Atherothrombosis of the extra-cranial cerebral arteries can cause arterioembolic TIA or ischemic stroke (< 25% of all ischemic strokes and TIA)
  • 1-year CV event rates increase with the number of symptomatic disease locations: risk rises sharply with diffuse vascular disease (p < 0.001)

blocks.alt: Clinical manifestations of atherothrombosis by vascular territory
blocks.cap: Atherothrombosis by territory: ischemic stroke and TIA, MI and stable/unstable angina, peripheral arterial disease with intermittent claudication, rest pain, gangrene and necrosis.

blocks.alt: Gross specimen of carotid bifurcation atheroma
blocks.cap: Carotid bifurcation atheroma: yellow plaque at the branch point, a site of turbulent flow.

blocks.alt: Gross specimen of atherosclerotic circle of Willis
blocks.cap: Circle of Willis with yellow atherosclerotic plaques along the basilar and cerebral arteries.

blocks.alt: Coronal brain section with left hemisphere infarct
blocks.cap: Infarct of the left hemisphere (ischemic stroke): softened, cavitating tissue in the lateral cortex.

blocks.alt: Foot with gangrene of the great toe
blocks.cap: Gangrene: black necrotic tissue of the great toe from peripheral arterial disease.

blocks.alt: Gross specimen of ischemic bowel
blocks.cap: Mesenteric vessel disease with ischemic gut: dark, hemorrhagic, infarcted bowel.

blocks.alt: Gross specimen of severely atherosclerotic aorta
blocks.cap: Opened aorta with extensive yellow atheromatous plaque and ulcerated, thrombus-covered lesions: the source of atheroemboli.

lectures.title: Infective Endocarditis (and Atherosclerosis)
lectures.framing: Infective endocarditis is infection of a damaged endocardial surface: injured endothelium forms a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus that transient bacteremia seeds into a vegetation. Everything follows from the vegetation: it destroys valves (heart failure), throws septic emboli (the peripheral signs) and hides in biofilm (weeks of IV antibiotics). The notes finish with atherosclerosis, a different chronic injury-and-repair disease of the arterial intima.
lectures.keypoints: Diagnose with Duke criteria: definite = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; majors are typical organism in 2 blood cultures, persistent bacteremia, Coxiella, or a positive echo. TTE first (sens 70%, spec 99+%); TEE (> 90%) for negative TTE with high suspicion, complications or devices. Early prosthetic IE is CNST; IVDU is S. aureus on the tricuspid valve. Treat with 6-12 weeks IV antibiotics; operate for HF, persistent infection, abscess/heart block, or vegetation > 10 mm, but delay at least 4 weeks after a major stroke or ICH. Atherosclerosis begins as chronic endothelial injury → fatty streak → fibrous plaque, and combined risk factors raise risk exponentially.

weeks.label: Week 3 - Ischemic Heart Disease & Vascular Pathology

lectures.name: Myocardial Infarction

blocks.html:
Coronary artery disease (CAD)
  • Coronary artery disease / ischemic heart disease: a group of cardiovascular diseases characterized by reduced blood supply to the heart – angina, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, sudden cardiac death
  • Death from heart disease has decreased due to less smoking, the importance of exercise, and pharmacological management (statins, antiplatelet agents) – but it still remains a common cause of mortality
  • Canada compares fairly well with other countries for heart-disease mortality
  • Every 26 seconds someone has an event; every 60 seconds someone dies from one
  • 1/5 deaths are from atherosclerotic disease; 37% of those who have an event die within a year

blocks.alt: Trends in age-standardized US death rates for the six leading causes of death, 1970-2002
blocks.cap: Heart-disease death rates fall steadily from 1970 to 2002 but remain the highest of the six leading causes.

blocks.html:
Coronary anatomy
  • Epicardial coronary arteries: run along the outer surface of the heart on the epicardium – right and left coronary arteries
  • Subendocardial zone: furthest from the blood supply; suffers first when circulation is compromised
  • The arrangement of the coronary circulation varies
  • Vascular territories overlap because of collateral vessels and anastomoses – the myocardium can tolerate some reduction or blockage without tissue damage
  • Coronary artery dominance: defined by the vessel that gives rise to the posterior descending artery, which supplies the myocardium of the posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum – RCA (85%), left circumflex (15%)

blocks.alt: Coronary artery anatomy: right coronary artery, left anterior descending, circumflex and their branches
blocks.cap: Right coronary (red) gives the AV nodal and posterior descending arteries; the left coronary (purple) divides into LAD and circumflex.

blocks.alt: Short-axis slice of the ventricles labelled with coronary territories
blocks.cap: Territories: anterior wall = LAD; septum = LAD (anterior 2/3) + RCA (posterior 1/3); lateral = circumflex; posterior = RCA.

blocks.html:
Coronary atherosclerosis
  • Vessels initially expand to accommodate plaque growth (compensatory enlargement) but eventually become stenosed
  • No symptoms until late in plaque formation – angina patients usually have > 70% narrowing
  • Disease is often in the proximal portions of medium and large arteries – reachable by surgery or catheters
  • Atheroma can be very focal along a coronary artery – the rate-limiting step for flow; normal flow can be restored locally with surgery
  • Many patients have severe disease in multiple vessels, which makes treatment much more challenging
  • Investigation of angina: treadmill stress testing (ECG), coronary angiography (contrast dye)
Measuring stenosis
  • Pathological assessment: percent reduction of cross-sectional lumen area compared with the normal vessel
  • Angiographic assessment: percent narrowing compared with the least stenosed area

blocks.lead: High-risk anatomic patterns – the thresholds that define them differ: 50% for left main, 70% elsewhere.

blocks.alt: Heart diagram with a stenosis in the left main coronary artery
blocks.cap: Left main stenosis.

blocks.alt: Heart diagram with stenoses in the proximal LAD and circumflex
blocks.cap: Left main equivalent: proximal LAD + circumflex.

blocks.alt: Heart diagram with stenoses in the LAD, circumflex and right coronary artery
blocks.cap: Triple vessel disease: LAD + circumflex + RCA.

blocks.alt: Heart diagram with stenoses in the LAD and right coronary artery
blocks.cap: Double vessel disease: here LAD + RCA.

blocks.html:
Surgical management: coronary angioplasty and stenting (PCI)
  • A catheter carrying a deflated balloon with a deployable stent around it is inserted and guided to the blocked artery
  • The balloon is inflated and expands the stent, which pushes the plaque against the sides of the artery and holds the vessel open
  • Plaques are intentionally ruptured and expanded by angioplasty, and may even dissect the vessel wall
  • Patients are anticoagulated to prevent thrombosis
  • Previously angioplastied and stented vessels can develop re-stenosis
  • Drug-coated stents are designed to reduce inflammation and slow re-stenosis
Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) – who benefits
  • Left main coronary stenosis, abnormal LV function, class III/IV angina

blocks.alt: Bar chart of months of survival gained with CABG by subgroup
blocks.cap: Survival gain from CABG is largest with left main disease (~19 months), then abnormal LV function; small for one/two-vessel disease.

blocks.alt: Cumulative total mortality, medicine vs CABG, over 12 years
blocks.cap: Pooled trials: mortality is lower with CABG than medicine for most of follow-up, with the curves converging by about 12 years.

blocks.html:
CABG procedure
  • A healthy vessel from elsewhere in the body is harvested and attached above and below the plaque to bypass the blockage
  • Most commonly the saphenous vein, radial artery, or internal thoracic (mammary) artery
  • 1998: endoscopic bypass-graft technique for taking out the saphenous vein – limited pain, infection and edema; quality identical to the open technique
  1. Vein harvest: incision above the knee; a fiberoptic scope is slid between the fat layer and the top of the vein. If more vein is needed, a counter-incision is made, the scope reinserted, and dissection continues towards the groin. Once dissection is complete and all branches divided, the vein is pulled out of the original incision and divided
  2. Median sternotomy (“mediastinotomy” in the source) with a reciprocating saw; sternal edges opened
  3. Internal thoracic artery is taken down and its branches divided; it stays attached at the axillary artery (as written in the source) and goes to the LAD
  4. Cannulation: pericardium opened; purse string in the upper ascending aorta for the arterial cannula of the heart-lung machine (brings in oxygenated, heated blood); aorta incised with a scalpel, cannula introduced and purse strings snugged down to secure it
  5. Venous outflow via the atrial appendage – purse string placed, appendage opened, larger cannula placed
  6. Vent placed in the mid ascending aorta; once on the heart-lung machine the aorta is cross-clamped and the heart arrested with high-potassium cardioplegia
  7. Distal anastomosis: coronary opened beyond the narrowing; anastomosis (5-6 mm) with 8-0 prolene continuous stitch. Quality can be checked with a flow probe (82 mL/min = exceptionally good graft)
  8. Proximal anastomosis: internal thoracic arteries keep their own blood supply, but radial arteries and saphenous veins do not – they are sewn to the aorta with 6-0 prolene continuous stitch
  9. Cross-clamp removed; blood flows back down the aorta through the coronary arteries and the bypass graft
  10. Once the heart is beating well, heart-lung machine flow is decreased, cannulas removed, and purse strings tightened (hemostasis)
  11. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin – allows clot formation
  12. Sternal edges brought together with stainless steel wires and the incision closed – can be painful for 3 weeks (divided bone)

blocks.html:
CABG mortality
  • Overall mortality after CABG is 2% – low mortality and low complication rates
  • Predictors of operative mortality: urgency of operation, older age, redo cardiac operation, female sex (more diffuse disease, smaller coronary arteries), LV ejection fraction, left main coronary stenosis, diabetes, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease
  • Predictors of late mortality: older age, LV ejection fraction, no internal thoracic artery graft, smoking, triple vessel disease/left main stenosis, hypertension, high cholesterol, incomplete revascularization, diabetes

rows:
Worst possible complication – risk of stroke during CABG, and aortic atherosclerosis, increase with age
Causes: emboli (ascending-aorta plaque compressed by the clamp embolizes on removal), hypotension, hypoxia
After a CVA: mortality 21%; 2-fold longer hospital stay; 6-fold more likely to be discharged to a nursing home

3% reoperation rate for hemorrhage
10% of blood transfusions go to cardiac surgery patients – 20% of cardiac patients use 80% of the blood products
Transfusion risks: older age, female, anemia, ASA, urgency, duration of CPB, recent thrombolytic therapy, reoperation, clopidogrel < 4 days ago, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab; prevent platelet aggregation)
Transfusion in CABG is associated with reduced long-term survival

Any operation has a risk of infection
Common sites: pneumonia (10%), wound (10%), urinary tract (4%), mediastinitis (1.5%)
• Mediastinitis: rare but devastating – mortality rises to 15-25%; reoperation with debridement and IV antibiotics for a minimum of 6 weeks
• Predictors: obesity, diabetes, previous cardiac surgery, significant post-operative bleeding, long operation, bilateral internal thoracic arteries (controversial)
Listed as a complication (no further detail in the note)
70% have changes at 1 month and 30% at 9 months – all patients are the same at 6 years

blocks.html:
CABG outcomes
  • Survival: 5-year = 92%, 10-year = 81%
  • Freedom from angina: 5-year = 83%, 10-year = 63%
  • One internal thoracic artery → 70% 12-year survival; bilateral internal thoracic arteries → 82% 12-year survival
Trends in revascularization
  • More arterial grafts (radial, bilateral internal thoracic), optimize graft patency, maximize quality of life, decrease the need for redo operation
  • Beating-heart surgery for a calcified aorta – no cannulation, cross-clamping or proximal anastomoses; benefits: decreased ICU/hospital stay, transfusions and delirium
    • Starfish = positioner – clamps the epicardium to help access vessels
    • Octopus = tissue stabilizer – straddles the coronary artery
  • ZEUS: Dr. Boyd (LHSC) performed the first robotically-assisted closed-chest beating-heart cardiac bypass operation
  • Da Vinci: surgeon sits at a console; hand motions on the gimbals move the robot
  • Automated anastomotic devices: punch in the aorta, place a preloaded stent with vein, push a button, and the stent comes out with an anastomosis; vein-graft thrombosis at the aorta was high, so it never took off commercially
Post-operative risk management
  • CABG is not a curative procedure
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, smoking cessation, referral to cardiac rehabilitation
  • Medical: ASA (lifelong), ticagrelor/clopidogrel (1 year), statins (lifelong), beta blockers (short term), ACEI (cardioprotective dose for life); SGLT2 inhibitors may be good; COMPASS medications (rivaroxaban 5 mg bid + ASA)

blocks.alt: Table of interventions found beneficial for post-CABG patients with class and level of evidence
blocks.cap: Class I, level A: antiplatelet therapy, ACE inhibitors, statins; lifestyle measures and beta-blockers are class I, level B.

blocks.html:
CABG vs. PCI vs. medical management
  • SYNTAX trial: at 10 years, no significant difference in all-cause death between PCI (first-generation paclitaxel-eluting stents) and CABG; however, CABG gave a significant survival benefit in three-vessel disease, but not in left main coronary artery disease
  • Diabetic patients do better with CABG than PCI

Module questions (CAD and CABG)
  1. Which statement is true?
    a) Coronary atherosclerosis is unique to the heart
    b) Following an MI it is unusual to have another atherosclerotic related event
    c) Total body atherosclerotic burden is inversely correlated to survival
    d) Cancer is a more common cause of death in North America
    e) CABG is the preferred treatment for isolated LAD stenosis
  2. Which statement is true?
    a) Minimally invasive conduit harvesting is cosmetically superior but slightly inferior in quality compared to traditional open techniques
    b) CABG is a profoundly fun operation but does not provide a survival benefit in most patients, only improvement in quality of life
    c) Complications such as stroke, bleeding, renal failure and mediastinitis limit the benefit of CABG to a small subset of patients
    d) The use of multiple arterial grafts, compared to veins, improves survival and freedom from recurrent angina
  3. Which statement is true?
    a) Optimal therapy following CABG includes ASA, ACE, statins, and cardiac rehabilitation
    b) Angioplasty and CABG are equally effective treatment options for most patients
    c) Collaboration between cardiologists and cardiac surgeons does not tend to improve individual patient outcomes
    d) Pharmacologic therapy can replace the role of exercise, weight loss and smoking cessation

Myocardial infarction
  • Myocardial infarction (heart attack): necrosis of heart muscle due to reduced or inadequate blood flow
  • Acute myocardial infarct = ischemic heart disease + acute coronary thrombosis – occurs in most ST-elevation MIs
  • Chronic myocardial infarct = severe ischemic heart disease
  • After about 30 min of ischemia, the myocardium may be irreversibly damaged (infarcted, necrotic) – needs prompt thrombolytics (tPA) or PCI (angioplasty with stent)
  • Necrosis begins in the subendocardial zone and spreads to become transmural

blocks.alt: Progression from normal artery to fixed plaque, plaque disruption and thrombus in acute coronary syndromes
blocks.cap: Fixed obstruction causes typical angina; plaque disruption with mural thrombus gives unstable angina/NSTEMI, and occlusive thrombus gives transmural MI or sudden death.

blocks.alt: Wavefront of necrosis from subendocardium to transmural infarct over 0, 2 and 24 hours
blocks.cap: Necrosis starts subendocardially and spreads outward until, by about 24 h, it can involve nearly the entire area at risk.

blocks.alt: Graph of salvageable vs dead myocardium over hours after occlusion
blocks.cap: The reversible phase is short: salvageable myocardium falls steeply over the first few hours – the reason reperfusion is time-critical.

rows:
Early MI: loss of banding in cardiomyocytes – probably a couple of days old
Cardiac enzymes rise as coagulation necrosis occurs and cell membranes become leaky
Vascular phase (vasodilation, edema); polymorphonuclear then mononuclear leukocytes

Early coagulation necrosis with neutrophils arriving – 12-24 h
Fully developed coagulation necrosis with maximal neutrophil infiltrate – 2-3 days
Macrophages phagocytose dead muscle
Neovasculature; fibroblast proliferation producing collagen, proteoglycans and myofibroblasts
Healing postero-lateral MI; dead muscle being replaced by fibrous tissue
Collagen remodelling, loss of blood vessels

Healed infarct / fibrous scar (turquoise collagen on connective-tissue stain) – 3-6 months
Large healed posterior-wall transmural MI scar
blocks.lead: Stages of MI healing – muscle does not regenerate; it is replaced by scar.

flowchart LR A["Coronary occlusion"] --> B["Stage I: ischemic injury
irreversible after ~30 min
necrosis, leaky membranes, enzymes rise"] B --> C["Stage II: inflammation
neutrophils 12-24 h

blocks.html:
MI pathophysiology
  • Major mechanism: plaque rupture with thrombus formation
  • Vulnerable plaque: fibrofatty plaques (thin fibrous cap; soft, lipid-rich, thrombogenic core) with high inflammation are more prone to rupture and thrombosis than fibrous plaques (calcified, stable)
  • Trigger to rupture: hemodynamic stress (shear stress on the plaque) or immune/inflammatory mediated
  • Plaques need not be flow-limiting before rupture – most occur in lesions < 50% stenosed

rows:
Plaque rupture/erosion with occlusive thrombus → STEMI
Plaque rupture/erosion with non-occlusive thrombus → NSTEMI
Atherosclerosis + oxygen supply/demand imbalance – e.g. a stenotic, fixed coronary lesion that cannot increase flow when demand rises

blocks.alt: Table classifying causes of myocardial injury (troponin elevation)
blocks.cap: Troponin rises in four groups: primary ischemia (plaque rupture), supply/demand imbalance, non-ischemic injury (contusion, myocarditis, cardiotoxins), and multifactorial (HF, Takotsubo, PE, sepsis, renal failure).

blocks.html:
Infrequent causes of MI
  • Fixed, severe coronary narrowing subjected to a sudden decrease in supply (blood loss) or increase in demand (exercise)
  • Primary coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal’s) – rare
  • Anomalous coronary arteries (young person) – rare
  • Embolus – clot in the LV or LA from atrial fibrillation or endocarditis
  • Cocaine – can induce spasm and thrombosis; suspect in the appropriate setting/population
Sudden cardiac death
  • Death within 1 hour of symptoms
  • Low incidence of MI and coronary thrombosis; high incidence of severe coronary atherosclerosis
  • Mechanism of death: arrhythmia – ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation
The big picture
  • Atherosclerosis → ischemic heart disease ± acute coronary thrombosis → myocardial infarction
  • Prevention is the best strategy – understand how risk factors influence pathogenesis
  • Many therapeutic options exist for established disease

fixed stenosis"] B -->|"fibrofatty, thin cap,

subendocardial"] C -->|"demand rises or

supply/demand imbalance"] J["Vasospasm, dissection,

rows:
Airway, breathing, circulation; BP (SBP difference > 20 mmHg between arms = think aortic dissection), HR (inferior MI = bradycardia, anterior MI = tachycardia), RR, temperature, O2 saturation
Oxygen by face mask; cardiac and O2-saturation monitors; good IV access ×2
Treat sustained ventricular arrhythmia rapidly (ACLS protocol)
ASA loading dose = 162-325 mg orally unless aortic dissection is being considered; rectal suppository if oral not feasible; clopidogrel if allergic
Presenting symptoms, PMHx, cardiac risk factors, medications, allergies

Classic presentation: > 15-30 min of crushing retrosternal chest pain or tightness – may radiate to shoulder, arm, forearm (L > R); ± shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea/vomiting
Other presentations: pain in other locations – back (think aortic dissection), neck/jaw, epigastrium; syncope or cardiac arrest – VT/VF (anterior MI), bradycardia (inferior MI); shock – low BP, reduced tissue perfusion; malaise – atypical presentation in older adults; silent – diabetic patients

Baseline neurologic function, particularly if fibrinolysis is planned
Heart failure: S3 or S4, JVD, pulmonary rales; signs of hemodynamic compromise
Pansystolic murmur (rare) – MR, ventricular septal rupture; exclude aortic dissection if an aortic-insufficiency murmur is heard
Pericardial rub is a late finding (> 24 h)

12-lead ECG within 10 min of arrival; repeat every 10 min if non-diagnostic but suspicion remains high
ST elevation – may have reciprocal ST depression in some leads; if ST segments are diffusely up across leads, think of other causes (pericarditis)
Q waves develop if reperfusion is not established – indicate necrosis and are permanent; pathologic = > 3 mm deep or > 1/3 the height of the R wave

Baseline cardiac biomarkers (troponin), electrolytes, coagulation studies, hemoglobin
Troponin may not be elevated/detectable for several hours after pain onset – do NOT wait for bloodwork to diagnose a STEMI
Consider the diagnosis: women, the elderly and patients with diabetes may have atypical presentations

Hx, PEx and ECG; presentation consistent with acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
Criteria: ST elevation of 1 mm (0.1 mV) in 2 anatomically contiguous leads, 2 mm (0.2 mV) in V2 and V3, or new LBBB
Complete occlusion: > 90% thrombotic arterial occlusion (common) or primary vasospasm (rare)

blocks.title: Do not wait for troponin
blocks.html: Troponin may be undetectable for hours after pain onset. STEMI is diagnosed on Hx, PEx and ECG – waiting for bloodwork delays reperfusion.

blocks.alt: List of false-positive and false-negative causes of ST elevation for MI
blocks.cap: ST-elevation mimics: early repolarization, LBBB, pre-excitation, Brugada, pericarditis, PE, SAH, hyperkalemia; prior MI with persistent ST elevation, RV pacing and LBBB can mask an MI.

rows: Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL ×3, q 5 min; add IV nitroglycerin for persistent chest discomfort, hypertension or HF – only if no hemodynamic compromise (hypotension or RV infarction)
AVOID generally; only if hypertensive, no signs of HF, not at high risk of HF, and no hemodynamic compromise, bradycardia or severe reactive airway disease – speak to a cardiologist first
Afterload reduction – nitroglycerin SL and/or IV; loop diuretic (furosemide IV)
Sit upright (reduce preload); furosemide 40-120 mg IV ± Foley catheter; morphine 2-4 mg IV q 5-10 min; consider BiPAP
Metoprolol IV – can result in shock; speak to a cardiologist first
Significant – reduces the amount of necrosis
Moderate – may reduce the amount of necrosis
blocks.lead: STEMI management: reperfusion. Re-establishing effective flow relieves pain, preserves myocardium and saves lives – benefit depends on time from pain onset.

blocks.html:
Reperfusion options
  • Primary PCI (coronary angioplasty and stenting) – gold standard; especially for large MI (especially anterior with marked ST elevation), cardiogenic shock, contraindication to thrombolysis
  • Fibrinolysis (thrombolytic therapy) – when primary PCI is unavailable or too far away/delayed
    • IV agents that dissolve fibrin – tenecteplase (TNK), tissue plasminogen activator derivatives (TNK, tPA, RPA), streptokinase
    • Complete restoration of flow in 50-55%; bleeding can occur (1% risk of stroke)
    • Effectiveness seen within 30-60 min
    • Criteria: 30 min of ischemic pain; ≥ 1 mm (0.1 mV) localized ST elevation in ≥ 2 contiguous leads (including posterior leads) or new LBBB; no contraindications (bleeding risk); within 12 h of onset – 24 h if ongoing pain + ST elevation
    • Signs of reperfusion: pain improves; ST reduction ≥ 50%; accelerated idioventricular rhythm (wide complex, HR 80-110 bpm)
  • Rescue PCI (thrombolytic failure): ongoing/unresolved ischemic pain; persistent ST elevation (> 50% of peak)
Adjunctive therapy
  • 2nd antiplatelet (in addition to ASA): clopidogrel if thrombolysis; clopidogrel, ticagrelor or prasugrel if primary PCI is planned
  • Anticoagulation (with thrombolysis): unfractionated heparin or LMWH (enoxaparin)

Module questions (MI)
  1. Which of the following (coronary plaque erosion, coronary plaque rupture, coronary plaque progression causing progressive stenosis, coronary vasospasm, anemia) best describes the most common pathophysiologic mechanism present during STEMI? Coronary plaque rupture
  2. What type of myocardial infarction is seen in this ECG? Anterolateral STEMI – ST elevation in leads V2-V6, I and aVL

blocks.alt: 12-lead ECG for module question 5

blocks.html:
1. What vessel is involved (occluded) in the previous case? Left anterior descending artery (LAD)
  2. Which of the following ECG patterns is consistent with those seen in NSTEMI?
    a) Wellen’s phenomenon (biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in the anterior precordial leads) → frequently indicates a significant stenosis in the proximal LAD
    b) Isolated T wave flattening or inversion
    c) Downsloping ST segment depression
    d) Normal ST segments and T waves
  3. Which approach to medical therapy is appropriate for a patient admitted with STEMI after primary PCI?
    a) Beta-blockers should be commenced (unless there is decompensated heart failure or significant hypotension or bradycardia) and have been shown to improve survival
    b) ACE inhibitors should be used in most patients following STEMI, particularly with hypertension, diabetes, LV systolic dysfunction (EF < 40%) and/or heart failure symptoms, in the absence of contraindication
    c) An aldosterone antagonist such as eplerenone should be commenced if there is LV systolic dysfunction (EF < 40%) and either diabetes or symptomatic heart failure, and no contraindication
    d) All patients should be on statin therapy unless contraindicated, regardless of LDL level
    e) All of the above
  4. Which statement regarding fibrinolytic therapy is true?
    a) Fibrinolytic therapy has its greatest efficacy within the first 1 hour of symptom onset → may be considered within 24 hours of onset; the longer the time after onset, the less likely fibrinolysis succeeds
    b) Fibrinolytic therapy should not be used to treat STEMI if symptom onset was greater than 6 hours
    c) Simultaneous anticoagulation during fibrinolytic therapy is optional → it is always given, using unfractionated heparin or LMWH
    d) Fibrinolytic therapy is indicated for high-risk NSTEMI patients at facilities not capable of PCI → not indicated for NSTEMI in any situation
  5. What is the proper dose of initial aspirin therapy during STEMI? a) 75 mg b) 81 mg c) 162 mg d) 325 mg

Aneurysms
  • Aneurysm: a persistent, focal dilation of a vascular structure with an increase of ≥ 50% of its normal diameter, forming a blood-filled, balloon-like bulge in the vessel wall
  • Can occur anywhere in the arterial or venous system
  • The size that counts as an aneurysm depends on location and the vessel’s normal diameter
  • Ectasia: an enlarged vessel with < 50% increase in diameter – precursor to aneurysm formation
  • Most common locations: aorta (> 3 cm), iliac (> 1.8 cm), popliteal (> 1.5 cm)

blocks.cap: Location hints at cause: berry (circle of Willis), syphilis and dissection (thoracic aorta), mycotic, and atherosclerotic (infrarenal aorta).

blocks.html:
AAA repair
  • Prophylactic operation to prevent complications – AAAs are asymptomatic (pain and embolic consequences are very rare)
  • Individualized: risk of rupture vs. life expectancy and operative risk of death
  • Aneurysm < 5 cm = watch and wait with yearly imaging
  • Indications for repair of an infrarenal degenerative AAA:
    • Size: ≥ 5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women – 4 RCTs confirm no survival benefit from repairing smaller aneurysms, even with endovascular repair
    • Significant growth: > 1 cm in a year
    • Higher rupture risk: symptoms, saccular morphology
    • Rupture
    • Fit for operation: no severe end-organ disease – CHF, COPD, ESRD, cirrhosis

rows: Dacron vascular graft, manually sewn into the aorta; aneurysm excluded from circulation
Stent placed by catheter under x-ray guidance
Minimally invasive – patient preference; not all patients are candidates (anatomy)
Yearly surveillance imaging; 10-20% re-intervention risk; endoleaks (blood flow outside the graft within the sac)

blocks.html:
AAA complications
  • Rupture: often lethal – overall mortality 80%; 40-50% among those who reach hospital
    • Presents with hypotension, abdominal pain radiating to the back, and a pulsatile abdominal mass – urgent surgical emergency
    • No such thing as a stable or leaking aneurysm – all are ruptured and presumed dead until proven otherwise
    • Median survival without repair = 6-8 hours; many die within minutes
    • Bleeding may be retroperitoneal or free intraperitoneal
  • Fistulization (e.g. aorto-esophageal fistula): an abnormal connection between vessels or organs that do not usually connect, due to disease, trauma or surgery
  • Embolization: blockage of arteries
  • Infection
  • End-organ ischemia

blocks.title: Ruptured AAA
blocks.html: Hypotension + abdominal pain radiating to the back + pulsatile mass = ruptured AAA until proven otherwise. There is no “stable leak”; median survival without repair is 6-8 h.

Thoracic aneurysms
  • More likely in women and in patients with aortic dissection, connective tissue disorders, FHx and multiple aneurysms
  • Benefits of endovascular over open repair are even greater – less death, major morbidity and paraplegia
  • Larger size threshold to operate: 6-6.5 cm

blocks.alt: Stages of endovascular stent-graft repair of a descending thoracic aortic aneurysm
blocks.cap: Thoracic EVAR: the stent-graft is advanced over a wire and deployed across the aneurysm.

blocks.html:
Thoracoabdominal aneurysms
  • Aneurysmal change of both the thoracic and abdominal aorta (entire aorta)
  • Very difficult to treat – endovascular and open repair are both complex with high mortality and morbidity
  • Open repair mortality = 10-20%; paraplegia = 10-20%
Popliteal aneurysms
  • Associated with AAA – 30-50% also have an AAA; all should be screened for AAA
  • Main concern is embolic or thrombotic events with risk of limb loss (> 30%)
  • Indications to repair: less about size, more about thrombus load; evidence of previous embolization; size > 3-4 cm
  • Usually repaired with open bypass; endovascular repair used less because of occlusion risk

blocks.html:
Module questions (aneurysms)
  1. Most common type and location of aneurysm? Degenerative, infrarenal aortic
  2. Most common symptom of an infrarenal aortic aneurysm? No symptoms – most are asymptomatic; embolization is rare, and pain occurs only with rupture or pre-rupture in larger aneurysms and should be treated as a surgical emergency
  3. Gold-standard test to diagnose an aortic aneurysm? CT with IV contrast – most accurate size and allows surgical planning
  4. Which group is at highest risk and recommended for US screening? Men 65-74 years, particularly with a history of smoking
  5. At what size is infrarenal AAA repair recommended in men? Diameter > 5.5 cm – an imperfect metric, but diameter is the best and most used predictor of rupture; women > 5 cm
  6. A 78-year-old man with a 6 cm AAA and CHF, CAD and COPD wants repair. Best method? EVAR – with significant comorbidities, EVAR has lower mortality and morbidity than open repair; no proven medical therapy “shrinks” an aneurysm

Dissection
  • Dissection: a tear within the wall of a blood vessel that lets blood separate the wall layers
  • Two lumens – the true lumen and a newly created false lumen
Aortic dissection
  • Type A: proximal – tear starts in the ascending aorta → surgical graft repair
  • Type B: distal – tear starts in the descending aorta → medical BP and HR control
  • Presentation: sudden, sharp, tearing chest pain radiating to the back
  • Trauma can cause either aortic dissection or complete aortic laceration
  • Complications: rupture (proximal = hemopericardium; distal = hemothorax or hemoretroperitoneum), stroke, MI, chronic dissection (carotid extension = stroke; coronary extension = MI; double-barrel aorta)
  • Ix: CXR; CT angiogram (stable) or TEE (unstable)
