lectures.title: Coronary Artery Disease, Myocardial Infarction & Complications of Acute MI
lectures.framing: Coronary atherosclerosis becomes an emergency when a vulnerable plaque ruptures and thrombus forms: an occlusive thrombus gives a STEMI (reperfuse now), a non-occlusive one an NSTEMI (stabilize, then angiography). The note then follows the damage through healing and its complications, and closes with aortic aneurysm and dissection.
lectures.keypoints: Most MIs arise from plaques < 50% stenosed – rupture, not stenosis, is the trigger. STEMI is diagnosed on ECG, not troponin: ASA 162-325 mg, then primary PCI (gold standard) or fibrinolysis within 12 h; benefit is maximal within 1 h. Inferior MI + hypotension, JVD, clear lungs = RV infarct – fluids, no nitro. Post-MI: ASA + P2Y12 (12 months) + beta-blocker + ACEI + high-intensity statin regardless of LDL. AAA: repair at ≥ 5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women, or growth > 1 cm/yr; the leading cause of death on surveillance is cardiovascular, not rupture. Dissection: type A = surgery, type B = medical.

lectures.name: Cardiac Rehab & Secondary Prevention
lectures.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation, Secondary Prevention and Peripheral Vascular Disease
lectures.framing: What happens after the first vascular event: cardiac rehab and drugs to prevent the next one, then the limb version of the same disease. The organising idea: collaterals decide the presentation – an embolus into a normal artery is catastrophic, while slow atherosclerotic occlusion is often tolerated.
lectures.keypoints: After MI, risk of another MI is 5–7×. Cardiac rehab is class I, level A (18–26% ↓ mortality in trials; ~50% in real-world programs); prescribe by F.I.T.T. Acute limb ischemia: 6 Ps, necrosis within 6–8 h, heparin then revascularize, watch for compartment syndrome → fasciotomy. ABI < 0.5 = rest pain, < 0.3 = tissue loss. PAD management is ABCDES – smoking cessation most important. Fibrinolyse STEMI if PCI cannot happen within 120 min; RV infarct: no nitrates, give fluids.

blocks.lead: Why secondary prevention matters – one vascular event multiplies the risk of the next.

blocks.html:
Principles of risk reduction
  • Cardiac rehabilitation (CR): a lifestyle intervention program that includes secondary prevention; a systematic model of chronic vascular disease care with proactive disease surveillance via a multifaceted approach:
    • Comprehensive targeted cardiovascular risk factor therapies
    • Behaviour modification for sustainable lifestyle and pharmacological adherence
    • Therapeutic exercise and physical activity programs
  • Encourages healthy lifestyles; addresses anxiety and depression
  • Sensible regular exercise is key: exercise HR set from a treadmill test (10 bpm below the ischemic threshold); avoid sudden severe stressing
  • Mediterranean diet: mainly grains, fruits, beans and vegetables; moderate fish and cheese; plenty of olive oil and garlic; very little red meat; wine – men 2 glasses daily, women 1

blocks.alt: Cardiac rehabilitation model from inpatient identification to outpatient evaluation, exercise, risk factor modification and long-term goals
blocks.cap: Inpatient: identify, counsel, refer. Outpatient: evaluate → prescribe exercise → modify risk factors → set physical, vocational and psychological goals.

blocks.html:
Evidence for cardiac rehab
  • Exercise-based rehab vs usual care: 18–26% relative risk reduction in mortality and hospitalization
  • Toronto CR: 50% risk reduction in mortality; high-level participants saved $3000/year in health service costs
  • SJH Hybrid CR: 50% reduction in death or hospitalization for MI or HF; NNT 6 to prevent 1 death or readmission; if 500 SJH patients finish CR with > 0.5 MET gain each year, 80 fewer might die or be readmitted (5000 in Ontario)
  • Participation in CR = class I, level A recommendation
  • ≥ 5 sessions of habitual exercise/week: > 6 METs and MI risk within 1 hour = relative risk of 2.4
  • Relative risk of death at > 8 METs is substantially less than at < 5 METs, with any underlying condition (hypertension, COPD, diabetes, smoking, BMI, hyperlipidemia)
  • Initial CR fitness is important for survival; aim to improve fitness > 0.7 METs (VO2 change > 2.5 cc/kg/min)

rows: ≥ 5–10 min of cardiovascular and/or muscular endurance activity at a target HR of 20–35% of HRR

40–80% of HRR
50–80% VO2 max, HR max or HR reserve
Target HR = (intensity factor) × (peak HR – rest HR) + rest HR
Intensity factor: deconditioned → start at 50%, work up to 70%
6–10 exercises for upper and lower body
≥ 5–10 min of cardiovascular and/or muscular endurance activity at a target HR < 60% of HR max
blocks.lead: Exercise prescription – F.I.T.T. (frequency, intensity, time, type) inside a warm-up and cool-down

blocks.html:
Module questions – cardiac rehab
  • 21. After MI, relative increase in risk of a subsequent MI vs the pre-MI risk? 5–7×
  • 22. After MI, relative risk reduction in mortality from exercise-based CR in clinical trials? 20–30%
  • 23. After MI or angioplasty/stenting/CABG, relative risk reduction in readmission or mortality from exercise-based CR in the real world? 40–60%
  • 24. F.I.T.T.? Frequency, Intensity, Time (duration), Type (activity)

Limb ischemia: whose leg would survive longer?
  • 50-year-old otherwise healthy marathon runner with atrial fibrillation and an acute embolus in the popliteal artery
  • 50-year-old smoker with HTN, hyperlipidemia and longstanding claudication, with acute occlusion of a high-grade popliteal stenosis → this leg: thanks to collaterals he might not even notice the occlusion

rows: Anything that travels from one place to another in the bloodstream; lodges at an arterial bifurcation, where vessels naturally narrow
Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing; robust collaterals develop as the atherosclerosis builds up

Catastrophic – usually in otherwise normal arteries with no established collaterals
Typical: acute white leg + complete neurosensory deficit
Progressive, as secondary thrombus forms proximal and distal to the occlusion

Less dramatic; usually a history of claudication, with critical ischemia as the end result
Depends on the size of the artery occluded and whether collaterals developed beforehand

Cardiac source most common:
• Atrial fibrillation – thrombus in the L atrial appendage
• Mural thrombus, acute MI
• Mechanical heart valves – mitral is highest risk (anticoagulate)
• Paradoxical – usually a young, obese woman on birth control; DVT crosses to the arterial side through a patent foramen ovale
• Endocarditis
• Cardiac tumour – send to pathology, especially if young with no other cause

• Progressive atherosclerosis of the leg arteries
• Hypercoagulability
• Arterial dissection
• Bypass graft occlusion

blocks.alt: Sources of arterial emboli: endocarditis vegetations, left atrial thrombus, mural thrombus after MI, ASD, aneurysm, atherosclerotic stenosis
blocks.cap: Most emboli are cardiac: AF left atrial thrombus, post-MI mural thrombus, valve vegetations; a septal defect allows paradoxical embolism.

blocks.alt: Sites where arterial emboli lodge, with frequencies
blocks.cap: Emboli lodge at bifurcations – the common femoral (34%) is the commonest site, then popliteal (14%) and common iliac (14%).

rows: Duration is the most important part of the history – irreversible muscle necrosis occurs within 6–8 hours if untreated
Ask about claudication, look for atrial fibrillation, use the 6 Ps
Palpable normal pulses in the contralateral leg → embolism
A strong pulse can mask an occlusion at that level → water-hammer effect
Thrombotic occlusion of the superficial femoral artery = asymptomatic

blocks.html:
Management of acute limb ischemia
  • A significant problem: 25% mortality; 20% result in amputation
  • Anticoagulation: heparin bolus 5000 U, then IV infusion 1000 U/hour; goal aPTT 2–3×
  • Oxygen by facemask
  • IV hydration and monitor urine output – at risk for kidney failure
  • Adequate analgesia
  • Thrombophilia screen if indicated
  • Endovascular: thrombolysis, angioplasty, stenting
  • Open surgical: thromboembolectomy, bypass, fasciotomy, amputation
Compartment syndrome
  • Pressure within a compartment rises, restricting blood flow and potentially damaging muscles and nerves
  • Lack of flow in ischemia damages the capillary walls; when flow is restored, the compartment swells
  • Muscles can die even with good blood flow, because they are so constricted
  • Treatment: fasciotomy – a surgical emergency

blocks.title: The clock in acute limb ischemia
blocks.html: Irreversible muscle necrosis within 6–8 hours. After reperfusion, watch for compartment syndrome – a surgical emergency needing fasciotomy – and for kidney failure.

Chronic arterial occlusive disease – risk factors
  • Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia
  • Operative risk: CAD, CVD, COPD
  • Genetics
Functional: intermittent claudication
  • Claudication: pain in a functional muscle group brought on by predictable exertion and promptly relieved by rest; reproducible
    • Aortic occlusion → buttocks, thighs, calves
    • Superficial femoral artery occlusion → calves
  • Clinical symptoms variable; 5% surgical intervention over 5 years; low amputation rate (2% over 5–10 years)
  • High mortality from co-existent CAD: 30, 50, 70% at 5, 10, 15 years
  • Non-invasive Ix: ultrasound, ankle-brachial index · invasive Ix: CT angiogram, angiography

blocks.lead: Ankle-brachial index: objective ratio of ankle systolic pressure to arm systolic pressure, quantifying arterial insufficiency.

blocks.html:
Medical management of PAD – ABCDES
  • Antiplatelet drugs – ASA, clopidogrel (Plavix), ticagrelor
  • Blood pressure management
  • Cholesterol management – statins
  • Diabetic management
  • Exercise – develops more collaterals
  • Smoking cessation – most important
Limb-threatening: critical limb ischemia
  • Ischemic rest pain and/or tissue loss and gangrene – in tissue most distal from the heart (toes)
  • Medical management: risk factor modification, antiplatelet therapy
  • Non-invasive Ix: vascular flow studies · invasive Ix: CT angiogram, catheter-based angiography
  • Surgical candidates: critical limb ischemia (unless saving the limb would threaten life → amputation); disabling claudication – more controversial (risk of worsening ischemia, cost)
  • Surgical considerations: age, anatomy, availability of venous conduit, comorbidities, life expectancy, indication, patient preference

rows:
Inflow: usually the common femoral artery; can be the aorta
Outflow: popliteal (above/below knee), anterior tibial, posterior tibial or peroneal arteries
Conduit: autogenous vein (long saphenous, small saphenous or arm veins) or synthetic (Gore-Tex)

Angiography suite, local anesthetic
Femoral puncture, balloon angioplasty, stents, atherectomy
Effective, inexpensive (unless complications arise), durable (with good anatomy and quality vein)
Effective (short- to mid-term), minimally invasive, outpatient, minimal risk of infection
General anesthetic, hospital stay, long recovery, wound complications
Graft thrombosis (thrombolysis, redo surgery); infected grafts (high rate of limb loss, high mortality)
Puncture-site complications (expanding hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arterial thrombosis); distal embolization (could limit other surgical options)

blocks.html:
Module questions – peripheral vascular disease
  • 25. Differential for embolic acute limb ischemia? Cardiac (AF, endocarditis, MI, prosthetic valves, paradoxical), emboli from aneurysmal disease with chronic thrombus, peripheral vascular disease
  • 26. Procedure of choice for compartment syndrome? Fasciotomy → a surgical emergency; releasing the fascia lets the muscles swell – otherwise neuropathy and even muscle necrosis leading to amputation
  • 27. Definition of critical limb ischemia? Rest pain and/or non-healing ulceration/gangrene
  • 28. Where is rest pain in CLI? Foot → the tissue furthest from the heart (foot and toes); claudication is in muscle groups such as the calf
  • 29. Most important in PAD management – stop smoking, aspirin, exercise, BP control? Stop smoking → smoking gives 3× risk of CLI; only diabetes matters more (4× risk of CLI)
  • 30. Symptom diagnostic of CLI: rest pain
  • 31. Medical management of PAD: ABCDES – antiplatelet, BP, cholesterol, diabetes, exercise, smoking cessation
  • 32. Options for lower-extremity revascularization: femoral-popliteal bypass, aorto-bifemoral bypass, angioplasty and stenting, axillary-femoral bypass

Meet the patient: chest pain
  • 63-year-old man; worsening chest pain for 8 hours; central, 8/10, radiating to the jaw, with dyspnea and diaphoresis; non-pleuritic; no cough, fevers, chills or infectious symptoms
  • PMHx: hypertension, GERD, osteoarthritis · FHx: no premature CAD
  • Social: truck driver, independent contractor; ex-smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 10 years ago; no significant alcohol or drug use
  • Medications: HCTZ 25 mg daily, lansoprazole 30 mg daily, naproxen as needed; no allergies
  • Exam: T 37.6°C; BP 135/90 (no arm difference); HR 64; RR 20; SpO2 95% RA; normal S1/S2, no S3/S4 or murmurs; JVP at the angle of the jaw, lungs clear, trace peripheral edema, normal peripheral pulses
  • Investigations: normal CBC, electrolytes, renal function; CK and troponin pending; CXR normal (no consolidation or edema)

blocks.alt: Case 12-lead ECG: inferior ST elevation with reciprocal changes and Wenckebach AV block
blocks.cap: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I, aVL and V2; the PR lengthens until a P wave is dropped.

blocks.html:
What does the ECG show? (choose 3)
  • ST elevation in the inferior leads – II, III, aVF: inferior STEMI
  • ST depression in the lateral leads – reciprocal depression in I, aVL (high lateral) and septal leads (especially V2), which may reflect posterior involvement
  • 2nd degree AV block, Mobitz I – progressive PR prolongation followed by a non-conducted P wave (Wenckebach)
  • Distractors: anterior or lateral ST elevation, inferior ST depression, Mobitz II, complete heart block
No PCI on site; nearest PCI centre is 150 minutes away – next step?
  • (b) Administer fibrinolytic therapy
  • In the absence of contraindications, give fibrinolysis for STEMI with symptom onset within 12 hours when primary PCI cannot be done within 120 minutes of first medical contact
  • Serial ECGs, repeat biomarkers, CT head or CT pulmonary angiogram only delay therapy once STEMI is diagnosed

symptoms within 12 h"] --> B{"Primary PCI possible within

to fibrinolysis?"} D -->|"No"| E["Fibrinolysis

rows: Known malignant intracranial neoplasm (primary or metastatic)
Ischemic stroke within 3 months (EXCEPT acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours)
Active bleeding or bleeding diathesis (excluding menses)
Significant closed-head or facial trauma within 3 months
Intracranial or intraspinal surgery within 2 months
Severe uncontrolled hypertension (unresponsive to emergency therapy)
blocks.lead: Which are absolute contraindications? (choose 3) Options: (a) ICH 5 years ago, (b) ischemic stroke 6 months ago, (c) lung adenocarcinoma with brain metastases, (d) trauma CPR, (e) suspected aortic dissection, (f) dementia, (g) pregnancy. Answer: (a), (c), (e); the rest are relative contraindications.

blocks.html:
Hypotension after nitrates
  • After fibrinolysis the patient receives ASA, clopidogrel, LMWH, nitrates for chest pain and oxygen, and is transferred
  • After nitrates he becomes hypotensive en route (BP 75/40)
  • Emergent catheterization: 100% occlusion of the proximal RCA with thrombus, successfully stented; LV angiography EF 45% with akinesis of the inferior/inferolateral walls
  • JVP at the angle of the jaw with positive Kussmaul’s sign; lungs clear; normal heart sounds, no murmurs; still hypotensive, negative pulsus paradoxus
  • Most likely cause: (b) right ventricular infarct (vs LV cardiogenic shock, acute VSD, papillary muscle rupture with MR, tamponade from free-wall rupture)
  • Hypotension after nitrates + distended neck veins with Kussmaul’s sign + clear lungs = RV infarct; no murmur, clear lungs and no pulsus paradoxus make the others less likely

blocks.title: RV infarct is preload-dependent
blocks.html: Impaired RV contractility makes the patient preload-dependent: vasodilators, particularly nitrates, cause hypotension. IV fluids are the mainstay of treatment. Suspect it in inferior STEMI with high JVP, Kussmaul’s sign and clear lungs.

Secondary prevention after MI
  • Discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy (ASA + ticagrelor) for a minimum of 1 year
  • Which provide secondary-prevention benefit (choose 2)? (b) Ramipril 5 mg daily and (c) atorvastatin 40 mg daily (not bisoprolol 2.5 mg, amlodipine 2.5 mg or ivabradine 5 mg)
  • ACE inhibitors: benefit greatest with co-existing hypertension, diabetes, LVEF < 40% or CKD, but guidelines recommend them for all patients post-infarct; if not tolerated (e.g. cough) → ARB
  • Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) provide secondary-prevention benefit
  • Beta blockers (e.g. bisoprolol) benefit patients with significant LV systolic dysfunction post-MI (EF < 40%), with or without clinical heart failure
  • Bisoprolol, calcium channel blockers and ivabradine can be effective anti-anginals but give no clear secondary-prevention benefit
Case follow-up
  • Referred to cardiac rehab; primary care follow-up within 1 month to review medication tolerance; cardiologist within 6 weeks
  • At 6 weeks: off work at least 3 months (commercial driving licence suspended after MI); significant financial constraints – has not renewed prescriptions; taking only ASA 81 mg; ticagrelor cost is prohibitive
  • Discussion points:
    1. What discussion would you have about his medical treatment?
    2. What changes would you make given his circumstances?
    3. How do geographic and socioeconomic factors affect his care, and the care of MI patients in general?

lectures.name: Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease

blocks.html:
Aortic valve
  • Three cusps
  • Ventricular systole: isovolumetric contraction, then the aortic valve opens and blood is rapidly ejected into the aorta; normally opens with a very small pressure gradient
  • Large pressure is generated across the valve → a lot of wear and tear over time
  • Aortic sclerosis: thickening/calcification of the valve without obstruction to flow; increases with age (50% of patients over 85 years)

blocks.alt: Aortic stenosis: calcified tricuspid valve and inset of a stenotic bicuspid valve
blocks.cap: Stenotic aortic valve: calcific nodules on a tricuspid valve (main) vs a congenital bicuspid valve (inset) — the two main causes of AS.

blocks.html:
Mitral valve
  • Allows passage of blood from the LA to the LV and prevents its return
  • Mitral annulus – fibrous ring attached to the leaflets
  • Two leaflets – anterior and posterior
  • Chordae tendineae
  • Papillary muscles – attached to the LV

(The moderator band is not part of the mitral apparatus — it carries conduction fibres through the RV.)

blocks.alt: Mitral valve apparatus: annulus, anterior and posterior leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles
blocks.cap: The mitral apparatus: annulus, anterior leaflet, posterior leaflet (3 lobes), commissures, chordae tendineae and the lateral and medial papillary muscles — dysfunction of any part causes MR.

blocks.html:
Aortic valve disease: stenosis vs regurgitation

Aortic stenosis is the most common acquired heart (valve) disease — a pressure load on the LV. Aortic regurgitation is a volume load.

rows:
Obstruction to flow from LV into aorta
↑ pressure gradient LV → aorta
↑ afterload on LV (Law of Laplace)
Compensatory hypertrophy:
• Good: maintains normal afterload
• Bad: ↓ LV compliance, ↓ coronary blood flow, ↑ O₂ demand
• Contractility maintained until late in course

Backflow from aorta into LV through a leaking valve
Annuloaortic ectasia: dilatation of the aortic root/valve annulus
• Usually idiopathic; may be associated with chronic hypertension
• ↑ risk of aortic dissection (tear/laceration)
Chronic AR: volume overload → LV dilatation, ↑ wall stress, compensatory hypertrophy; LV systolic function preserved initially, CHF eventually
Acute AR: sudden onset (endocarditis, dissection) into a normal-sized, normally compliant LV → sudden ↑ LV pressure; LVEDP transmitted back to LA and pulmonary circulation → pulmonary edema; dyspnea, hypotension, short (possibly inaudible) murmur; emergency surgery usually indicated

Degenerative/calcific (etiology unclear)
• Pathophysiology similar to atherosclerosis; calcium deposition
• Presents later in life (60s-80s) – wear and tear
• Genetic markers being identified
• Statins (atherosclerotic regression) have no benefit
Congenital/bicuspid
• 1% of population, male preponderance
• Presents in 40s-50s
• 1/3 AS, 1/3 AR, 1/3 clinically insignificant
• Abnormal, dilated aortas – intrinsic defect in the media

Leaflet: calcific degeneration, bicuspid valve, endocarditis, lupus
Root enlargement (leading cause in the Western world):
• Age-related degeneration/enlargement – most common
• Hypertension – stretches the annulus
• Cystic medial necrosis – Marfan syndrome
• Bicuspid aortic valve aortopathy
Acute AR: endocarditis, dissection

"ASD": Angina, Syncope, Dyspnea (CHF)
Asymptomatic: survival similar to general population; < 1% SCD
Symptomatic: 10% SCD with angina, higher with CHF
Overall survival 75% at 3 years; normalises with AVR
Dyspnea/HF carries the worst prognosis

Long asymptomatic period – good prognosis
Early: exertional dyspnea, fatigue
CHF as LV systolic function fails: orthopnea, PND
Angina can occur – low diastolic pressure, LVH

Systolic murmur at the base; later peak = more severe (loudness does not grade severity)
Soft S2: stenotic valve does not close properly, so only P2 is heard
S4: stiff hypertrophied LV
Pulsus parvus et tardus: reduced, delayed
LV heave: strong apical impulse; apex may be displaced

Diastolic murmur at the (left sternal) border; later peak = more severe
LVH with dilated LV: apex displaced down and out
S3: CHF; S4: stiff LV
Widened pulse pressure – narrows as CHF develops:
• Quincke: capillary pulsations
• Müller: systolic pulsation of the uvula
• Duroziez: systolic murmur when femoral artery compressed proximally, diastolic when compressed distally
• Traube: pistol-shot sounds over the femoral artery
• Corrigan: collapsing pulse

ECG: not diagnostic
Echocardiogram: gold standard – valve gradients, valve area, LV function (EF), other valve disease, LVH, aortic root size

ECG: not diagnostic
CXR: may show LVH or enlarged aorta
Echocardiogram: gold standard – etiology, severity, LV response (EF), aortic root size, other valve disease

Asymptomatic: watch and wait; no clear benefit to surgery (growing evidence for surgery in some asymptomatic patients)
Symptomatic: valve replacement
• Bioprosthetic: porcine cusps or bovine pericardium sewn on a synthetic frame; limited lifespan (~15 years); no long-term anticoagulation
• Mechanical: long life expectancy; oral anticoagulation

Asymptomatic: no medication improves survival; endocarditis prophylaxis historically, no longer suggested
Surgery if LV failing or significantly dilated: LVEF < 50%, LVESD > 50 mm, LVEDD > 65 mm (LVH alone is not a criterion)
Symptomatic: depends on etiology
• Leaflets → aortic valve replacement
• Root dilation → aortic valve-sparing surgery

blocks.html:
Mitral valve disease: stenosis vs regurgitation

Both lesions raise LA pressure and push it back into the pulmonary circulation, ending in pulmonary hypertension and right-heart failure. MS under-fills a normal LV; MR volume-loads the LV until it fails.

rows:
Obstruction to flow from LA into LV:
• Fusion of leaflet commissures
• Thickening, fibrosis, calcification of cusps
• Thickening, fusion, shortening of chordae
LV underfilled → reduced systemic CO
Pooling in LA → stasis → clot/stroke risk
↑ LA pressure → distension of pulmonary veins
RV compensatory hypertrophy → pulmonary arterial hypertension
RV distortion → tricuspid dysfunction, RA dilatation

Backflow from LV into LA through a leaking valve
LV systolic function preserved initially; fails over time → reduced systemic CO
↑ LA pressure and volume → transmitted to pulmonary circulation
• Rate of rise depends on LA compliance
• Pulmonary hypertension eventually
Primary MR: intrinsic valve pathology
Secondary MR: distortion of a normal valve by dilatation or dysfunction of surrounding structures

Rheumatic fever/heart disease – most common globally (> 99%)
• Group A strep pharyngitis → autoimmune process (molecular mimicry, cross-reactivity with GAS antigens)
• Female preponderance
• Developing countries: common, short asymptomatic period
• Western world: uncommon, long asymptomatic period (15 years)
• 25% MS, 40% MS + MR, 35% multivalvular
• Mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary
Mitral annular calcification (MAC) – aging, atherosclerosis, abnormal Ca²⁺ metabolism, CKD
Radiation-induced – late manifestation in survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma
Congenital MS

Acute:
• Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture
• Infective endocarditis with chordal rupture
• Acute rheumatic fever
• Myxomatous chordal rupture
• Acute LV dilation (myocarditis, ischemia)
• Mechanical failure of a prosthetic mitral valve
Chronic:
• Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous MV disease)
• Infective endocarditis
• Rheumatic MV disease
• Cardiomyopathy
• Ischemic heart disease

Exertional dyspnea (most common presentation), fatigue
LHF: orthopnea, PND
Hemoptysis: rupture of thin-walled dilated bronchial veins
RHF: peripheral edema, ascites, congested liver
Angina: RVH, pulmonary hypertension
Hoarseness: compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Earlier in high-output states (pregnancy, anemia, hyperthyroidism, fever) – ↑ CO and HR against a fixed valve

Acute: pulmonary edema (↓ SV, ↑ LA pressure); sudden dyspnea, hypotension, HF/cardiogenic shock
Chronic: initially asymptomatic; then dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, palpitations

Diastolic murmur at the apex
S1: loud initially, softens as the valve stiffens
S2: loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
Pulse: atrial fibrillation (LA dilation)
Malar flush: rosy cheeks from cutaneous vasodilatation
LHF: pulmonary congestion, poor CO
RHF: high JVP, tricuspid regurgitation, peripheral edema, ascites

Holosystolic murmur at the apex, accentuated in left lateral decubitus; may be soft/inaudible in acute MR
Normal carotid upstroke (vs AS)
S2: loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
S3: rapid LV filling in diastole
Apical impulse enlarged, sustained, displaced (LV dilation)
Pulse: atrial fibrillation (LA dilation)
Diffuse precordial lift in severe MR (LA enlargement)

ECG: LA enlargement, atrial fibrillation (clues, not diagnostic)
CXR: LA enlargement, double density/border sign, straightened left heart border, splayed carina, RV enlargement
Echocardiogram: gold standard – MV morphology, function, severity, effects on other structures (LA dilatation, pulmonary pressure, RV size/function), likely etiology

ECG: LA enlargement, atrial fibrillation
CXR: LA enlargement, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema
Echocardiogram: gold standard – etiology, severity, LV and RV size/systolic function, LA size, pulmonary pressures

Asymptomatic: watch and wait
Sinus rhythm: salt restriction + diuretics if pulmonary congestion
AF: beta blockers (slow HR, ↑ diastolic filling time) + anticoagulation (thrombus/stroke)
Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty (rheumatic MS):
• Catheter via femoral vein → IVC → RA → interatrial septum → LA
• Balloon inflated inside the valve to ↑ valve area
• Only if less than moderate MR
• Delays or avoids surgery
• Contraindications: LA thrombus, significant MR, calcific MS
Mitral valve replacement (stenotic valves must be replaced)
• Bioprosthetic: older, history of bleeding
• Mechanical: younger, or another indication for anticoagulation
MAZE procedure: restore/maintain sinus rhythm
Left atrial appendectomy: ↓ stroke risk in AF

Asymptomatic: watch and wait
Blood pressure control; diuresis for volume overload
AF: rate control + anticoagulation
Severe MR: endocarditis prophylaxis
Surgery indications:
• Symptomatic severe primary MR
• Asymptomatic severe primary MR with mild/moderate LV dysfunction
• Not favourable once LV dysfunction is severe
Repair > replacement if anatomy suitable – no prosthesis, no anticoagulation, less endocarditis
Transcatheter repair: MitraClip – expanding evidence (EVEREST II, COAPT)

blocks.html:
Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)

Via median sternotomy or a minimally invasive approach.

  1. Aorta, right atrial appendage and base of the heart are exposed
  2. Cardiopulmonary bypass – cannula in the distal ascending aorta or proximal arch; aorta is cross-clamped
  3. Aortic valve exposed
  4. Cardioplegic arrest – stop the heart
  5. Valve removed; annular stitches placed through the prosthesis
  6. Aortic incision closed – sutured anastomosis
  7. Finished – pacing wires placed
Outcomes
  • Mortality risk 1-2%
  • Recovery: 4-5 days in hospital; 1 month at home
  • Expect dramatic improvement in quality of life – complete resolution of symptoms; improved long-term survival

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Sternotomy or minimally invasive access"] --> B["Expose aorta, RA appendage,
base of heart"] B --> C["Cardiopulmonary bypass
aorta cross-clamped"] C --> D["Expose aortic valve"] D --> E["Cardioplegic arrest"] E --> F["Excise valve
annular stitches through prosthesis"] F --> G["Close aortotomy"] G --> H["Pacing wires placed"]

blocks.alt: Sequential illustrations of the steps of surgical aortic valve replacement
blocks.cap: SAVR step by step (left to right): exposure, aortotomy, valve exposure, excision, placing annular sutures through the prosthesis, seating it, and closing the aorta.

blocks.html:
Surgical approach: conventional vs minimally invasive

Conventional (sternotomy)

  • Used when access to the rest of the heart is needed – bypass grafting, arrhythmia procedure/ablation

Minimally invasive (mini-thoracotomy, hemi-sternotomy)

  • Provides exposure to only the relevant anatomy
  • Outcomes in RCTs equal to conventional
  • Fewer blood transfusions; lower incidence of atrial fibrillation
  • Cosmetic benefits; quicker return to activity

blocks.alt: Surgical incisions: conventional sternotomy vs minimally invasive mini-thoracotomy and hemi-sternotomy
blocks.cap: Conventional full sternotomy vs the two minimally invasive routes: right mini-thoracotomy and upper hemi-sternotomy.

blocks.html:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
  • Femoral arterial or alternative access (subclavian, carotid, LV apex)
  • Fluoroscopic/echo guidance
  • Rapid ventricular pacing to allow accurate placement of the valve
  • Access-site hemostasis

blocks.alt: TAVI access routes: transfemoral catheter, CT reconstruction of aorta, transapical access
blocks.cap: TAVI access: transfemoral (left), CT of the aorta and iliofemoral vessels used to plan access (centre), and transapical via a small left thoracotomy (right).

blocks.alt: TAVI valve crimped onto a catheter and deployed within the native aortic valve
blocks.cap: The TAVI valve is crimped onto or inside the catheter, advanced retrograde, and expanded within the diseased native valve.

blocks.html:
TAVI acute complications
  • Injury to adjacent structures: membranous septum (heart block, VSD or LV-RA fistula); anterior mitral leaflet (mitral regurgitation)
  • Inadequate seating of the prosthesis: coronary obstruction/MI, paravalvular leak
Bottom line for aortic stenosis
  • No medical therapy for severe AS; without intervention survival is poor
  • SAVR: excellent outcomes; gold standard for patients expected to survive > 5-7 years
  • TAVI: standard of care for moderate-to-high-risk elderly patients with severe AS; long-term data in low-risk patients awaited
  • Treating AS saves lives and improves quality of life

Myxomatous mitral valve disease
  • Affects 2% of the general population
  • Results in leaflet prolapse
  • Spectrum: fibroelastic deficiency (FED) → Barlow's
  • Highly amenable to valve repair – can restore normal life expectancy and quality of life
Surgical candidates
  • Severe, symptomatic MR
  • Declining LV function
  • Dilating LV
  • New-onset atrial fibrillation
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension

blocks.alt: Spectrum of degenerative mitral disease from fibroelastic deficiency to Barlow's disease
blocks.cap: Degenerative MV spectrum: FED → FED+ → forme fruste → Barlow's, with progressively more (redundant) leaflet tissue.

blocks.html:
Repair techniques

Quadrangular resection ± sliding plasty

  1. (A) The prolapsing, redundant segment is completely excised
  2. (B) Sliding plasty – mobilisation of the remainder of the posterior leaflet
  3. (C) An annular band is placed to support the repair – improves durability

Other techniques

  • Triangular resection – removes less tissue
  • Neochordae reconstruction – reconstructed chordae attached to papillary muscles
  • Folding plasty
  • 'Haircut'/resection + chordal transfer

blocks.alt: Quadrangular resection of the posterior mitral leaflet with sliding plasty and annuloplasty band
blocks.cap: Quadrangular resection: (A) excise the prolapsing segment, (B) sliding plasty of the remaining posterior leaflet, (C) annuloplasty band to support the repair.

blocks.html:
Minimally invasive mitral approaches
  • Avoid sternotomy
  • Faster recovery, shorter hospital stay
  • Improved cosmesis and patient satisfaction
  • Superior visualisation; excellent repair results
  • Same 3-4 cm mini-thoracotomy can be used to replace with tissue or mechanical valves
Videoscopic repair
  • All the same repair techniques as via open sternotomy
  • Superior visualisation of the MV and subvalvar apparatus
  • Need to get used to different angles; specialised tools (knot pusher)
Emerging transcatheter therapies
  • Percutaneous MitraClip – based on edge-to-edge repair: prolapsing posterior segments are clipped to the corresponding anterior segment
    • Improves outcomes in heart failure: COAPT trial (Cardiovascular Outcomes Assessment of the MitraClip Percutaneous Therapy) – heart failure hospitalisations significantly reduced at 2 years in severe MR treated with MitraClip plus best medical therapy
  • Transcatheter/transapical implants – e.g. Tiara (NeoVasc, Canada), first-in-man December 2014; worldwide experience growing
    • Device sits in the mitral annulus and prevents regurgitation, or opens the valve in stenotic lesions
    • At present no good transcatheter options for mitral insufficiency – many devices in development
Bottom line for the mitral valve
  • Myxomatous mitral insufficiency can be repaired with excellent long-term outcomes and restored normal life expectancy
  • Replacement for other indications: non-repairable, stenotic, or endocarditis-destroyed valves
  • Some data suggest replacement for functional MR gives less recurrent regurgitation than repair
  • Emerging therapies will play an increasing role in selected patients

Theoretical risks of a prosthetic valve
  • Structural valve deterioration (SVD)
  • Non-structural dysfunction – paravalvular leak, pannus ingrowth
  • Thrombosis, thromboembolism
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Death
  • Patient effect: survival, quality of life, inferior hemodynamics (higher gradients), morbidity
Mitral valve repair restores life expectancy
  • Once patients become increasingly symptomatic, observed survival falls below expected

blocks.alt: Survival after mitral repair by preoperative NYHA class and ejection fraction
blocks.cap: After MR surgery, NYHA I-II patients achieve expected survival (A) while NYHA III-IV patients fall well below it (B); lower preoperative EF predicts worse survival (C) — operate before symptoms and LV decline.

blocks.html:
Early repair for flail mitral valve saves lives
  • Flail MV is associated with ↑ morbidity and mortality; surgery is unavoidable
  • Do not replace flail mitral valves – repair gives longer survival (10-15 years after surgery)
  • Early surgery on a regurgitant MV before NYHA III-IV symptoms beats medical management long-term – preserves survival, reduces HF risk
  • MV repair techniques are simple, straightforward and becoming routine
  • Evidence is emerging that aortic valve repair also better preserves survival

blocks.alt: Survival after flail mitral leaflet: early surgery vs initial medical management
blocks.cap: Flail-leaflet MR: early surgery gives better 20-year survival than initial medical management, in both the overall and propensity-matched cohorts.

blocks.alt: Survival after mitral repair vs replacement for anterior and posterior leaflet prolapse
blocks.cap: Repair (dashed) outlives replacement (solid) for both anterior- (AL-MVP) and posterior-leaflet (PL-MVP) prolapse.

blocks.html:
Advantages of valve repair
  • Hemodynamics – replacement is limited by the prosthesis itself; most repairs leave more aortic/mitral valve area
  • Durability
  • Lower risk of infection, thrombosis and thromboembolism – native tissue in contact with blood
  • Fewer bleeding complications – no anticoagulation
  • Insufficient (regurgitant) valves can commonly be repaired – stenotic valves need to be replaced
  • Successful repair restores life expectancy and survival; outcomes are excellent
  • The most perfect valve is your own!

blocks.title: Repair or replace?
blocks.html: Leaky → repair; tight → replace. Regurgitant valves (especially myxomatous/flail MR) are repaired; stenotic valves (calcific AS, rheumatic MS) must be replaced.

Ideal valve prosthesis
  • Long-term durability
  • Easy to implant
  • No intrinsic thrombogenicity
  • No predilection for endocarditis
  • Widely available
  • Hemodynamics similar to a native valve – no increased work for the heart, no residual gradient, near-normal flow, no hemolysis, no activation of coagulation/inflammatory cascades
Valve prosthesis options
  • Slight survival benefit for mechanical prostheses – much debate, no randomised data

lectures.title: Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management
lectures.framing: The four big left-sided lesions — aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation — each load the heart in a characteristic way (pressure vs volume, LV vs LA/pulmonary circulation), and that load predicts the symptoms, the signs and the timing of surgery. The organising surgical idea: regurgitant valves can usually be repaired, stenotic valves must be replaced — and the best valve is your own.
lectures.keypoints: Echocardiography is the gold standard for every valve lesion; ECG is never diagnostic. Severe AS: valve area < 1 cm², mean gradient > 40 mm Hg; once symptoms start, 50% survival is 5 y with angina, 3 y with syncope, 2 y with heart failure — there is no medical therapy, so replace (SAVR, or TAVI in elderly moderate-to-high-risk patients). Operate on asymptomatic severe AR when LVEF < 50%, LVESD > 50 mm or LVEDD > 65 mm. Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic (Jones: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor); balloon valvuloplasty is contraindicated with LA thrombus or significant MR. For MR, repair beats replacement and early surgery before NYHA III-IV symptoms preserves survival. Mechanical valves last but need lifelong anticoagulation (INR 2-3 aortic, 2.5-3.5 mitral); bioprosthetic valves need none but deteriorate (~15 years).

weeks.label: Week 4 - Heart Failure, Hypertension & Congenital Disease

lectures.name: Physiology of Heart Failure

blocks.html:
Definitions of heart failure
  • Historic physiologic: the heart cannot maintain a cardiac output adequate for metabolic requirements and cannot accommodate venous return – no mention of EF
  • Clinical: a syndrome in which reduced heart function is associated with diminished exercise capacity, a high incidence of ventricular arrhythmia and shortened life expectancy
  • Better clinical definition: a clinical syndrome of typical symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling, fatigue), possibly with signs (elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, peripheral edema), caused by a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality, resulting in reduced cardiac output and/or elevated intracardiac pressures at rest or during stress
  • Layman's terms: the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's oxygen and nutrient demands
  • 2005 clinical definition = symptoms of HF (rest or exercise) + objective evidence (echo) of systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction + (if in doubt) response to HF-directed treatment
  • 2008 clinical definition = symptoms (breathlessness at rest or on exercise, fatigue, tiredness, ankle swelling) + signs (tachycardia, tachypnea, pulmonary rales, pleural effusion, raised JVP, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly) + objective evidence of structural/functional abnormality at rest (cardiomegaly, S3, murmurs, echo abnormality, raised natriuretic peptide)

HF is a clinical syndrome, NOT a disease – a constellation of signs and symptoms + some type of structural heart disease. Ejection fraction is NOT required to make the diagnosis.

Compensated vs decompensated
  • Compensated: asymptomatic despite ↓ pumping function – enlarged heart, ↑ HR
  • Decompensated: symptomatic; can no longer compensate; needs treatment and often hospitalization

Epidemiology
  • Fastest-growing global CVD – substantial morbidity, mortality and economic burden; 40 million affected worldwide
  • 42-50% die within 5 years of diagnosis
  • 74% have ≥ 1 comorbidity (renal disease, diabetes, hematological)
  • 27% re-hospitalized within 30 days
  • #1 reason for hospitalization in patients > 65; number one driver of unplanned admission; 1.4 million hospital days/year
  • Canada: > 600 000 affected and rising; > 50 000 diagnosed each year; 1 in 2 Canadians touched by HF
  • Costs Canadians > $2.8 billion/year; 10 billion spent annually on HF hospital costs
  • Annual HF deaths in Canada exceed breast + colon + prostate cancer combined
  • There is no cure for HF

Pathophysiology
  • Over time, damage to any major structure/system – ventricles, atria, coronary arteries, valves, electrical system, pericardium, pulmonary arteries/lungs – alone or together can result in HF
  • Patients often develop HF after the heart has been weakened or damaged by other cardiovascular conditions

blocks.alt: The cardiovascular continuum: risk factors → CAD → MI → remodeling → HF → end-stage disease
blocks.cap: The cardiovascular continuum: risk factors → CAD → MI → remodeling → HF → end-stage disease.

blocks.alt: LV dysfunction ↓ cardiac output → neurohormonal activation → Na+ retention, arrhythmia, further remodeling → congestion, sudden death, pump failure
blocks.cap: LV dysfunction ↓ cardiac output → neurohormonal activation → Na+ retention, arrhythmia, further remodeling → congestion, sudden death, pump failure.

blocks.html:
Stages of HF development
  1. Injury/induction – all at once (MI, inflammation) or slow cumulative effects (risk factors, genetics)
  2. Cellular changes – lead to anatomic changes (cardiac remodeling)
  3. Functional changes – cardiac dysfunction and physiologic responses to accommodate the damage
  4. Symptomatic HF ± acute pulmonary edema/shock – clinical signs and symptoms are always the last thing to occur

Renal function also declines as HF worsens.

blocks.alt: Survival is poor in both HFpEF and HFrEF, slightly worse with HFrEF
blocks.cap: Survival is poor in both HFpEF and HFrEF, slightly worse with HFrEF.

blocks.html:
Left vs right heart failure

Biventricular HF: both sides affected; LHF can lead to RV disease.

rows:
Systolic = failure to pump: reduced EF (HFrEF); LV loses normal contraction, less ejection force; ↑ preload
Diastolic = failure to fill: preserved EF (HFpEF); LV does not relax fully between beats; ↑ afterload

Most commonly from pulmonary hypertension due to chronic lung disease – COPD, PE, pulmonary fibrosis, sleep apnea, myasthenia gravis, poliomyelitis
Causes RV dilation and RVH
Reduced forward flow (fatigue, ↓ exercise tolerance, lightheadedness, low BP) and reduced filling from the lung (SOB, orthopnea/PND)
Blood backs up in the veins from the RV → venous congestion
Fatigue, ↑ capillary wedge pressure, pulmonary congestion, PND, confusion, restlessness, orthopnea, tachycardia, exertional dyspnea, cyanosis
Fatigue, ↑ peripheral venous pressure, ascites, enlarged liver/spleen, distended jugular veins, dependent/pitting edema, anorexia/GI complaints, swelling of legs, ankles, abdomen

blocks.cap: Left HF: reduced forward flow and lung congestion; right HF: venous congestion.

blocks.cap: Left-sided failure: pulmonary congestion, PND, orthopnea.

blocks.cap: Aging heart: hypertrophic cardiomyocytes with perimysial, endomysial and perivascular fibrosis.

blocks.html:
Neurohormonal dysregulation (Q10-11)
  • Baroreceptors become dysfunctional – no longer respond to changes in vessel stretch → afferent signals to the CNS
  • Neural: efferent sympathetic activation to heart, kidney, peripheral vasculature, skeletal muscle
  • Hormonal: baroreceptor unloading stimulates cardioregulatory centres → AVP release from the posterior pituitary
  • Sympathetic activity ↑ renin → ↑ angiotensin II → ↑ Na+ and water reabsorption and ↑ aldosterone
  • This is the body's response to dehydration – not appropriate in HF
AVP/ADH in heart failure
  • Circulating AVP is 2× higher than in healthy controls in HF with decompensation and hyponatremia
  • Seems paradoxical – should be lower given ↑ atrial pressure and blood volume
  • Sympathetic and RAAS activation may override volume/pressure receptors and hypothalamic control of AVP release
  • AVP → vasoconstriction and ↑ systemic resistance; ↑ collecting duct permeability → fluid reabsorption; net ↑ arterial resistance

blocks.html:
Atrial fibrillation and heart failure
  • 20% of HF patients have AF, but whether it is causal or consequential is unknown
  • AF → rapid, irregular rate and loss of atrial systole → ↓ cardiac output → HF; HF → ↑ filling pressures and LA size → AF

blocks.alt: HF and AF feed each other through ↑ LA size, fibrosis, neurohormonal activation and ↓ cardiac output
blocks.cap: HF and AF feed each other through ↑ LA size, fibrosis, neurohormonal activation and ↓ cardiac output.

blocks.html:
Causes of heart failure
  • Most common: MI, CAD, chronic hypertension, valve disease, arrhythmias, chronic pulmonary disease
  • Less common: idiopathic cardiomyopathy, viral/bacterial cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, pericarditis, congenital heart disease, diabetes, thyroid disease, pregnancy, septic shock

rows: Myocardial scar, stunning/hibernation, epicardial CAD, abnormal coronary microcirculation, endothelial dysfunction
Recreational substances, heavy metals, medications, radiation

Infection-related – bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites
Non-infectious – autoimmune disease, hypersensitivity, eosinophilic myocarditis

Acquired – mitral, aortic, tricuspid, pulmonary valve disease
Congenital – atrial and ventricular septal defects

Constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion
Hypereosinophilic syndrome, endomyocardial fibrosis

Most have prior MI or CAD – present with an infarct and HF
A blocked vessel puts downstream myocardium at risk of ischemia/necrosis; remodeling → dilated, thin-walled ventricle
Ischemic cardiomyopathy: HF with LVEF < 40% plus prior MI, viable hibernating myocardium, or severe CAD
Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of HF in developed countries
Occult CAD is not uncommon – angiography helps when etiology is unclear
Irreversible (prior MI) or reversible (chronically ischemic but viable) loss of contractility

Ischemic dilated CM = based on underlying ischemic heart disease – pathologists call this HF secondary to ischemic heart disease with LV dysfunction

Regurgitation makes large hearts: normal 250-300 g; diseased 500-600 g; severe MR/AR 750-1000 g (cor bovinum, “cow's heart”)

Still a major cause worldwide; less common in the West with effective drugs
Two patterns: LVH + pressure overload → HF with normal EF (→ low EF if an MI occurs); or dilated, poorly functioning heart → HF with low EF

Case example

A 54-year-old man presents to the ER with severe SOB at rest. Echo: moderate RV dysfunction, severe LV dysfunction (EF ~20%). History of heart attacks. Admitted, treated with evidence-based therapy, discharged on day 7 feeling much better. At 1 month: no orthopnea, PND or edema, but still short of breath after 1 city block, often stopping to rest.

  • a) On admission: acute biventricular HF secondary to ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF ~20%); NYHA IV; AHA stage C
  • b) 1 month later: acute biventricular HF secondary to ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF ~20%); NYHA II; AHA stage C

blocks.html:
Management principles
  • Goals: improve quantity and quality of life; ↓ symptoms and hospitalizations; coordinated, patient-centred, evidence-based care
  • Seek reversible causes in every patient
  • Plans must account for comorbidities, systolic dysfunction and presenting symptoms
  • Vaccination
  • HFrEF = evidence-based therapy; HFpEF = no evidence-based therapy other than diuretics – treat risk factors; control BP, HR, diabetes
Diuretics – acute congestion
  • Essential for decongestion
  • Forced salt/water loss ↑ neurohormonal (RAAS) activation
  • Can cause hyponatremia and hypokalemia – use the lowest dose that keeps symptoms and weight stable
  • Loop (block Na+K+2Cl– cotransporter; most potent) – furosemide
  • Thiazide (block Na+Cl– transporter) – chlorthalidone
  • Combinations when loop diuretics alone fail

blocks.html:
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI)
  • Natriuretic peptides help in HF – vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, inhibit fibrosis
  • LCZ696 (Entresto) = sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) + valsartan (ARB)
  • Neprilysin breaks down natriuretic peptides (neprilysin = BAD) → sacubitril ↑ natriuretic peptide levels
  • Neprilysin also breaks down angiotensin II (neprilysin = GOOD) → sacubitril keeps angiotensin II high (vasoconstriction)
  • Valsartan blocks AT1 (angiotensin II binding) and inhibits the RAAS – offsetting that
  • PARADIGM-HF (enalapril vs LCZ696) → guidelines: use an ARNI in place of ACEI/ARB in symptomatic HFrEF to ↓ CV death, HF hospitalization and symptoms
  • Stop ACEI 36 hours before starting LCZ696 (interaction)

blocks.alt: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin (↑ natriuretic peptides); valsartan blocks the AT1 receptor
blocks.cap: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin (↑ natriuretic peptides); valsartan blocks the AT1 receptor.

blocks.html:
If channel inhibitors – ivabradine
  • If is the main diastolic depolarization current generating a new action potential
  • Ivabradine selectively inhibits If in the SA node → slows diastolic depolarization and HR without affecting contractility, BP, bronchioles/asthma or renal function
  • Lowering HR reduces mortality – the higher the baseline HR, the greater the benefit
  • SHIFT → guidelines: consider ivabradine in symptomatic HFrEF with resting HR > 70, sinus rhythm, and an HF hospitalization within 12 months; larger benefit if HR ≥ 77

blocks.alt: Ivabradine flattens the diastolic depolarization slope, lengthening the RR interval
blocks.cap: Ivabradine flattens the diastolic depolarization slope, lengthening the RR interval.

blocks.html:
SGLT2 inhibitors
  • Block sodium-glucose transporter 2; act on multiple pathways → cardiac protection
  • Developed for diabetes – found to reduce HF events in diabetic patients
  • DAPA-HF: dapagliflozin ↓ mortality in HFrEF regardless of diabetes; benefits patients on an ARNI
  • EMPEROR-Reduced: empagliflozin ↓ CV death and hospitalization regardless of diabetes, age, sex and race
  • Guidelines: SGLT2i recommended in mild-moderate HFrEF with or without type 2 diabetes to improve symptoms and QOL and ↓ hospitalization and CV mortality
  • Introduce early in diabetic patients; add in non-diabetic patients once optimized on triple therapy

blocks.alt: Rationale: SGLT2i benefits in trials were largely independent of glucose
blocks.cap: Rationale: SGLT2i benefits in trials were largely independent of glucose.

blocks.html:
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators and CRT
  • Patients can die suddenly at any point, even when apparently stable
  • An ICD reduces sudden death from ventricular arrhythmia by shocking the heart to reset the rhythm
  • HFrEF patients should be considered for ICD therapy – only those with LVEF ≤ 35% (Q30)
  • LBBB → dyssynchronous wall motion and function → progressive HF and worse symptoms; interventricular conduction delay ↑ sudden death risk
  • Asynchronous LV activation: abnormal septal motion, ↓ pulse pressure, ↓ EF and CO, ↓ diastolic filling time, prolonged MR
  • CRT: device under the L clavicle in subcutaneous tissue; RV and LV leads paced synchronously
  • RAFT: ICD-CRT patients do better than ICD alone

Proposed model of integrated care

Care matched to risk and complexity (Q31): stable low-risk patients with primary care (spoke); moderate risk at a community hub/local hospital; high-risk complex patients at an advanced cardiac centre (tertiary node).

blocks.html:
Donkey analogy of heart failure
  • Decompensated CHF: cardiac output cannot keep up with demand; preload ↑ (fluid/Na+ retention), afterload ↑ (SNS activation, vasoconstriction)
  • ACEIs/ARBs: ↓ afterload/preload by blocking angiotensin/aldosterone
  • Loop diuretics: ↓ preload by ↓ fluid/Na+ retention
  • Hydralazine/nitrates: ↓ afterload/preload by blocking vasoconstriction / venodilation
  • Beta blockers: inhibit negative remodeling from the activated SNS
  • Inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine, milrinone): ↑ contractility and cardiac output
  • Ventricular assist device: assists the ventricle with contraction and pumping

Meet the patient: acute decompensated HF

A 45-year-old man presents to the ER with dyspnea at rest and 3 weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea, with PND, orthopnea and ankle edema. No chest pain, cough or sputum. PMHx unremarkable apart from ongoing smoking.

  • BP 90/70, HR 100, SpO2 90% on room air
  • CVS: normal S1, S2; S3; 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the apex; JVP 7 cm ASA
  • Chest: basal crackles; abdomen normal
  • 2+ bilateral peripheral edema with cool extremities

Next investigations (choose all that apply): (a) CBC, electrolytes, BUN/Cr; (b) ECG; (c) CXR; (d) BNP; (e) spirometry; (f) CT chest; (g) echocardiogram.

blocks.cap: Labs: Na+ 125, BNP 1100 pg/mL (normal < 100), troponin negative.

blocks.cap: ECG: septal Q waves in V1-V3 – old anterior MI.

blocks.cap: CXR: vascular redistribution and fluid in the fissure – congestive heart failure.

blocks.html:
• ECG: septal Q waves in V1-V3, suggesting an old anterior MI
  • CXR: vascular redistribution and fluid in the fissure, most likely CHF

Initial therapy?

  • a) Supplemental O2 and IV diuretics – clinically in HF, needs decongestion with IV diuretic (furosemide); hypoxic, needs O2
  • b) Beta blocker – contraindicated in class IV HF; can cause hemodynamic compromise
  • c) Heparin – ECG suggests an old MI, troponin negative, no chest pain; no need for anticoagulation
  • d) Spironolactone – not used acutely; wait to demonstrate EF < 40%

Profile with the worst prognosis? Cold and wet – suggestive of cardiogenic shock. “Cold” = cold extremities (high SVR or low cardiac index, poor perfusion); “wet” = volume overload (elevated JVP, crackles, S3, BNP, CXR).

blocks.alt: Warm/cold and wet/dry profiles; hypoperfusion is not synonymous with hypotension
blocks.cap: Warm/cold and wet/dry profiles; hypoperfusion is not synonymous with hypotension.

blocks.html:
Echocardiogram
  • Severely dilated LV, EF 25%, akinetic septum and apex; no thrombus
  • Normal RV size and function
  • Mild MR

Options if no response to initial therapy? IABP, inotropes, LVAD, transplant – all are possibilities: start with inotropes (milrinone, dobutamine) to ↑ CO and perfusion; if that fails, mechanical circulatory support with an IABP (most helpful with ischemia); if still deteriorating, emergency LVAD or transplant listing.

He responds to IV diuretics, is hospitalized for a week, loses 15 lb and feels much better; milrinone is needed initially, then stopped.

HFrEF < 40% – which drugs improve mortality? ACEI, ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta blockers, spironolactone, ivabradine – all have proven mortality benefit; digoxin ↓ hospitalization but has no mortality benefit.

Follow-up: GDMT started; discharged on a flexible diuretic regimen; referred to the outpatient HF Clinic; primary care follow-up in 1 week with bloodwork for electrolytes and renal function.

Module questions 1-14
  1. Causes and symptoms of HF? Causes: MI, CAD, chronic hypertension, valve disease, arrhythmias, chronic pulmonary disease. Symptoms: dyspnea, fatigue and weakness, edema in feet and ascites, rapid/irregular heartbeat, ↓ exercise tolerance, wheezing and productive cough, nocturia, poor appetite, nausea, poor concentration/↓ alertness
  2. Compensated vs decompensated? Compensated: asymptomatic despite ↓ function (enlarged heart, ↑ HR). Decompensated: symptomatic, needs treatment, increasingly frequent hospitalizations
  3. NYHA classes? Four categories based on limitation of physical activity (breathlessness or angina), from Class I (no limitation) to Class IV (symptoms at rest)
  4. Types of HF? Left-sided, right-sided, biventricular
  5. Right vs left symptoms? See the left vs right table above
  6. Two types of left-sided HF? Systolic (pumping problem; ↓ EF; ↑ preload) and diastolic (filling problem; preserved EF; ↑ afterload)
  7. Preload and afterload? Preload: ventricular stretch at end-diastole; reflects venous pressure/return and filling – a volume measure. Afterload: pressure the chambers must generate in systole; set by SVR/PVR, arterial pressure and vascular tone – a pressure measure
  8. Cor pulmonale? RHF, often from chronic lung disease or other causes of pulmonary hypertension; ↑ RA and RV pressure → maladaptive remodeling
  9. Concentric vs eccentric remodeling? Eccentric: adaptive to volume overload (e.g. pregnancy), reversible; walls thin, sarcomeres in series. Concentric: compensates for pressure overload by thickening the wall; pathological; HFpEF; sarcomeres in parallel. Concentric can progress to maladaptive eccentric remodeling (mitochondrial dysfunction, cell death) → HFrEF; may partly reverse with a VAD
  10. Neurohormonal dysregulation? See the neurohormonal section and flowchart above
  11. AVP in HF? See the AVP section above
  12. Identifying HF etiology? Categorize as HFrEF/HFmrEF, HFpEF, or congenital; consider common causes first (tachyarrhythmia, valve disease, known CAD or CAD risk factors, LVH), then less common ones (toxins, nutritional deficiency, genetic defects, infiltrative disease)
  13. Drug classes? ACEI, ARB, beta blockers – BP lowering; MRA – diuretic and BP lowering; ARNI (sacubitril/losartan); If inhibitors – slow pacemaker activity and HR; vasodilators – relax vascular SMC, ↓ afterload, useful in systolic HF; positive inotropes (digoxin) – ↑ contractile force, no proven effect on long-term outcomes
  14. HF and arrhythmia? AF → ↑ and irregular rate → ↓ cardiac output → HF; HF → atrial enlargement → AF. Causality unclear, but many with AF also have HF

True – late manifestation of almost any heart disease; progressive and ultimately fatal
A syndrome results from a specific disease process
False – syndromes occur in the absence of a specific disease process

True – frequent hospitalization, high morbidity and mortality

True – prognosis is set by symptoms plus structural disease
The most common etiology is end-stage ischemic heart disease

blocks.html:
1. Which sign (PND, orthopnea, lung crackles, liver congestion/ascites) suggests right rather than left HF? Liver congestion/ascites
  2. Which perfusion/congestion profile has the worst prognosis? Cold and wet
  3. Prevalence and incidence of HF in Canada? Prevalence > 600 000; incidence > 50 000/year
  4. Classic HF drugs target: angiotensin II (ACEI, ARB), sympathetic activity (beta blockers), aldosterone (MRA)
  5. Do higher resting heart rates carry worse outcomes? Yes – lowering HR reduces mortality
  6. ICD/CRT for all HF or only LVEF ≤ 35%? Only LVEF ≤ 35% – increased risk of sudden death from ventricular arrhythmia
  7. How could an integrated care model reduce morbidity and mortality? (reflection – see the integrated care model above)

lectures.title: Heart Failure: Physiology, Classification and Management
lectures.framing: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome, not a disease: symptoms and signs plus structural heart disease. Its engine is neurohormonal activation (SNS, RAAS, AVP) – an appropriate response to dehydration turned harmful – and nearly every HFrEF drug blocks one limb of it.
lectures.keypoints: EF is not needed for the diagnosis; symptoms are always the last stage. HFpEF is 60%, HFrEF 40% (ischemic 65% of HFrEF). AHA stages never go backwards; NYHA class can. Low BNP rules out HF; a normal ECG makes it very unlikely. Cold and wet has the worst prognosis. HFrEF: ACEI/ARB→ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i, ivabradine if sinus HR ≥ 70; ICD/CRT if LVEF ≤ 35%. HFpEF has no proven therapy beyond diuretics.

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Elevated blood pressure: a BP level associated with an increase in long-term risk
  • Hypertension: a BP level at which treatment is associated with a decrease in long-term risk
Why it matters
  • Most attributable risk factor for global disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs)
  • Leading reason patients present to primary care and specialty offices
  • Second most important risk factor for stroke, after atrial fibrillation

blocks.html:
BP variability
  • BP varies throughout the day, which makes assessment a challenge; white coat hypertension is also a problem
  • Readings vary with who takes them – retraining is important for normalization

blocks.alt: Figure from the Hypertension: Diagnosis, Causes and Risk notes

blocks.html:
BP and age
  • Systolic BP rises linearly with age
  • Diastolic BP begins to fall around age 55 due to loss of compliance → widened pulse pressure

blocks.html:
1) Determine that the patient with high BP has hypertension
  • One high BP reading ≠ hypertension
  • Manual BPM accuracy is affected by device, provider and patient factors: conversation during the reading, only one reading recorded, no rest period, rapid cuff deflation, rounding to 0 or 5, patient anxiety in a healthcare setting
  • Routine clinical BP is 9/6 mm Hg higher than standardized research BP
Proper BP procedure
  • Sit in a comfortable chair, back supported, feet flat on the floor, arm at heart level
  • 5-minute rest; take a first and second reading, and a third if they differ significantly
  • NEVER record BP on an exam table or supine in a hospital bed to determine future CV risk

blocks.lead: BP measurement methods – HBPM and ABPM predict CV risk better than office BPM; night-time BP correlates best with future CV events.

blocks.title: Fun fact: standing upright
blocks.html: One adaptation that lets humans stand on two legs is increased afterload: nerves to the leg arteries constrict the vessels on standing so BP does not fall. BP can change beat to beat as the body adapts it to what we are doing.

blocks.alt: Figure from the Hypertension: Diagnosis, Causes and Risk notes

blocks.html:
BP and cardiovascular risk
  • MRFIT: SBP 120-129 → ↑ CV risk; SBP > 140 → significant ↑ CV risk; a drop in DBP → ↑ CV risk
  • High-normal BP increases the risk of developing CVD
  • SHEP: a 12 mm Hg drop in SBP was associated with a 40% reduction in stroke
  • In general, lowering SBP lowers stroke risk – trials use a baseline of 140-160 mm Hg

Endocrine: pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly

blocks.html:
• Modifiable aggravating factors: alcohol, excess salt, recreational drugs, NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, anabolic steroids, erythropoietin, calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), ephedrine/pseudoephedrine, black licorice (glycyrrhizic acid ↑ cortisol levels), sleep apnea
  • Preliminary Ix: urinalysis; blood chemistry (K+, Na+, Cr); serum Ca2+ and albumin; TSH; HbA1c; lipid profile; standard 12-lead ECG
3) Determine the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes
  • Hypertension is a risk factor for cerebrovascular disease (dementia), CHF, AF, renal failure, CAD, peripheral vascular disease, erectile dysfunction
  • Benefits of lowering BP: ↓ CHF 60%, ↓ stroke 40%, ↓ CAD 15%
  • Risk assessment: clinical impression, risk factor counting/equation tools, Framingham risk score, cardiovascular age score
4) Make a plan to lower risk with lifestyle and medications
  • Lifestyle management for all
  • More aggressive management for higher CV risk – early pharmacotherapy, lower BP targets
  • Choose medications by patient factors (drug plan, adverse events), disease factors (ACEI for CHF), drug factors (long-acting once daily; low, fixed-dose combinations)
  • Details: see Management of Hypertension

Module questions

37. The pharmacist told your patient to go to the ER because his pharmacy BP was 176/105. Which are true? (select all)

  • a) Based on BP alone, he should go straight to the ED – false: nothing indicates urgency/emergency
  • b) He is going to die soon – technically true, but probably not soon
  • c) He has a high blood pressure – true
  • d) He has hypertension – false: one high reading ≠ hypertension
  • e) His BP needs re-evaluation before hypertension can be diagnosed – true
  • f) Checking your blood pressure while shoplifting is not a good idea
  • g) He should be encouraged to do a series of “out of office” BP measurements – true

38. Which of eggs, salt, excess adiposity, obstructive sleep apnea, excess water, excess alcohol, lectures about hypertension cause hypertension? Salt, obstructive sleep apnea, excessive alcohol consumption

lectures.title: Hypertension: Diagnosis, Causes and Risk
lectures.framing: Hypertension is defined by treatment benefit, not a number alone. The lecture follows the four-step approach: confirm it is really hypertension, find a cause, estimate CV risk, then plan treatment.
lectures.keypoints: One high reading ≠ hypertension; clinic BP runs 9/6 mm Hg high, and ABPM is the gold standard (night-time BP best predicts events). SBP rises with age; DBP falls after ~55. OSA (10%) is the commonest secondary cause, then renal disease, primary aldosteronism, alcohol/substances and medications (5% each). Lowering BP cuts CHF 60%, stroke 40%, CAD 15%.

blocks.alt: Figure

blocks.html: First-line treatment of systolic/diastolic hypertension without compelling indications

blocks.alt: Target < 135/85 (automated): health behaviours, then thiazide/thiazide-like, ACEI, ARB, long-acting CCB, beta blocker, or a single-pill combination (ACEI+CCB, ARB+CCB, ACEI/ARB+diuretic)
blocks.cap: Target < 135/85 (automated): health behaviours, then thiazide/thiazide-like, ACEI, ARB, long-acting CCB, beta blocker, or a single-pill combination (ACEI+CCB, ARB+CCB, ACEI/ARB+diuretic).

blocks.html:
• BP > 10 mm Hg above target → start 2 medications as a low-dose single-pill combination
  • Plan for most patients to be on a 3-drug cocktail: RAAS inhibitor (ACEI/ARB) + diuretic/dihydropyridine CCB
  • Longer-acting (thiazide-like) diuretics are preferred over shorter-acting (thiazide) diuretics
  • RAAS inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy; caution in women of childbearing potential
  • Beta blockers are not recommended first line for patients ≥ 60 without another compelling indication (angina, CHF)
  • Avoid diuretic-induced hypokalemia by using K+-sparing agents when possible (ACEI, ARB)
  • ACEI are not used as monotherapy for Black patients without another compelling indication – higher rates of low-renin hypertension, so drugs that stimulate renin are preferred first line
Combination therapy
  • If BP does not improve on one drug, add a second drug rather than doubling the first – much more effective, fewer side effects
  • ALLHAT: BP control rates depend on physician willingness to escalate (use of 3+ drugs)

blocks.alt: Adding a second drug gives the full additive SBP reduction (ratio ~1.0); doubling the dose gives only ~0.2 of it
blocks.cap: Adding a second drug gives the full additive SBP reduction (ratio ~1.0); doubling the dose gives only ~0.2 of it.

rows: Do NOT use RAAS blockers (significant hyperkalemia or further renal impairment)

blocks.lead: Effective combinations = column A + column B. Preferred 3-drug cocktail = diuretic + ACEI/ARB + long-acting CCB. Monitor electrolytes when giving 2 drugs from the same column.

blocks.html:
Case example
  • 60-year-old man; annual check-up BP 165/95 by AOBP, confirmed with multiple HBPM readings
  • FHx of hypertension in parents and siblings; no OSA or other secondary causes
  • Initial investigations normal; S4 present

Best recommendation? All are reasonable: (a) Na+ < 2000 mg; (b) exercise ≥ 30 min, 5/7 days; (c) lose weight; (d) vegetables and high-K foods; (e) avoid eggs.

Despite complying, readings are identical. Medications? Yes – the usual office threshold to start drugs in low/moderate risk is ≥ 160 mm Hg.

Preferred long-acting medication? (a) ACEI (perindopril, trandolapril); (b) ARB (telmisartan, candesartan, irbesartan); (c) diuretic (indapamide, chlorthalidone); (d) DHP CCB (amlodipine, nifedipine); (e) beta blocker (bisoprolol).

What dose of the first medication? (a) ¼ dose (start low, go slow); (b) ½ dose (80% of the effect); (c) full dose (go big or go home).

blocks.alt: Dose-response: half the maximum dose gives ~80% of the SBP lowering of the full dose
blocks.cap: Dose-response: half the maximum dose gives ~80% of the SBP lowering of the full dose.

blocks.html:
Go ahead with combination therapy now? (a) No, starting two is dangerous; (b) absolutely, go big or go home; (c) yes, but as a low-dose single-pill combination – starting point 165/90 vs target 140/90: 25 points away = 3+ drugs.

If you add a second drug: ACEI + diuretic or ACEI + CCB.

Adherence strategies
  • Quality information on the consequences of hypertension and benefits of lifestyle and drugs
  • Ask about side effects and record them
  • Tie pill taking to a daily routine (same time/place/situation)
  • Simplify the drug and lifestyle regime; make it affordable
  • Involve family and friends
  • Regular BP follow-up
  • Blister packs or other adherence aids; self-measurement of BP
  • Record refill dates on a calendar; consider self-monitoring pill counts

BP drug treatment for the average patient (Dr. George Dresser)
  • Step 1: RAAS inhibitor – ACEI vs ARB: what are the odds the patient will complain of a cough on treatment?
  • Step 2: synergy and side effects – diuretic vs CCB: look at serum K+ and volume status (pedal edema)

blocks.alt: Step 2: normal/low K+ with little edema → DHP CCB; high K+ or marked edema → thiazide-like diuretic
blocks.cap: Step 2: normal/low K+ with little edema → DHP CCB; high K+ or marked edema → thiazide-like diuretic.

blocks.html:
• Step 3: more synergy – diuretic or CCB: add the one not added in step 2
  • Step 4: spironolactone (MRA) vs doxazosin (α1 antagonist) vs beta blocker: look at serum K+ and heart rate
  • Step 5: monitor: this 4-drug cocktail controls BP in 95% of average patients; a patient not at target is either very exceptional or not taking the medication. Directly observed therapy: in clinic, on an ABP monitor, watch them take all 4 agents and monitor BP for 4-6 hours to confirm an inadequate response
  • Step 6: beta blocker vs doxazosin, based on K+ and kidney function: poor kidney function → switch to a renal-impairment algorithm; K+ > 3.7 mmol/L → more thiazide-like diuretic; K+ < 3.7 mmol/L → increase spironolactone

blocks.alt: Step 4: low K+ → spironolactone; high K+ → doxazosin; high heart rate (> 85) → beta blocker
blocks.cap: Step 4: low K+ → spironolactone; high K+ → doxazosin; high heart rate (> 85) → beta blocker.

blocks.html:
Module questions

39. Faced with a patient with high BP, which is most accurate about starting active treatment?

  • a) If BP is above the population mean for age, weight and sex, treatment is beneficial
  • b) The absolute BP level is more important than the patient's global CV risk
  • c) Treatment should only be offered if experimental evidence shows treating similar patients reduces CV risk
  • d) Drugs are generally harmful and should be avoided unless the patient asks for them
  • e) Most patients can be managed with healthy behaviours and one medication

40. Preferred combinations for the average hypertensive patient? (a) diuretic + CCB; (b) ACEI + beta blocker; (c) ARB + spironolactone; (d) ACEI + diuretic; (e) beta blocker + any RAAS inhibitor

41. In low-risk patients, guidelines advise not starting treatment until SBP > 160, while in high-risk patients the threshold can be as low as 130. Is the wide variation warranted? Recommendations are based on treatment trials lasting at most 7-8 years; in low-risk patients it is impossible to accumulate enough outcome events to show benefit until BP is quite high.

lectures.title: Treatment of Hypertension
lectures.framing: Treatment intensity follows global CV risk: thresholds and targets tighten as risk rises. Most patients need several drugs combined (RAAS stimulator + RAAS inhibitor), added rather than dose-doubled.
lectures.keypoints: Start drugs at ≥ 160 (low risk), ≥ 140 (moderate), ≥ 130 (diabetes, high risk); targets < 140/90, < 130/80 diabetes, ≤ 120 high risk. > 10 mm Hg above target → low-dose single-pill combination. Add a drug rather than double one – half dose gives 80% of the effect. Preferred 3-drug cocktail: diuretic + ACEI/ARB + long-acting CCB. No RAAS blockers in pregnancy or renovascular disease; no BB first line at ≥ 60.

lectures.name: Congenital Heart Disease

blocks.html: Congenital heart disease (CHD): any alteration in the structural development of the heart. The most common congenital defect – 1% of all births, not counting bicuspid aortic valve and small muscular VSDs.

Embryology of the heart
  • Day 14: primary heart field in a crescent on the cranial side of the embryo; as the embryo grows, the heart tube rotates on the transverse axis to lie ventral and caudal
  • Day 20: bilateral endocardial tubes filled with cardiac jelly
  • Day 21: tubes bulge towards each other at the dorsal end and fuse in the midline
  • Day 22: primitive heart tube with precursors of the main structures – truncus arteriosus + bulbus cordis → great arteries; primitive ventricle → ventricles; primitive atrium → atria; tube elongates by proliferation of secondary heart field cells
  • Day 24: cardiac looping anterior and to the right, as top and bottom are anchored
  • Day 35: atria move cranially, giving a common AV canal; RV gives rise to both outflow tracts
  • Septation: muscle walls grow toward the middle between atria, ventricles and outflow tracts; foramen ovale forms in the atrial septum; the outflow septum spirals down to the ventricles, giving blood two paths out of the heart
  • Then valve formation and branching of the great arteries and veins

blocks.html:
Fetal circulation
  • Goals: deliver oxygenated placental blood to the coronaries and brain; protect the non-aerated lungs
  • Shunts bypass the lungs (in parallel): oxygenated blood to head/heart, deoxygenated back to the placenta
  • 100% of blood goes to the body, only 10% to the lungs
  • Ductus venosus – placental blood bypasses the hepatic circulation
  • Foramen ovale – placental blood bypasses the right heart
  • Ductus arteriosus – deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs into the descending aorta
What can go wrong?
  • Looping stage: different connections between atria, ventricles and great arteries; different heart orientations
  • Septal stage: septal defects – “holes in the heart” (ASD, VSD)
  • Later stages: valve stenosis/regurgitation, abnormal venous connections, distal aorta and PA abnormalities
  • Persistent fetal circulation: patent shunts

blocks.alt: Fetal circulation: ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus
blocks.cap: Fetal circulation: ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus.

blocks.html:
Cardiac hemodynamics
  • The impact of a shunt depends on the pressure gradient (location), resistance of the capillary beds (PVR/SVR), and resistance of the hole/tube (radius, length)
Approach to CHD

1) Pink (acyanotic) or blue (cyanotic)?

  • Deoxygenated Hb is blue-toned; oxygenated Hb red-toned
  • Cyanosis appears when deoxygenated Hb > 5 g/dL in the systemic circulation – there must be deoxygenated blood in the systemic circulation
  • Requires desaturation, but is less prominent with anemia

2) Degree of pulmonary blood flow (PBF)

  • ↑ PBF = lighter lungs (fluid); vascular markings reach the lung edges; proximal branch PAs more prominent
  • ↓ PBF = darker lungs; proximal branch PAs look smaller

blocks.cap: Increased pulmonary blood flow: vascular markings extend to the periphery.

blocks.alt: Decreased pulmonary blood flow: dark lung fields, small branch PAs

3) Associated findings

  • Symptoms: congestive symptoms
  • Signs: abnormal precordium, pulses, heart sounds, murmurs – lesion specific
  • Ix: ECG and CXR (less specific, more available); echocardiogram (usually definitive, less available)

Acyanotic lesions: left-to-right shunts
  • Communication between the right and left heart
  • In isolation, blood moves left → right because of higher left-sided pressures and lower pulmonary vascular resistance

Hemodynamics: ↑ flow – volume overload of the pulmonary circulation

Acyanotic obstructive lesions
  • 6-8% of CHD; usually normal PBF – no shunts; isolated valve lesions picked up on exam
  • Coarctation of the aorta: narrowing where the ductus arteriosus inserts → ↓ flow to the lower body – ↓ femoral pulses and leg BP
    • Less critical: murmur, hypertension as an older child
    • Critical: ↓ gut perfusion, HF as a neonate
    • Tx: surgery or stenting of the narrowed segment

Cyanotic lesions: cardiac or non-cardiac?
  • Most cyanosis is respiratory or infectious – management is very different
  • Hyperoxia test: PaO2 response to 100% inspired O2
  • PaO2 < 100-150 on 100% O2 suggests a cardiac cause – it should be ~600

1% of CHD
Single artery leaves the heart and gives rise to aorta and PAs; large VSD with the trunk committed to both ventricles
Blood mixes on exit → cyanosis; easy lung flow → high PBF at the expense of organ perfusion

Tx: surgery in the first 1-2 weeks – VSD patched so the trunk becomes the aorta; PAs connected to the RV by a conduit

Transposition of the great arteries
2 – cross two fingers
↑ PBF

Circulations in parallel (two independent circuits) instead of series
Survival depends on fetal shunts letting red blood reach the systemic circulation
5% of CHD – most common cyanotic CHD presenting as a neonate

Profound cyanosis in the newborn period with minimal respiratory distress for the saturation; little/no murmur
Severe cyanosis is life-threatening

3% of CHD
Absent tricuspid valve – single ventricle lesion

6% of CHD – most common cyanotic CHD

Severity follows the RV outflow obstruction: mild – harsh SEM, subtle/late cyanosis; severe – newborn cyanosis
Tet spells: dynamic loss of pulmonary outflow → babies go extremely blue (life-threatening)
Un-operated: progressive cyanosis, tet spells, limited lifespan
Tx: surgery at 4-6 months – close VSD, open RV outflow
