blocks.html:
Treatment of cyanotic CHD
  • All cyanotic CHD needs surgery to survive – usually curative, sometimes needing further surgery; single-ventricle lesions get palliative surgery to reach adulthood
  • Prostaglandin keeps the PDA open → ↑ PBF; helpful when cyanosis is due to ↓ PBF (tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot)

Case example: Ali

A 1-month-old boy sent to the ED by his GP for a murmur and cyanosis.

  • History: feeding and growing normally; no ↑ work of breathing; murmur and ‘duskiness’ noted at the 1-month check; no medical history; normal development and pregnancy; FHx: Tetralogy of Fallot in a maternal uncle, VSD in his sister
  • Two most important next steps: general inspection – ABCs; full vital signs – BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation
  • Exam: well, no distress; vitals normal except SpO2 86% on room air; harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB radiating to axilla and back; rest normal
  • No echo available – next test? Chest x-ray – shows whether PBF is decreased or normal, and any subtle lung pathology

blocks.cap: Ali's chest x-ray: decreased pulmonary blood flow; boot-shaped heart.

blocks.html:
Most likely diagnosis? (a) isolated VSD; (b) obstructed TAPVR; (c) TGA; (d) Tetralogy of Fallot – pulmonary stenosis murmur, ↓ PBF, most common cyanotic CHD, “boot”-shaped heart; (e) bicuspid aortic valve.

Next: refer to pediatric cardiology for full assessment and echo; surgery around 4-6 months; follow for progressive desaturation and tet spells.

Module questions

42. A 3-month-old with a pansystolic murmur, poor weight gain, moderate ↑ work of breathing, tachypnea, hyperdynamic precordium and enlarged liver. Most likely diagnosis?

  • a) ASD – no pansystolic murmur or congestion
  • b) Small muscular VSD – no congestion
  • c) Moderate perimembranous VSD
  • d) Bicuspid aortic valve – no pansystolic murmur or congestion
  • e) PDA – continuous murmur ± congestion

43. NICU: a 12-hour-old ‘dusky’ baby in minimal distress, SpO2 65%, otherwise normal exam. Most likely?

  • a) Transposition of the great arteries – most common CHD presenting in newborns; no significant murmur, severe cyanosis
  • b) TAPVR – presents later with less cyanosis
  • c) Sepsis – cyanosis but ↑ work of breathing
  • d) Pneumonia – cyanosis but ↑ work of breathing
  • e) Hypoplastic left heart syndrome – single ventricle lesion presenting with ↓ cardiac output

Pediatric heart murmurs: scope of the problem
  • Extremely common: up to 80% of children have a murmur at some point; 98-99% are not CHD
  • Innocent murmurs are benign sounds from blood ejected out of a NORMAL heart
  • They cause significant parental and clinician anxiety; GPs need to distinguish innocent from pathologic and counsel families
  • Referral is common, and most referred murmurs are innocent; many can be diagnosed by careful history and exam
  • Pediatricians and neonatologists diagnose murmurs with reasonable accuracy

blocks.html:
Pediatric cardiology case 1

A 3-year-old boy referred for a murmur: new doctor; no parental concerns, symptoms or relevant history; murmur found incidentally, rest of exam normal. Murmur: 2/6 systolic ejection, vibratory, low-pitched, LLSB with minimal radiation, louder supine.

Most likely cause? (a) pulmonary stenosis – harsh with click; (b) innocent murmur – Still's murmur; (c) VSD – pansystolic; (d) AR – diastolic; (e) PDA – continuous.

Case example: Budi

A 6-year-old boy referred for a murmur found on a routine check, with no other concerns. No chest pain, palpitations, SOB, cyanosis, syncope or presyncope; normal energy and activity; normal history, development, pregnancy and diet; no FHx of CHD, arrhythmia, HF, early CAD or sudden unexplained death.

Describing a murmur: timing (systolic, diastolic, continuous); type (ejection/crescendo-decrescendo, pansystolic; early, mid, late diastolic); intensity 1-6; quality (harsh, blowing, musical); location, radiation, changes with maneuvers.

The murmur is a 2/6 continuous murmur just above the right clavicle that disappears with firm pressure on the neck and on lying down. Cause? (a) peripheral PA stenosis; (b) Still's murmur; (c) venous hum; (d) aortic stenosis; (e) PDA.

Venous hum diagnosed – next steps? (a) reassure the child and parents that no further intervention is required; (b) refer to cardiology; (c) ECG; (d) restrict all physical activity; (e) send to the ED to start beta blockers.

Pediatric chest pain
  • Normal children do not have heart attacks – some populations may be at higher risk from other medical problems
  • Growing pains are common; muscles and bones often hurt
  • The rib cage is more cartilaginous in children; ossification occurs in adolescence
  • Most parents worry that chest pain = heart attack

Quality (often hard for children to describe), quantity, location (discrete vs vague), associated symptoms
FHx, PMHx

Reproducible pain

Non-cardiac abnormalities – signs of respiratory disease (wheeze)
Random, including rest; pleuritic; body position
Exercise (and only exercise); predictable degree of exertion

blocks.html:
Pediatric cardiology case 2

A 10-year-old girl referred for chest pain. What would suggest a cardiac cause?

  • a) Pain only with activity (never at rest) – consistent exertional pain is the hallmark of cardiac chest pain
  • b) Sharp, left-sided – MSK
  • c) Easily reproduced by palpation – MSK
  • d) Wakes the patient from sleep – non-specific
  • e) Also has a systolic murmur – common in innocent murmurs

Kawasaki disease
  • Acute, self-limited febrile illness; cause unknown – possibly an abnormal immune reaction to an infectious trigger
  • 21/100 000 children – most common acquired pediatric heart disease in the developed world
  • At risk: children < 5 years; males > females (1.5:1); Asian (especially Japanese) highest risk, Caucasian lowest
Diagnostic criteria (clinical diagnosis)

At least 4-5 days of fever and 4 of 5:

  • Bilateral, non-purulent conjunctivitis
  • Mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips)
  • Rash
  • Indurated, red hands and feet
  • Unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy ≥ 1.5 cm

blocks.title: Kawasaki criteria mnemonic: fever + 4 of CREAM
blocks.html: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Extremity changes (red, indurated hands/feet), Adenopathy (unilateral cervical ≥ 1.5 cm), Mucosal changes – with ≥ 4-5 days of fever.

rows:
Microvascular angiitis, acute endarteritis; classic symptoms
Labs: thrombocytopenia, aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria, ↑ CRP
Rarely HF, dysrhythmia

Panvasculitis of coronaries with aneurysms and thrombus
Desquamation of hands/feet; fever resolves
Labs: thrombocytosis
Coronary scarring, stenosis, calcification, recanalization; myocardial fibrosis; CRP normalizes

blocks.html:
Risk of coronary artery aneurysms
  • Untreated: 25%; with treatment within 10 days of fever onset: 4%
  • Asian (Japanese) > Hispanic > Caucasian > African

blocks.alt: Coronary aneurysm risk in Kawasaki disease
blocks.cap: Coronary aneurysm risk in Kawasaki disease.

blocks.html:
Treatment
  • To prevent coronary complications: IVIG (↓ aneurysm formation) + ASA (prevents clots)
  • If coronary complications: ongoing antiplatelets; anticoagulation; exercise restriction and lifelong follow-up; possible coronary stenting/CABG

blocks.html:
Pediatric cardiology case 4

A 5-year-old girl with a persistent fever for 6 days (responds to acetaminophen); parents at their wits' end with how fussy she is. Exam: miserable but not in extremis; a single large (2 cm) mobile, mildly tender left cervical node; red sclera (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis); cracked, dry, strawberry-like lips and tongue; diffuse non-specific erythematous rash.

Diagnosis: Kawasaki disease.

blocks.alt: Kawasaki features: conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue and cracked lips, rash, hand and foot changes
blocks.cap: Kawasaki features: conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue and cracked lips, rash, hand and foot changes.

lectures.title: Congenital Heart Disease
lectures.framing: CHD is sorted with two questions: pink or blue? and how much pulmonary blood flow? The answers group the lesions (left-to-right shunts, obstructions, right-to-left shunts, mixing lesions, separate circulations), and each group follows from where development went wrong. The lecture also covers pediatric murmurs, chest pain and Kawasaki disease.
lectures.keypoints: CHD affects 1% of births. Cyanosis needs > 5 g/dL deoxygenated Hb; a hyperoxia PaO2 < 100-150 points to the heart. ASD: wide fixed split S2, often found in adults; VSD: pansystolic murmur, congestion at 6-12 weeks; PDA: continuous murmur, bounding pulses. TGA is the commonest cyanotic lesion in neonates; ToF the commonest overall. 98-99% of pediatric murmurs are innocent (Still's most common). Kawasaki: fever ≥ 4-5 days + 4/5 features; IVIG + ASA within 10 days cuts aneurysms from 25% to 4%.

Pediatric cardiology case 3

A 15-year-old male is referred for palpitations. First question: what is meant by “palpitations” – fast? irregular? hard? slow?

rows: What the palpitations feel like (fast? irregular?), onset and offset, triggers, actual heart rate if measured
Not particularly helpful – usually not having palpitations in clinic

Try to capture the rhythm while symptomatic
Resting ECG may be normal, but may show patterns predisposing to arrhythmia
ECG during palpitations is diagnostic
Longer-term rhythm monitoring: Holter (2-lead continuous ECG, 24-48 hours, rarely 1-2 weeks) or longer continuous/intermittent monitors (3-8 weeks)

Sinus tachycardia – exercise, anxiety, presyncope (dehydration, position changes, prolonged standing), organic (hyperthyroid, hypertension)
Sinus rhythm – increased awareness of a normal heart rate
Supraventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is more likely to present with syncope than palpitations
Less than maximal HR; usually < 150-180 bpm at rest
Usually > 200 bpm (slightly slower in older adolescents); too fast to count
Rapid (may be slower if anxiety adds a sinus tachycardia)
May have presyncope or SOB with or before palpitations; normal exam
Presyncope, chest pain or SOB follow the onset of palpitations; usually normal exam

lectures.title: Pediatric Palpitations
lectures.framing: In an adolescent with palpitations, the task is separating sinus tachycardia (gradual, rate-appropriate) from SVT (abrupt, > 200 bpm) – and the exam rarely helps, so the diagnosis comes from history and capturing the rhythm.
lectures.keypoints: An ECG during symptoms is diagnostic; Holter 24-48 h or 3-8 week monitors capture it. SVT: abrupt onset (1-5 s), usually > 200 bpm; sinus tachycardia: slow onset (> 10-30 s), < 150-180 at rest. Resting ECG may show WPW. VT presents with syncope rather than palpitations.

lectures.name: Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

blocks.html:
Recognizing advanced heart failure
  • Low perfusion at rest = COLD
  • Cold + wet = cardiogenic shock

blocks.alt: HF stages A-D: therapies escalate step by step; stage D (refractory) adds inotropes, VAD/transplant, hospice
blocks.cap: HF stages A-D: therapies escalate step by step; stage D (refractory) adds inotropes, VAD/transplant, hospice.

blocks.html: A patient approaching end-stage HF will tell you – I NEED HELP:

rows: Previous or ongoing dobutamine, milrinone or dopamine
Persistent NYHA III/IV symptoms or persistently high BNP
Persistent edema or frequent diuretic dose adjustments
Need to reduce / inability to uptitrate goal-directed therapies

blocks.html:
Referral
  • Once advanced HF is identified, refer to a centre providing advanced care – mechanical devices (ventricular assist devices) or transplant
  • Being referred or seen at a transplant centre does NOT mean the patient is “listed” – one of the options will be considered
  • Very few advanced HF patients meet transplant criteria – only 50 people on the waitlist in Ontario
Patients approaching stage D
  • Recognize your limits as a physician in treating a complex condition
  • Allow your patient to be considered for specialized therapies, usually concentrated in a few centres
  • Inform your patient about the seriousness of their condition and provide information on prognosis and outcomes
Inotropic therapy
  • Most HF therapies slow or reverse progression, but beyond a point they may give no benefit – cold patients
  • Beta blockers may not help at this stage because of their negative inotropy (which tries to preserve ventricular function) – consider reducing them, recognizing this marks advancing disease
  • Inotropes improve symptoms but do NOT prolong life and may precipitate arrhythmias
  • Inotropy is a bridge to a durable therapy (transplant/LVAD) or palliation

Cardiac transplantation
  • Orthotopic: recipient heart explanted and the donor heart implanted in its place
  • Heterotopic: recipient heart left in situ; donor heart placed in series

blocks.alt: Orthotopic transplant: aorta, pulmonary artery, SVC and IVC connections
blocks.cap: Orthotopic transplant: aorta, pulmonary artery, SVC and IVC connections.

blocks.html:
Components of transplant assessment
  1. Does the patient want transplant/advanced options?
  2. Is the condition advanced enough to warrant transplant? Severe symptoms, supplemented by cardiopulmonary exercise testing and invasive hemodynamics
  3. Any contraindications? Significant comorbidities, psychosocial considerations, immunological issues, surgical considerations, age
  • The ethical principle of justice matters – there are usually too few donors for those who might benefit
Post-transplant care
  • Patients are often frail and deconditioned – intensive rehabilitation pre- and post-operatively
  • Immunosuppression: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone
  • Prophylaxis against opportunistic infection – pneumocystis, CMV
  • Routine endomyocardial biopsies to assess for rejection
Outcomes
  • Graft half-life: at 12 years, 50% of hearts are no longer functioning
  • Early deaths: infection, rejection, vasoplegia, cerebrovascular events
  • Later deaths: cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, infection/rejection
  • Transplant numbers rose in the mid-1980s with better immunosuppression (cyclosporine)

blocks.alt: Transplant survival by era: median 8.4 years (1982-1991) and 10.7 years (1992-2001)
blocks.cap: Transplant survival by era: median 8.4 years (1982-1991) and 10.7 years (1992-2001).

blocks.alt: US heart transplants rose sharply from the mid-1980s
blocks.cap: US heart transplants rose sharply from the mid-1980s.

blocks.html:
Ventricular assist devices (VAD)
  • Surgically implanted, electrically driven pump moving blood from the ventricle(s) into the arterial circulation
  • Durations: temporary and durable
  • Designs: axial and centrifugal
  • Brands: HeartMate II and III, HeartWare HVAD

rows: Blood travels in the same direction as the rotor's orientation
Blood enters perpendicular to the rotor's orientation
Blood can contact static devices – stators
Rotor need not contact any static surface – magnetic levitation
Less sensitive to physiological factors like afterload
More sensitive to afterload changes because of the 90° entry
Physiological changes affect the device's ability to offload

blocks.alt: Figure from the Advanced Heart Failure notes
Figure from the Advanced Heart Failure notes
Figure from the Advanced Heart Failure notes

blocks.html:
VAD components
  1. Well-positioned, unimpeded pump – inflow cannula, rotor (propeller), outflow cannula
  2. Intact driveline – delivers power and operating information to the pump
  3. Functioning controller – tells the pump what to do and monitors it
  4. Power supply – battery or wall socket
  • Batteries and controller are outside the patient; the driveline tunnels in to the pump
Indications
  • Bridge to another therapy (temporary → durable VAD) or to transplant
  • Destination therapy for non-transplant candidates – a patient may not qualify for transplant but may for a VAD
Complications
  • Foreign body providing non-physiologic flow – pulseless
  • Driveline infection – most patients develop this; surface or deep
  • GI bleeding
  • Stroke/intracranial hemorrhage
  • Device thrombosis
  • Pump malfunction

Palliative care in advanced HF
  • No advanced therapy cures HF (not even transplant) – at best it trades an imminently lethal condition for a manageable one
  • Patients need to understand the main goal: improving symptoms, which may prolong longevity
  • Patients often die from HF itself or an HF-related complication
  • Palliative care traditionally focused on conditions with more predictable trajectories (cancer); HF is unpredictable, so palliative care should be considered earlier – but is often considered late
  • A “palli-active” approach is common: destination VAD, home inotropes, home IV diuretics, telehomecare

blocks.alt: HF trajectory: repeated decompensations, then transition to advanced HF – oral therapy failing, consider MCS/transplant, shift toward palliative care
blocks.cap: HF trajectory: repeated decompensations, then transition to advanced HF – oral therapy failing, consider MCS/transplant, shift toward palliative care.

blocks.html:
Module questions
  1. Which of narrow pulse pressure, worsening renal function, slow heart rate are signs of poor perfusion in HF? Narrow pulse pressure, worsening renal function
  2. Which of LVAD, implantable defibrillator, spironolactone, beta blockers is initiated in end-stage HF? Left ventricular assist device
  3. Criteria consistent with approaching end-stage HF: (a) LVEF < 20%; (b) reduction in beta-blocker dose; (c) recent inotropic therapy – all are I NEED HELP criteria
  4. Common (> 5%) VAD complications? Stroke, driveline infection
  5. Why is palliative care challenging in HF? The trajectory is unpredictable

lectures.title: Advanced Heart Failure
lectures.framing: Advanced (stage D) heart failure is recognized when standard therapy stops working – the patient is cold. The decision is then which durable option fits: transplant, VAD, or palliation, with inotropes as a bridge.
lectures.keypoints: I NEED HELP flags advanced HF. Cold + wet = cardiogenic shock. Inotropes improve symptoms but do not prolong life – bridge or palliation. Referral ≠ listing; transplant needs desire, severity, no contraindications. Post-transplant: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone, graft half-life ~12 years; late death from allograft vasculopathy. VADs are pulseless; driveline infection is nearly universal.

lectures.name: Mechanism of Arrhythmia

blocks.html:
Functions of the electrical system
  • Impulse initiation
    • Failure to initiate an impulse → bradycardia
    • Abnormal rapid repetitive initiation → tachycardia
  • Impulse conduction
    • Failure to conduct to all parts of the heart → bradycardia (conduction block)
    • Circular conduction (short circuit) → tachycardia
Automaticity
  • Automaticity: specialized cardiac tissue can initiate impulses and spontaneously depolarize
  • SA node determines when and how quickly the heart beats
  • Under normal physiologic stimuli the heartbeat accelerates and decelerates – neural control (autonomic input)

rows: P waves before each QRS complex
Narrow regular QRS complex without a preceding P wave
blocks.lead: Hierarchy of pacemaker automaticity – each lower site is slower.

blocks.html:
Abnormal automaticity
  • Pathologically suppressed automaticity → bradycardia
    • Sinus node disease – scarring with age, fibrosis, sick sinus syndrome
    • Metabolic conditions reducing sinus node automaticity – electrolyte disturbances, thyroid disease
  • Tissues can become automatic under pathologic conditions
    • Atrial tachycardia – an atrial focus rapidly and repetitively fires
    • During myocardial ischemia/infarction, ventricular muscle may develop automaticity → ventricular tachycardia
Case example

A 78-year-old woman is monitored for syncope.

blocks.alt: AF stops, then a 6-second pause with no atrial activity and no junctional escape
blocks.cap: AF stops, then a 6-second pause with no atrial activity and no junctional escape.

blocks.html:
• Rhythm strip shows reduced automaticity → a 6-second pause
  • Initially HR is rapid, irregular, with no P waves (atrial fibrillation)
  • When AF stops, nothing happens in the atrium for 6 seconds and no junctional escape beat takes over
  • Suppressed automaticity → bradycardia, dizziness, syncope
  • A pacemaker may be indicated to depolarize during the pause

Re-entry

Re-entry: re-stimulation of cardiac muscle due to circular conduction abnormalities.

  • Impulse conducts abnormally (usually circularly around an obstacle) and perpetuates itself
  • Common cause of tachycardia; does NOT cause bradycardia
Refractoriness protects against re-entry
  • Cardiac tissue has a long absolute refractory period after activation, caused by the long recovery phase of the AP
  • All ventricular muscle depolarizes in 80 ms, but repolarization takes 400 ms (QT interval)
  • This prevents re-stimulation of tissue and is anti-tachycardic

blocks.alt: Depolarization of the ventricle takes 80 ms (QRS); repolarization takes 400 ms (QT)
blocks.cap: Depolarization of the ventricle takes 80 ms (QRS); repolarization takes 400 ms (QT).

blocks.html:
Requirements for re-entry
  • A potential circuit – usually two halves (limbs)
  • Different refractoriness in each limb
  • Slow conduction in one region – lets previously activated tissue recover and be re-activated
  • Temporary conduction block in one direction – uni-directional block

blocks.alt: A premature beat blocks in the longer-refractory β limb, conducts slowly down α, then returns retrograde up β once it has recovered
blocks.cap: A premature beat blocks in the longer-refractory β limb, conducts slowly down α, then returns retrograde up β once it has recovered.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Premature beat - PAC"] --> B{"Both limbs refractory?"} B -->|"Yes"| C["No conduction"] B -->|"No"| D["Blocks in limb with longer refractoriness
uni-directional block"] D --> E["Conducts slowly down the other limb"] E --> F{"Blocked limb recovered
by the time impulse arrives?"} F -->|"No - conduction too fast"| G["Still refractory
no re-entry"] F -->|"Yes"| H["Retrograde conduction up the blocked limb"] H --> I["Circuit re-stimulates itself
re-entrant tachycardia"]

blocks.html:
1) AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) – Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)
  • Extra short circuit: an accessory pathway connecting atrium to ventricle outside the AV node
  • Sinus conduction goes normally down the AV node, around the ventricular conduction system, and back up the accessory pathway
  • Forms a circuit that re-stimulates the AV node, creating a heartbeat each time – 120-250 bpm

blocks.alt: Circuit: down the AV node into the ventricle, back up the accessory pathway to the atrium
blocks.cap: Circuit: down the AV node into the ventricle, back up the accessory pathway to the atrium.

blocks.alt: Possible accessory pathway locations around the mitral and tricuspid annuli
blocks.cap: Possible accessory pathway locations around the mitral and tricuspid annuli.

rows: Uni-directionally blocked first beat comes down the AV node (slows conduction) and up the accessory pathway, back to the AV node
Uni-directionally blocked first beat comes down the accessory pathway and up the AV node, opposite to normal conduction
Conduction to the ventricle uses the AV node and His-Purkinje system
Conduction to the ventricle uses the accessory pathway

blocks.alt: Orthodromic AVRT
blocks.cap: Orthodromic AVRT.

blocks.alt: Orthodromic: antegrade down the AV node, retrograde up the accessory pathway
blocks.cap: Orthodromic: antegrade down the AV node, retrograde up the accessory pathway.

blocks.alt: Antidromic: antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the AV node
blocks.cap: Antidromic: antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the AV node.

blocks.html:
2) AV node re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
  • Both limbs of the circuit are within the AV node (small microcircuit)
  • One limb moves slowly down towards the ventricle; the other travels around and re-enters
  • Narrow complex regular tachycardia – common in young people
  • Responds to beta blockers, CCB, or catheter ablation of the slow pathway in the AV node
3) Ventricular tachycardia in myocardial infarction scarring
  • Limb 1: slow conduction through the scar
  • Limb 2: outside and around the scar
  • Wide complex regular tachycardia
  • Can be life-threatening with poor EF and prior MI
  • Management: medications (sotalol, amiodarone) or catheter ablation of the scar tissue

blocks.alt: Scar VT: slow conduction through the peri-infarct zone, returning around the scar
blocks.cap: Scar VT: slow conduction through the peri-infarct zone, returning around the scar.

rows: Down AV node, up accessory pathway
Down accessory pathway, up AV node
Two limbs within the AV node

blocks.html:
Triggered activity: abnormality of impulse initiation
  • Abnormal ion currents produce an abnormal AP
  • Re-depolarizations are triggered after depolarizations → repetitive firing
  • Long QT syndrome: phase 3 (K+ outflow) is prolonged, stretching out the AP
  • Extended repolarization lets Na+ and Ca2+ channels recover, allowing another inward current to start before repolarization is complete
  • Early afterdepolarizations can perpetuate → repetitive depolarizations

blocks.alt: Early afterdepolarization: recovered Na+/Ca2+ channels allow a new inward current during a prolonged phase 3
blocks.cap: Early afterdepolarization: recovered Na+/Ca2+ channels allow a new inward current during a prolonged phase 3.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Prolonged phase 3 K+ outflow
long QT"] --> B["Extended repolarization"] B --> C["Na+ and Ca2+ channels recover"] C --> D["New inward current before
repolarization completes"] D --> E["Early afterdepolarization"] E --> F["Repetitive depolarizations"] F --> G["Torsades de Pointes
polymorphic VT"] H["Bradycardia or pauses"] --> G

blocks.title: Torsades de Pointes is a medical emergency
blocks.html: Polymorphic VT with a long QT interval at baseline and bradycardia/pauses at initiation. Manage with IV Mg2+ and by speeding up the baseline heart rate (isoproterenol or external pacing) to avoid the pauses that lead to these lethal rhythms.

Module questions
  1. Where does the impulse for each heartbeat usually occur? Sinus (SA) node
  2. What structure in the atrial septum slows conduction before it enters the His-Purkinje fibres? Atrioventricular (AV) node
  3. What condition consists of lack of normal automaticity and impulse formation, leading to pauses or junctional escape rhythms? Sinus bradycardia
  4. When ventricular tissue is partly depolarized due to infarction, it can cause increased automaticity and a rhythm called? Ventricular tachycardia
  5. Name 3 tachycardias caused by re-entry: AV re-entrant tachycardia (AV node + accessory pathway); AV node re-entrant tachycardia; scar-related ventricular tachycardia
  6. What type of beat is required to initiate a re-entrant circuit? An early beat (premature atrial contraction, PAC) that blocks in one limb and conducts down the other
  7. What must differ between the two limbs to perpetuate re-entry? Conduction velocity and refractory periods
  8. In VT with a remote MI, what are the two limbs? Through the scar (slow conduction, short refractoriness) and around the scar (rapid conduction, longer refractoriness)

lectures.title: Mechanisms of Arrhythmia
lectures.framing: Every arrhythmia is a failure of one of two functions – impulse initiation or impulse conduction. Failure of either gives bradycardia; abnormal excess of either (automaticity, triggered activity, re-entry) gives tachycardia.
lectures.keypoints: Pacemaker hierarchy: sinus 40-90 → junction 35-50 → His-Purkinje 20-40 → ventricle <30 bpm. Re-entry causes tachycardia, never bradycardia, and needs two limbs with different refractoriness, slow conduction and a uni-directional block triggered by a premature beat. Orthodromic AVRT (90%) is narrow, antidromic is wide; AVNRT is narrow, scar VT is wide. Long QT → early afterdepolarizations → Torsades, treated with Mg2+ and faster heart rate.

lectures.name: Bradycardia

blocks.html: The two categorical mechanisms of bradycardia: sinus node dysfunction (a problem with the battery → not enough P waves) and AV block (a problem with the wiring → normal P waves, not enough QRS complexes).

Sinus node dysfunction = problem with the battery
  • Not enough P waves
  • Degenerative process that becomes more prevalent with aging
1) Sinus bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence
  • Inappropriate response to sympathetic drive – adrenaline, exercise
  • Symptoms: fatigue, exertional limitation

blocks.alt: Chronotropic incompetence (CI): peak heart rate with exercise is blunted compared with controls
blocks.cap: Chronotropic incompetence (CI): peak heart rate with exercise is blunted compared with controls.

blocks.html:
2) Sinus pauses, sinus arrest
  • Intermittent pauses of the SA node
  • Symptoms: presyncope, syncope
3) Conversion pauses
  • Sinus pause triggered by conversion of a tachycardia
Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome
  • Tachy = AF with rapid rates
  • Brady = sinus conversion pauses
  • Management challenges

blocks.alt: Rapid AF treated with metoprolol, then conversion to a slow sinus rhythm with long pauses
blocks.cap: Rapid AF treated with metoprolol, then conversion to a slow sinus rhythm with long pauses.

blocks.html:
Sick sinus syndrome vs asymptomatic dysfunction
  • Sick sinus syndrome (SSS) = symptomatic sinus node dysfunction → treatment is appropriate (pacemaker)
  • Asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction ≠ SSS → no indication for treatment

AV block = problem with the wiring
  • Normal P waves, not enough QRS complexes
  • Site of block: AV node or infra-nodal (His bundle, bundle branches) – lower levels of block have a worse prognosis

rows: At least 1 non-conducted P wave; more P waves than QRS

Group beating: QRS complexes appear bunched in groups
Site of block: AV node or infra-nodal; pacemaker likely indicated
Gradual PR prolongation before the block
No PR prolongation preceding the block
Every second P wave non-conducted; no consecutive PR intervals to judge whether they prolong or are fixed
No conducted P waves; more P waves than QRS

AV dissociation – QRS regular, PR variable
Regular escape rhythm: junctional (narrow QRS) or ventricular (wide QRS)
Site: AV node (> 40 bpm) or infra-nodal (< 40 bpm)
Regular QRS with fibrillatory waves at baseline (AF is normally irregularly irregular)

blocks.html:
Bundle branch blocks (BBB)
  • Warning sign of degenerative conduction disease, which may evolve into complete heart block
  • Same number of P waves and QRS complexes, because the other bundle branch still works
  • Wide QRS > 120 ms – left and right bundles depolarize consecutively instead of together

Torsades de Pointes / polymorphic VT = long QT interval
  • Usually triggered by a premature ventricular contraction landing on the T wave – “R on T phenomenon”

Bradycardia management
  • Treat for mortality (risk of sudden death): 2nd degree AV block type II, 3rd degree AV block
  • Treat for morbidity (symptomatic): sinus node dysfunction, 2nd degree AV block type I
  • No need for treatment (asymptomatic): sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, Mobitz I Wenckebach, 1st degree AV block, BBB

ECG: sharp spikes followed by a wide QRS

Module questions
  1. The 2 main categorical mechanisms of bradycardia are: sinus node dysfunction and AV block
  2. All of the following (sinus arrhythmia, sinus bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence, sinus pauses) are manifestations of sinus node dysfunction EXCEPT: sinus arrhythmia – physiologic sinus variation with respiration; normal
  3. First degree AV block is defined by: a long PR interval > 200 ms, but all P waves are conducted
  4. Types of second degree AV block include all EXCEPT: (a) intermittent non-conducted P waves preceded by prolonging PR intervals; (b) … preceded by fixed PR intervals; (c) AV dissociation – a manifestation of third degree (complete) heart block; (d) 2:1 AV block
  5. This ECG shows: sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and normal axis – QRS wide and positive in V1; QRS positive in leads I and II

lectures.title: Bradycardia
lectures.framing: Bradycardia is either a battery problem (sinus node dysfunction – too few P waves) or a wiring problem (AV block – P waves without QRS). Whether to pace depends on mortality risk and symptoms, not the heart rate alone.
lectures.keypoints: SSS = symptomatic sinus node dysfunction; asymptomatic dysfunction needs no treatment. Lower (infra-nodal) blocks carry a worse prognosis. Mobitz II and complete heart block are paced for mortality even if asymptomatic. AF with a regular QRS means complete AV block. LBBB is negative in V1, RBBB positive.

lectures.name: Syncope

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Syncope: a transient loss of consciousness (LOC) with spontaneous recovery that does not require intervention
    • Blackout, faint, spell, collapse; not the same as coma, cardiac arrest, drowsiness or generalized seizure
    • Usually due to a reduction in cerebral blood flow (hypotension)
  • Presyncope: sensation of impending loss of consciousness without progression to LOC
    • Dizzy, lightheaded; must be differentiated from vertigo
    • May be a less severe manifestation of reduced cerebral blood flow
  • Prodrome: the symptoms that precede syncope

rows: Usually structurally normal hearts, otherwise healthy; any age
Vasovagal variant with a recognized trigger – micturition, cough, pain
Baroreceptors in the carotid vasculature become stimulated
Aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumours

blocks.alt: Survival by cause of syncope: vasovagal tracks no-syncope; cardiac syncope has the worst survival
blocks.cap: Survival by cause of syncope: vasovagal tracks no-syncope; cardiac syncope has the worst survival.

blocks.html:
Taking a syncope history
  • Confirm LOC – not a fall/trip, weakness or dizziness
  • Circumstances – standing for long periods, dehydration, warm weather
  • Prodrome or sudden (vasovagal vs arrhythmic) – HR, sweating, chest pain, flushing, nausea, SOB
  • Recovery (post-drome) – heart racing, chest pain, SOB, fatigue
  • Witnesses
  • PMHx – structural heart disease
  • FHx – sudden, unexplained death
Case example

A 65-year-old woman with recurrent syncope – 6 events over 17 years. PMHx: high cholesterol, osteoarthritis. Medications: simvastatin, ibuprofen.

What does this patient need first? (a) echocardiogram, (b) ambulatory monitor, (c) tilt table test, (d) more history – ask questions that push towards or away from a neurally-mediated (benign) cause, (e) straight to pacemaker.

bloodwork, ECG, echo"] F --> G["Ambulatory monitoring
symptom-rhythm correlation"] G --> H["Provocation
tilt, stress test, EP study"] H --> I["Treat underlying cause
surgery, pacemaker, ablation, ICD"]

rows:
Common situations: post-prandial, warm day, prolonged standing; post-exertion, post-cough, post-micturition; triggered by pain, anxiety, stress, illness
Prodrome (seconds-hours before): fatigue, weakness, nausea, sweating, pallor, visual disturbance, abdominal discomfort
Post-episode: fatigue, malaise – whereas cardiac syncope with heart block may feel back to normal after the episode

Absence of QRS complexes – the heart is affected by the vasovagal reflex, it does not cause it
Parasympathetic tone hits the sinus node and AV node at the same time: sinus node → P waves slow; AV node → Wenckebach or AV block
Simultaneous sinus slowing and heart block is diagnostic of a vasovagal reflex

Vasovagal reflex ↓ systemic vascular resistance → BP falls
Pure vasodepressor – HR stays stable
Cardioinhibitory/mixed – HR also drops

Reassurance – VVS is generally benign (simply a bodily reflex)
Salt (electrolytes) and water (hydration)
Trigger avoidance

Feeling a prodrome – do NOT stand to “walk it off”; sit/lie down
Squeeze/cross the legs to increase perfusion to the brain

Beta blockers – block the SNS overdrive that leads to the reflex PNS surge
Fludrocortisone – retains salt in the kidney, ↑ BP
Midodrine – ↑ vascular resistance, ↑ BP

Generally not warranted; rare instances – refractory patients, occupations where an event is high risk
Patients often still faint: pacing addresses only the cardioinhibitory component, not the vasodepressor component
Surgical placebo is very effective at treating VVS

Routine bloodwork

Echocardiogram; cardiac MRI or CT if high suspicion – structural heart disease increases the risk of malignant arrhythmia

Patients are often seen AFTER the event – only useful if another episode occurs during monitoring
Symptom-rhythm correlation diagnoses arrhythmic causes (brady, tachy); the patient keeps a symptom diary to compare with the rhythm
Monitors: Holter (24-48 h); external loop recorder; implantable loop recorder (2-3 year battery)

Tilt test, stress test, drug infusions
Electrophysiology testing (invasive): catheters through the veins into the heart; stimulate and measure electrical activity; look for conduction disease or inducible tachycardia

Treat the underlying cardiac condition:
Structural – surgical correction of the obstruction
Bradycardia – pacemaker
Tachycardia – medications, cardiac ablation, implantable defibrillator
Fainting during exercise is NOT vasovagal – suggests cardiac causes; obstruction and arrhythmia can be provoked by exertion/↑ demand
3-year survival after the onset of symptoms
Diagnosed by echocardiogram; cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy people

FHx of sudden death can point to arrhythmia
Long QT syndrome → Torsades de Pointes – triggered by alarm clocks and swimming
Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (bidirectional) – triggered by exercise

Ask “What was the last thing you remember before fainting?”
No memory of any problem = sudden syncope
Injury with the event often means it was sudden and they could not protect themselves
Feeling unwell beforehand is not sudden syncope
Known CAD, prior MI, poor LVEF

Bradycardia risk: conduction disease – LBBB, RBBB, 1st degree AV block
Tachycardia risk: structural disease – Q waves, long QT, WPW (delta waves), Brugada syndrome

blocks.title: Exertional syncope is never vasovagal
blocks.html: Syncope during exercise points to obstruction (AS, HOCM) or arrhythmia. Vasovagal syncope may follow exertion, but is not triggered during it.

Module questions
  1. The most common cause of syncope is: reflex syncope (vasovagal, orthostatic)
  2. Common triggers of vasovagal syncope include: post-micturition, coughing, pain, post-exertion – it should not be triggered during exercise
  3. The vasovagal reflex can result in: (a) sudden ↓ SVR (drop in BP); (b) sudden ↓ sinus rate; (c) sudden ↓ AV conduction (heart block); (d) all of the above
  4. Common treatments for vasovagal syncope include all EXCEPT: (a) education and reassurance; (b) ↑ salt and water; (c) avoid triggers; (d) pacemaker implantation – can be considered for resistant severe cases, but not a common treatment
  5. For high-risk features on history (sudden or exertional syncope), helpful cardiac investigations include: exercise stress test, echocardiogram, ambulatory monitor

lectures.title: Syncope
lectures.framing: Syncope is transient LOC from reduced cerebral blood flow. Most is benign reflex (vasovagal) syncope; the job is to find the minority with cardiac syncope, which carries the worst prognosis, and the history does most of that sorting.
lectures.keypoints: Reflex syncope is 75%; cardiac syncope (15%) has the worst survival. Simultaneous sinus slowing + AV block is diagnostic of vasovagal reflex. VVS treatment is reassurance, salt and water, trigger avoidance, counter-pressure; pacemakers rarely help because they miss the vasodepressor component. Red flags: exertional or sudden syncope, structural disease, abnormal ECG, FHx of sudden death.

Recurrent symptoms but NO sudden death; excellent prognosis
Can cause hemodynamic collapse and sudden death if untreated

Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)

SVTs are classified by whether the arrhythmia needs the AV node – which is what blocking the AV node (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) reveals.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
  • Conduction occurs over both the AV node and an accessory AV pathway
  • Fused QRS complex with a preceding delta wave

Accessory pathways and their ECGs

  • B: SVT with bundle branch block → wide QRS tachycardia
  • C: down the accessory pathway, up the normal pathway → wide QRS tachycardia
  • D: conduction down the normal pathway + accessory pathway (AF) → irregularly irregular

blocks.html:
Ventricular tachycardia (VT)
Monomorphic VT – QRS complexes all look identical
  • Associated with organic heart disease – CAD, cardiomyopathy
  • Idiopathic VT – structurally normal heart; primary electrical problem

blocks.html:
Polymorphic VT – QRS complexes change beat-to-beat in a single lead
  • Repolarization (QT) syndromes
  • With ischemia, cardiomyopathy, “genetic” heart disease
  • Generally presents with syncope and cardiac arrest, NOT palpitations
  • Prolonged QT Torsades de Pointes can lead to polymorphic VT

Ventricular fibrillation
  • Rapid, disorganized rhythm that can lead to cardiac arrest

blocks.html:
Prognosis with VT
  • Depends mainly on ventricular function – good LV = good prognosis
  • Extent and degree of coronary stenosis is a major factor – treatable (statins, risk reduction) vs fixable (revascularization)
  • Sudden death can occur with QT syndromes despite a good LV

  • Sudden severe light-headedness that settled, but his heart was racing, so his wife drove him to the ER
  • BP 90/60, HR 160 bpm, a little tachypneic
  • ECG: rate 150 bpm, wide QRS complexes → wide complex tachycardia / VT
  • Give adenosine or cardiovert right away

• a) The ECG shows SVT – narrow complex tachycardia
  • b) IV adenosine is appropriate – will likely make it stop
  • c) The patient is at risk for stroke or cardiac arrest – FALSE: benign condition
  • d) Catheter ablation is a reasonable long-term option – based on the frequency of the spells

21. A 74-year-old patient arrives in the ED and this ECG is recorded. Which statements are true?

blocks.alt: Question 21: wide complex tachycardia – VT

• a) The ECG shows wide complex tachycardia – true
  • b) The best treatment is cardioversion – true; works for both VT and aberrant conduction (RBBB)
  • c) Adenosine will stop this arrhythmia – false; VT does not stop with adenosine
  • d) This looks like SVT with RBBB – false
  • e) This looks like VT – true; QRS axis is very abnormal and V5-V6 have Q waves (unusual for standard RBBB)

22. A 55-year-old man arrives in the ED with chest pain and a rhythm strip is recorded. It shows: polymorphic VT – asterisks show PVCs; during the rapid arrhythmia each QRS is wide compared with sinus rhythm (not SVT or AF) and each QRS looks different (not monomorphic VT).

23. Following the rhythm strip, this 12-lead ECG is recorded. The cause of the arrhythmia is:

blocks.alt: Question 23: ST elevation in the inferior and lateral leads
blocks.cap: Question 23: ST elevation in the inferior and lateral leads.

blocks.html:
• a) Idiopathic – primary electrical problem with a structurally normal heart
  • b) Unsuspected cardiomyopathy
  • c) Acute ischemia – ST elevation in inferior and lateral leads (inferolateral STEMI); most common cause of polymorphic VT; treat the arrhythmia with STEMI treatment (IV amiodarone in the ED, transfer to the cath lab for primary PCI to the RCA)
  • d) Long QT syndrome
  • e) A genetic defect

lectures.title: Tachycardia: SVT and VT
lectures.framing: Tachycardia sorts first by QRS width: narrow = supraventricular (benign, no sudden death), wide = VT until proven otherwise (can cause collapse and sudden death). For SVT, the next question is whether it depends on the AV node.
lectures.keypoints: SVT has an excellent prognosis; VT can kill. AV node–dependent SVTs (AVNRT, AVRT) terminate with AV block; atrial tachycardia, flutter and AF continue. WPW = delta wave + fused QRS. For an uncertain wide complex tachycardia, adenosine then cardioversion – cardioversion is always appropriate if unstable or uncertain. Polymorphic VT presents with syncope/arrest, and acute ischemia is its most common cause. VT prognosis tracks LV function.

lectures.name: Atrial Fibrillation

blocks.html:
ECG manifestations
  • Multiple re-entrant circuits meander through the atria – multiple waves in the atrium
  • Fibrillatory waves – disorganized, continuous; can be very small
  • Irregular RR intervals – irregularly irregular ventricular rate
Etiology
  • Age-dependent: risk rises after 50; 10% of those 80+ have AF
  • Cardiac: hypertension, ischemic heart disease, valvular disease (MS, MR, AS), sick sinus syndrome, cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic)
  • Non-cardiac: alcohol, metabolic (thyroid disease), pulmonary (COPD, pneumonia, sleep apnea)
  • Reversing the underlying disease can make AF easier to treat

rows:
Highly symptomatic self-terminating episodes, minutes to hours
Patients are well when back in sinus rhythm
Does not stop spontaneously – antiarrhythmic agents or DC cardioversion required

In AF all the time – agents slow the ventricular rate and control symptoms
No attempt is made to restore sinus rhythm

blocks.html: AF causes harm through three consequences, and each has its own therapy: thromboembolism → anticoagulation; rapid irregular ventricular rate → rate control; loss of atrial kick → rhythm control.

flowchart TD A["Atrial fibrillation
chaotic atrial activation"] --> B["1 Stasis of blood
+ LA enlargement"] A --> C["2 Rapid irregular
ventricular rate 130-170"] A --> D["3 Loss of atrial kick"] B --> E["Clot → stroke, embolism"] E --> F["Anticoagulation
by CHADS2"] C --> G["Palpitations, dyspnea,
chest discomfort"] G --> H["Rate control
beta blocker, CCB, digoxin"] D --> I["↓ LV filling and CO
breathlessness, fatigue"] I --> J["Rhythm control
antiarrhythmics, DC cardioversion"]

blocks.html:
1) Thromboembolic events
  • Rapid, chaotic atrial activation → disorganized mechanical function and stasis of blood
  • Causes of AF also cause LA enlargement, adding to stasis
  • Once formed, clots can embolize → stroke and other thromboembolic events
  • Mitral stenosis is also a very high risk factor for stroke
  • Stroke prophylaxis (any 1 risk factor): anticoagulation (warfarin) or antiplatelet therapy (ASA)

blocks.alt: Annual stroke risk (%) rises with CHADS2 score: 1.9% at 0, 4.0% at 2, 18.2% at 6
blocks.cap: Annual stroke risk (%) rises with CHADS2 score: 1.9% at 0, 4.0% at 2, 18.2% at 6.

blocks.alt: Where anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, fondaparinux, dabigatran) and antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) act
blocks.cap: Where anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, fondaparinux, dabigatran) and antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) act.

blocks.html:
2) Rapid irregular ventricular rate
  • The AV node allows rapid ventricular activation: 130-170 bpm
  • Symptoms: palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort
  • Tx: rate control with AV nodal blocking drugs – beta blockers, CCB, digoxin
  • AF can also give a normal rate or bradycardia; rate slowing may or may not be needed depending on AV node function
3) Loss of atrial-ventricular synchrony
  • Loss of atrial mechanical function removes the atrial contribution to ventricular filling – the atrial kick
  • In some heart diseases this ↓ LV filling and cardiac output → breathlessness, exertional dyspnea, fatigue
  • Tx: rhythm control
    • Class I (Na+ channel blockade): flecainide, propafenone
    • Class III (K+ channel blockade): sotalol, amiodarone, dronedarone
    • DC cardioversion: synchronized electrical shock to return AF to sinus – patient anaesthetized (propofol), paddles anterior and posterior, 50-200 J, patient wakes in sinus rhythm

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Rhythm control planned"] --> B{"AF duration?"} B -->|"Under 48 hours"| C["OK without anticoagulation"] B -->|"Over 48 hours or unknown"| D["Rate control +
3 weeks anticoagulation"] C --> E["DC cardioversion
propofol, 50-200 J synchronized"] D --> E E --> F["Sinus rhythm"]

blocks.title: AF > 48 hours or of unknown duration
blocks.html: Rate-control and give 3 weeks of anticoagulation before cardioversion – thrombus may already have formed. AF < 48 hours without anticoagulation is okay to cardiovert.

Case example
  • A 42-year-old man in the ER with rapid palpitations and dyspnea for 12 hours
  • Hypertension for years, on enalapril
  • ECG: rapid AF (140-160 bpm); BP 110/85

Management

  • Rate control: acutely IV metoprolol or diltiazem; oral metoprolol or diltiazem on discharge
  • Antithrombotic Rx: has hypertension, CHADS = 1 → needs oral anticoagulation: apixaban 5 mg bid
  • Rhythm control (only 12 hours, young, symptomatic): judgement call

Module questions: atrial fibrillation
  1. All of the following are ECG manifestations of AF EXCEPT: (a) rapid irregular QRS; (b) fibrillatory waves; (c) rapid regular atrial activity – atrial flutter; (d) irregular QRS at 80-90 bpm; (e) rapid irregular atrial activity
  2. Common causes of AF include: hypertension, CHF due to prior MI, MR due to mitral valve prolapse, pericarditis, aging – almost any cardiac condition and some non-cardiac conditions can contribute
  3. CHADS2 score of a 72-year-old man with AF, hypertension, diabetes, no MI or other heart disease – does he need anticoagulation? CHADS2 = 2 (hypertension, diabetes); he needs anticoagulation – any patient with CHADS2 > 1 should be anticoagulated unless there is a strong contraindication
  4. The same man presents in AF at 125-135 bpm, anxious, palpitations, mild dizziness, BP 100/65; onset unknown; no medication. Reasonable EXCEPT: (a) IV metoprolol; (b) IV diltiazem; (c) oral metoprolol; (d) cardioversion – thrombus can form in the LA (especially the LA appendage) as early as 48 hours after AF onset; unless there is a clear, believable onset < 48 hours or the patient is already therapeutically anticoagulated, cardioversion raises the risk of thrombus dislodgement and stroke (if already anticoagulated, thrombus risk is low and cardioversion is reasonable)

lectures.title: Atrial Fibrillation
lectures.framing: AF is chaotic re-entry in the atria producing an irregularly irregular rhythm. It harms in three ways – stroke, rapid rate, lost atrial kick – and management matches each: anticoagulate, rate-control, rhythm-control.
lectures.keypoints: Irregularly irregular with fibrillatory waves. 10% of over-80s have AF. CHADS2: CHF, HTN, age > 65, diabetes (1 each), stroke/TIA (2); mitral stenosis is also very high risk. Rate control = beta blocker, CCB, digoxin; rhythm control = class I/III drugs or DC cardioversion. > 48 h or unknown → 3 weeks anticoagulation before cardioversion.

lectures.name: Antiarrhythmic Therapies

blocks.alt: Vaughan Williams classes mapped to the action potential: class 1 phase 0 (Na+), class 2 phase 4 (β), class 3 phase 3 (K+), class 4 phase 2 (Ca2+)
blocks.cap: Vaughan Williams classes mapped to the action potential: class 1 phase 0 (Na+), class 2 phase 4 (β), class 3 phase 3 (K+), class 4 phase 2 (Ca2+).

blocks.html:
Drug effects on the ECG
  • Changing the slope of phase 0 → widening of the QRS
  • Prolonging the plateau phase → prolonged QT
Basic principles of therapy

1) Identify and treat precipitating factors

  • Electrolyte abnormalities – low K+, Mg2+, PO4 3–
  • Myocardial ischemia
  • Hypoxemia
  • Catecholamines – endogenous (anxiety, pain, fever), exogenous (epinephrine, dopamine)
  • Other modifiable risk factors – weight reduction, alcohol, smoking cessation
  • Medications – drugs may prolong QT; antiarrhythmics may be proarrhythmic

2) Decide on your goal

  • Not all arrhythmias need treatment – sinus tachycardia (treat the underlying cause)
  • AF – rate control vs restoring sinus rhythm; thrombosis prophylaxis if indicated

3) Minimize risk

  • Drug-drug interactions
  • Renal dysfunction – many drugs are renally excreted; know renal function and the drug's pharmacology to avoid side effects or toxicity
  • Non-pharmacologic therapy may be most appropriate – pacemaker, implantable cardiac defibrillator

Proarrhythmia

Proarrhythmia: the ability of drugs (including antiarrhythmics) to cause arrhythmias.

  • Digoxin – toxicity may cause virtually any arrhythmia, including triggered activity
  • QT-prolonging drugs – Torsades de Pointes
  • Drug-induced bradyarrhythmia – beta blockers, CCB

• Many drugs act in multiple classes – sotalol is a beta blocker (II) with K+ channel blockade (III); amiodarone is class III but has class I, II, III and IV effects

  • Some drugs fit no class – atropine (bradycardia), digoxin (slows rate in AF), adenosine (AV nodal blocker)

Indirect vagal effect ↓ intrinsic SA node rate
Prolongs AV conduction – rapid but very short response

Rate control in AF, but: will not convert AF to sinus; poor rate control for recurrent AF; vagal effect is overcome by sympathetic outflow (ICU patients, exercise)
Possibly useful in sedentary patients

Terminates a re-entrant arrhythmia (AVNRT) or diagnoses an SVT / regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia
AV re-entry → converts to sinus
AF or sinus tachycardia → slows the rate

Try a vagal maneuver first
IV bolus, very quickly, with monitor and continuous ECG
If the first dose fails, repeat at double dose
Toxicity may cause virtually any arrhythmia

Bronchospasm in asthma/COPD
Flushing and possible chest pain – warn the patient

blocks.html:
Case example 1

A middle-aged man comes to the ED from home with heartburn, diaphoretic.

  • Vitals: HR 78, BP 167/98, afebrile, O2 sat 99% on nasal prongs
  • Suddenly moans and falls back; no response when shaken
Is this patient…
  • Stable? → drugs
  • Unstable? → electricity (cardioversion/defibrillation)
  • Dead? → CPR + electricity + drugs

What is the rhythm on the monitor? Wide complex tachycardia.

blocks.html:
• On the second shock (200 J): reversion to sinus rhythm; intubated, oxygenation stable
  • BP 96/68, cold and clammy, but opens eyes, squeezes hands and wiggles toes to command
  • Next step: antiplatelet agent and emergent PCI might be most reasonable; if PCI is not available, thrombolysis is reasonable

blocks.alt: Cardiac arrest algorithm: continuous CPR, rhythm check every 2 minutes, shock VF/pVT, epinephrine every 3-5 min, amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VF/pVT, treat reversible causes (Hs and Ts)
blocks.cap: Cardiac arrest algorithm: continuous CPR, rhythm check every 2 minutes, shock VF/pVT, epinephrine every 3-5 min, amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VF/pVT, treat reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

Case example 2

A patient awaiting liver transplant assessment had a transvenous liver biopsy yesterday; vitals have suddenly changed:

  • HR 178 bpm, BP 86/56, breathing comfortably on nasal prongs with good O2 saturation, afebrile
  • Blood glucose normal
Is this patient…
  • Stable? → drugs
  • Unstable? → electricity (cardioversion/defibrillation)
  • Dead? → CPR + electricity + drugs
  • Adenosine to help diagnose and convert to sinus rhythm

blocks.alt: Case 2 rhythm
blocks.cap: Case 2 rhythm.

Case example 3

Internal Medicine call for a rapid heart rate: a 76-year-old man, HR 146 irregularly irregular, BP 148/72, just after open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) of a hip fracture under general anesthetic.

  • PMHx: chronic AF (5+ years), prior NSTEMI, hypertension; no heart failure
  • Medications: metoprolol, ASA, ACEI, statin, DOAC – may have missed some doses over the last day
  • Vitals: HR 145, BP 140/78, nasal prongs at 2 L/min (not much oxygen), afebrile
  • No chest pain or SOB; wonders what the ‘fuss is about’

Stable, chronic AF at a fairly fast rate – consider slowing it. Options:

rows: Slows pre-existing AF, then wears off
Slows rate, but needs a loading dose – not the best choice
Already takes it chronically and tolerates it

blocks.html:
Case example 4

Code Blue: a patient has collapsed. What is the most immediate therapy? Dead → CPR + electricity + drugs.

  • Rhythm on the monitor: wide complex polymorphic tachycardia – Torsades de Pointes
  • Back in sinus rhythm; chart review: K+ 3.2 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.5)
  • Medications: methadone (chronic opioid), haloperidol (antipsychotic started 2 days ago for delirium), levofloxacin (antibiotic started yesterday)
  • Electrolyte abnormality + QT-prolonging drugs → long QT → Torsades
After ROSC
  • Check the baseline ECG after return of spontaneous circulation and identify the QT
  • Consider Mg2+
  • Correct K+ (slowly!)
  • Stop medications that may prolong QT – exception: methadone (withdrawal symptoms)
  • Increase baseline HR – as HR increases, QT decreases

methadone, haloperidol, levofloxacin"] --> D D --> E["Torsades de Pointes"] E --> F["Arrest: CPR + defibrillation"] F --> G["ROSC: check baseline QT"] G --> H["Mg2+, correct K+ slowly"] G --> I["Stop QT drugs
except methadone"] G --> J["Increase baseline HR
to shorten QT"]

blocks.html:
Module questions: antiarrhythmics and emergencies
  1. Which of lidocaine, verapamil, digoxin, metoprolol would NOT slow the ventricular rate in AF? Lidocaine – acts only on ventricular myocytes; not effective for supraventricular arrhythmias

Amitriptyline overdose. Amitriptyline (Elavil®) is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) with a very large volume of distribution (Vd): drug levels do not reflect toxicity and it cannot be dialyzed out. TCA toxicity causes:

  • Na+ channel blockade
  • Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) effects
  • Alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade
  • GABA receptor antagonism in the brain → seizures
32. Palpitations and chest pain; bicuspid aortic valve with asymptomatic moderate AS; no prior AF. BP 80/60, ↓ level of consciousness. Most immediate therapy?

blocks.alt: Question 32: narrow complex, irregularly irregular tachycardia – AF with fast ventricular response
blocks.cap: Question 32: narrow complex, irregularly irregular tachycardia – AF with fast ventricular response.

blocks.html:
• Cardioversion (electricity) – unstable (low BP, chest pain, ↓ LOC); strip shows a narrow complex irregularly irregular tachycardia (most likely AF with fast ventricular response)
  • AS means AF is poorly tolerated – loss of atrial ‘kick’ with a hypertrophied ventricle
  • Beta blockers and CCBs may lower BP further and do not work quickly

33. An 18-year-old with an actively bleeding stab wound to the left groin: HR 148, BP 78/56, RR 28, cold and clammy, ↓ capillary refill. Rhythm most likely: sinus tachycardia – P waves before each beat, regular; aberrancy would widen the QRS.

34. Therapy: fluids and blood products with direct pressure to the wound – the sinus tachycardia is compensation for hypovolemia; treat the cause – drugs that slow the rate would worsen hypotension.

35. A continuous 30+ second rhythm strip; at about 15:21:34 an IV drug is given. Most likely drug?

blocks.alt: Question 35: narrow complex tachycardia ~170-180, a transient slow rate, then sinus rhythm – adenosine
blocks.cap: Question 35: narrow complex tachycardia ~170-180, a transient slow rate, then sinus rhythm – adenosine.

blocks.html:
• IV adenosine – narrow complex tachycardia at ~170-180, followed by a slow rate, then conversion to sinus rhythm

36. Consult-liaison psychiatry (delirium develops in 70-80% of ICU patients): the patient would benefit from haloperidol (QT-prolonging). Baseline ECG QT = 0.6 seconds – prolonged (> 0.4-0.48 s). Do not give a QT-prolonging drug (risk of Torsades); ensure electrolytes are normal and no other QT-prolonging drugs are prescribed.

37. Post-op hip replacement under spinal anesthetic; dizzy; BP 85/56; bradycardic rhythm. Appropriate therapy: IV atropine, possibly followed by transcutaneous pacing (pacing shocks through pads at a regular rate – like an implanted pacemaker but needs higher energy to capture). Find the cause: rule out a high spinal block affecting the cardiac sympathetic innervation (from the high thoracic cord); if so, management is supportive until the block wears off, including ventilatory support if respiratory muscles are affected.

38. Match the rhythm strip or ECG to the diagnosis (strips not reproduced): premature atrial contraction; first degree AV block; second degree AV block; third degree AV block (complete heart block); ventricular fibrillation; atrial flutter; premature ventricular contractions.

lectures.title: Antiarrhythmic Pharmacology
lectures.framing: Antiarrhythmics act on specific phases of the action potential (Vaughan Williams classes I-IV), and every one can also cause arrhythmias. Therapy starts with precipitating factors and a clear goal, not with the drug.
lectures.keypoints: Class I = Na+ (phase 0, widens QRS); II = beta blockers (phase 4); III = K+ (phase 3, prolongs QT); IV = Ca2+ (phase 2, AV node). CCBs are not for ventricular arrhythmias and are avoided in HF. Amiodarone: long half-life, lung, thyroid, cornea, skin toxicity, little proarrhythmia. Digoxin does not convert AF and fails with high sympathetic tone. Adenosine terminates AVNRT, slows AF/sinus tachycardia, can cause bronchospasm. In emergencies: stable → drugs, unstable → electricity, dead → CPR + electricity + drugs. Torsades: Mg2+, correct K+ slowly, stop QT drugs, raise HR. Lidocaine does not slow AF; TCA overdose widens the QRS.

lectures.name: In Class - ECG Review

blocks.html:
Meet the patient: palpitations

A 65-year-old woman with a week of “palpitations” – skipped, irregular heartbeats. No chest pain, SOB or syncope. Personal stress (caring for her husband after his stroke); attributes symptoms to stress. Recently diagnosed hypertension; diet-controlled diabetes.

Appropriate next step? (e) All of the above – all are reasonable starting points:

  • a) Physical exam – pulse regularity, vitals, clues of structural heart disease
  • b) Bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, TSH) – palpitations can signal common systemic disease such as anemia or thyroid disease
  • c) ECG – shows rhythm or clues to structural heart disease
  • d) Holter monitor – captures the rhythm during symptoms
Based on the ECG, what is the diagnosis?

blocks.alt: Narrow complex, irregularly irregular rhythm – atrial fibrillation
blocks.cap: Narrow complex, irregularly irregular rhythm – atrial fibrillation.

rows: Flutter or “F waves” in the inferior leads

blocks.html:
Findings
  • AF at 110 bpm in the office; otherwise unremarkable exam – no murmurs, no elevated JVP
  • BP 130/80; currently well and asymptomatic, but concerned by the new diagnosis
  • Echocardiogram: no structural disease
What are the next appropriate steps?

(a) anticoagulate; (b) beta blocker for rate control; (c) antiarrhythmic medication; (d) elective electrical cardioversion; (e) A and B.

For THIS patient: anticoagulation + beta blocker for rate control. All answers can be acceptable in certain situations. The question highlights the two key AF principles: (1) the need for anticoagulation and (2) rate vs rhythm control.

  • Stroke risk uses the CHADS2 score: hers is 2 (age and hypertension) → annual stroke risk 4%
  • Stable, new AF → no need for emergency cardioversion or an urgent antiarrhythmic
  • Rate control with a beta blocker or CCB is a good first step – it controls the ventricular rate during exercise
  • Duration unknown and could be > 48 hours → high thrombus risk → anticoagulate

blocks.title: Cardioversion in AF of unknown duration
blocks.html: If AF has lasted, or may have lasted, > 48 hours and the patient is not appropriately anticoagulated, cardiovert only for hemodynamic instability or once an intracardiac thrombus is excluded by imaging (transesophageal echocardiogram).

lectures.title: ECG Review: New Atrial Fibrillation
lectures.framing: A case of palpitations in a 65-year-old woman worked from ECG to management. The ECG settles the diagnosis (AF: narrow, irregularly irregular); management then rests on two principles – anticoagulation and rate vs rhythm control.
lectures.keypoints: Palpitations workup: exam, CBC/electrolytes/TSH, ECG, Holter – all reasonable. Narrow + irregularly irregular = AF; narrow + regular = SVT; F waves in inferior leads = flutter; wide + regular = VT. Stable new AF → anticoagulate (CHADS2 2 = 4%/yr) + rate control. No cardioversion if > 48 h/unknown and not anticoagulated, unless unstable or TEE excludes thrombus.
